questions.questionText: What does LLD stand for, and what is its primary focus?
questions.explanation: LLD (Low Level Design) focuses on how code is written within each infrastructure component — maintainability, extensibility, encapsulation. It is not about network infrastructure (that is HLD) nor about database schema design in isolation.

options.optionText: Large Level Design — designing the overall system architecture
Low Level Design — designing how the actual code is written well
Low Level Design — designing the network infrastructure
Logical Level Design — designing database schemas

questions.questionText: Which of the following best describes High Level Design (HLD)?
questions.explanation: HLD is a bird's-eye view: load balancers, app servers, databases, queues, how they interact. LLD (code structure inside components) is separate.

options.optionText: Writing clean, maintainable code inside individual components
Defining what components exist in a system and how they connect
Designing the internal logic of a single class
Writing unit tests for backend services

questions.questionText: In a horizontally scaled system, what is the primary role of a Load Balancer?
questions.explanation: The load balancer sits between users and application servers, routing each request to an available server using algorithms like round-robin or least-connections. It is not responsible for session storage (that is the database layer) or encryption (a separate concern) or vertical scaling.

options.optionText: To store user session data across multiple servers
To upgrade the existing server to a more powerful machine
To decide which server handles each incoming request
To encrypt all incoming user requests before processing

questions.questionText: Which of the following is the core problem with Procedural Programming as the codebase scales?
questions.explanation: In Procedural style, data is passive and behaviour is active. This creates a debugging nightmare at scale: if a field is wrong, you must search every function everywhere that touches it. OOP solves this by centralising behaviour (methods) with data (state) inside the entity.

options.optionText: Procedures cannot call other procedures
Entities are passive — any procedure can read or modify any entity's data freely
Procedural code does not support functions
Procedural code cannot work with databases

questions.questionText: In Object-Oriented Programming, what does an Entity own?
questions.explanation: OOP bundles data and behaviour together. An entity owns both; it is the unit of cohesion and control. This ownership is what enables invariant enforcement at the point where the data lives.

options.optionText: Only its attributes (data)
Only the functions that act on it
Both its data (what it IS) and its behaviour (what it DOES)
References to all other entities in the system

questions.questionText: Which of the following code snippets represents the OOP style of thinking?
questions.explanation: driver.acceptRide(trip) makes the subject (driver) the active agent performing the action. This is entity-first thinking. The alternatives are procedural — the action comes from outside the entity, not from the entity itself.

options.optionText: printStudent(student)
processPayment(trip, driver, rider)
driver.acceptRide(trip)
calculateFare(source, destination, vehicle)

questions.questionText: In a Java Trip class representing a ride-sharing trip, which approach best ensures encapsulation and guards against accidental state corruption?
questions.explanation: Option A (public state) is the Procedural trap in Java syntax: anyone anywhere in the codebase can corrupt Trip.status. Option B enforces that all state transitions go through the class's logic, protecting invariants. This is especially critical in a distributed system where multiple servers might try to update the same trip — the Trip object must be the single arbiter of valid transitions.

options.optionText: Option A is better because it allows flexibility and direct access
Option B is better because it centralises validation and enforces invariants at the single source of truth
Both are equivalent for a small team
Option A is better for performance; Option B is better for safety only

questions.questionText: You need to extend the Trip entity to handle two trip types: LocalTrip (within a city) and OutstationTrip (across cities). Both share common state (passenger, driver, status, fare) but differ in pricing logic and cancellation policies. Which approach better reflects LLD principles?
questions.explanation: Option B avoids the "Anemic Domain Model" trap (procedural code in OOP syntax). Each entity owns its behaviour. As you add PetDeliveryTrip, MedicineTrip, etc., you extend the hierarchy instead of adding more conditionals to a monolithic class. This is extensibility — a core LLD goal — in practice.

options.optionText: Create a single Trip class and add conditional logic: if (tripType == "outstation") { pricing logic A } else { pricing logic B }
Create LocalTrip and OutstationTrip as separate classes inheriting from a Trip base class, each overriding pricing and cancellation rules

Option B (inheritance) is better because it separates concerns and allows each trip type to encapsulate its own rules; Option A (conditional) couples different types and makes the class fragile to new trip types
Both are equivalent; pick based on team preference

questions.questionText: A ride-sharing application runs across 15 backend servers, all behind a load balancer. If an individual server tries to store user session state (e.g., "Driver 123 is currently logged in") in that server's memory:
questions.explanation: Horizontal scaling requires stateless servers — each server must be interchangeable. Any server must handle any request for any user. This constraint directly impacts LLD: you cannot have objects hoarding per-user data across request boundaries; that data must live in the Trip entity, User entity, etc., persisted in the database, not on the server.

options.optionText: It is efficient and reduces database load, so it is fine
It works as long as all requests from the same driver are routed to the same server (session affinity)

It will fail when a second request from the driver lands on a different server, because that server has no knowledge of the session; the only robust solution is to externalise session state to a shared database or cache layer
It is a problem only if the number of servers exceeds 10

questions.questionText: You have designed a Trip entity and want to prevent subclasses from breaking its invariant-protection contract. Which statement is most accurate about using the final keyword?
questions.explanation: LLD is about intentionality. Marking Trip as final says "this entity's contract is non-negotiable; subclassing is not the extension path." Marking tripId as final says "identity does not change." This protects invariants. It is not paranoia; it is documenting design intent to the next engineer who reads the code.

options.optionText: Using final everywhere is always good practice; it guarantees the class is immutable
Using final on the class prevents extension, which restricts flexibility

Using final on the class prevents careless subclassing that might violate Trip's business rules (like invalid status transitions); using final on certain fields (like tripId) prevents accidental reassignment; this is a deliberate LLD design decision
final is a performance optimisation with no semantic value for design

questions.questionText:
Consider the following two systems:
System A: A real-time trading engine processing millions of transactions per second, written in C, where every microsecond of latency matters and a team of 5 engineers maintains it full-time.
System B: An e-commerce platform with 200+ engineers, frequent feature additions, complex business logic, and new payment/shipping integrations every quarter.
Which paradigm is most appropriate for each, and why?
questions.explanation: Paradigm choice is a constraint-driven engineering decision, not a philosophical preference. C's performance characteristics — no GC pauses, predictable memory layout, zero-cost abstractions, direct hardware access — matter when microseconds are the competitive unit. For System B, the engineering constraint is 200 engineers shipping concurrent features without stepping on each other's code; OOP's boundaries and method contracts provide exactly that structure.

options.optionText: System A → OOP, because it has a small team; System B → Procedural, because it has more engineers

System A → Procedural, because performance is the critical constraint and the team is small enough to manage it; System B → OOP, because maintainability, extensibility, and team collaboration are the critical constraints
Both systems should use OOP because OOP is always better than procedural
Both systems should use procedural because it performs better in all cases

questions.questionText: A junior engineer argues: "OOP and Procedural are basically the same thing — in both, you have data and functions. OOP just puts them together in a class. It is just a syntactic difference." Which response most accurately addresses this argument?
questions.explanation: In Procedural, the procedure is the primary cognitive unit — you think "what do I do to this data?" In OOP, the entity is the primary cognitive unit — you think "what is this entity responsible for?" In Procedural, cancelTrip(trip) is a free-floating concern that any module can invoke or duplicate. In OOP, trip.cancelTrip() is the Trip entity's declared responsibility — one canonical location, one authority over that state transition.

options.optionText: The junior engineer is correct — OOP and Procedural are functionally identical, just with different syntax
The junior engineer is wrong — OOP does not use functions at all, whereas Procedural does

The junior engineer is partially right about grouping, but misses the fundamental shift: in Procedural, procedures are the core active concept and entities are passive data; in OOP, entities become the core active concept, owning both their data and their behaviour, and controlling what can be done to them — this is a philosophical shift in how you structure and reason about an entire system
The junior engineer is wrong — OOP is only about inheritance and polymorphism, not about grouping data and functions

questions.questionText: A Spring backend for a payment platform has a Payment class with private fields and only public getters and setters, and a PaymentService class containing validatePayment(Payment p), applyDiscount(Payment p, Discount d), and markComplete(Payment p, String newStatus). A senior engineer in code review comments: "This is procedural code dressed in Java syntax." Which analysis is most accurate?
questions.explanation: This is the Anemic Domain Model anti-pattern. A class with only getters/setters and no behaviour is functionally identical to a C struct — it is passive data that external procedures manipulate. Real OOP dictates that entities govern their own state transitions (e.g. payment.markComplete()), while service classes coordinate workflows across entities.

options.optionText: The engineer is wrong — using classes with private fields and a separate service class qualifies as OOP by definition

The engineer is correct — Payment has no behaviour; all business logic lives in PaymentService, making Payment an anemic data container that external functions operate on, recreating the exact Procedural problem OOP was designed to solve
The engineer is partially right — the fix is to merge PaymentService into Payment as static methods
The engineer is wrong — Spring service classes are a standard architectural pattern and are not procedural by nature

questions.questionText: What does the following code print?
questions.explanation: d2 = d1 copies the reference (heap address), not the object. Both variables point at the same Driver. Writing d2.name modifies that shared object, so d1.name returns "Suresh".

options.optionText: Rahul
Suresh
null
A NullPointerException is thrown

questions.questionText: After calling `new Driver("Rahul", 4.8)` with the constructor below, what is the value of the driver's `name` field?
questions.explanation: name = name reassigns the local parameter to itself — a legal no-op. The instance field this.name is never touched and stays null. The fix is this.name = name.

options.optionText: "Rahul" — assigned correctly
A compile error — name appears twice
null — the parameter assigned to itself, field untouched
"Rahul" — Java auto-infers this.name when names match

questions.questionText: A `Driver` class needs a counter that tracks how many `Driver` objects have ever been created across the entire application. A developer writes this code. What is wrong with this design?
questions.explanation: An instance field belongs to each individual object. If five Driver objects are created, there are five separate `totalDrivers` fields, each holding the value 1 (or whatever the constructor set). No single number reflects the total. The fix is `static int totalDrivers = 0` — a static field belongs to the class itself and is shared by every instance, so incrementing it in any constructor accumulates the true total.

options.optionText: Nothing — `totalDrivers` will correctly track the total across all Driver objects
Every Driver object gets its own copy of `totalDrivers`, each starting at 0; the field tracks nothing meaningful at the application level
The field will cause a compile error because counters must be declared `final`
The field is private and cannot be incremented from the constructor

questions.questionText: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between a class and an object in Java?
questions.explanation: The class definition (bytecode) is the template. Each new call allocates a separate heap block for one object with its own copy of every instance field. Class and objects are independent.

options.optionText: A class holds all its objects — deleting the class deletes the objects
A class is a blueprint with minimal memory; each object is a separate heap allocation created by new
A class and an object are the same thing; "object" is just informal for a class at runtime
An object is stored on the stack and the class is stored on the heap

questions.questionText: A Driver class has `public double rating`. Which statement is most accurate?
questions.explanation: Convention-based protection fails at scale. Any code with a Driver reference can write any value to a public field. Private + setRating() means the compiler rejects direct writes and the method is the single enforcement point.

options.optionText: Acceptable — developers will know not to set invalid values
Should be protected to prevent subclass corruption
Any code anywhere can write driver.rating = 10.0; making it private with a validated setRating() is the only design that enforces the rule
Fine to keep public; a validateRating() method called by callers is sufficient

questions.questionText: Which access modifier restricts a field so that only the class that declares it can read or write it?
questions.explanation: private limits access to the declaring class only. protected allows same-package + subclasses. Package-private allows the same package. public allows everywhere.

options.optionText: private
protected
public
package-private (no modifier)

questions.questionText: A developer lists "four pillars of OOP: Abstraction, Encapsulation, Inheritance, Polymorphism." A senior engineer says the framing is imprecise. Which response is most accurate?
questions.explanation: Abstraction is the destination (represent a system as bounded ideas). The three pillars are mechanisms to get there. Treating all four as equal obscures the hierarchy.

options.optionText: The developer is correct — all four are independent equal pillars
Abstraction is not part of OOP; it belongs to functional programming
Abstraction is the overarching principle OOP exists to implement; Encapsulation, Inheritance, and Polymorphism are the three mechanisms that achieve it
Abstraction and Encapsulation are synonyms; the real pillars are only Inheritance and Polymorphism

questions.questionText: A `Driver` object is created with `Driver d = new Driver()` using only the no-argument constructor (which has an empty body). The code then calls `System.out.println(d.name.length())`. What happens, and why?
questions.explanation: Java initializes unassigned instance fields to type-specific zero-equivalents: reference types (including `String`) default to `null`, not to `""`. Calling any method on a null reference throws `NullPointerException` at runtime. This is why constructors exist: to replace null defaults with real values before the object is used. The fix is either a constructor that sets `this.name` explicitly, or a null guard before the call. NullPointerException is the most common Java runtime error and almost always traces back to a field or return value that was assumed to be non-null but was not initialized.

options.optionText: It prints 0 — Java initializes String fields to an empty string `""`
It prints the length of the class name "Driver"
A NullPointerException is thrown — reference-type fields default to null, and calling `.length()` on null dereferences a null reference
It prints -1 — Java uses -1 to indicate an uninitialized String

questions.questionText: Which access modifier makes a member accessible to subclasses in a different package, but NOT to unrelated classes in that same different package?
questions.explanation: `protected` grants access within the declaring package AND to subclasses in any package. An unrelated class in a different package has no access. `public` removes all restrictions and is therefore too permissive. `private` and default are both too restrictive.

options.optionText: `private`
default (no modifier)
`protected`
`public`

questions.questionText: In Java, where must a `this(...)` constructor call be placed within a constructor body?
questions.explanation: The Java Language Specification (JLS §8.8.7) requires that both this(...) and super(...) appear as the first statement of a constructor body. The compiler enforces this at compile time — any code before this(...) is a compile error.

options.optionText: Anywhere before the first field assignment
After all field assignments are complete
As the very first statement in the constructor body
Only in a constructor that takes no arguments

questions.questionText: What keyword designates a member as class-level in Java — shared across all instances rather than belonging to any individual object?
questions.explanation: `static` designates a member as class-level: one copy lives in the method area regardless of how many instances exist. `const` is reserved but unused in Java. `final` makes a variable unresettable but does not make it class-level. `auto` does not exist in Java.

options.optionText: `const`
`final`
`auto`
`static`

questions.questionText: A Fare class must be fully immutable — no subclass should be able to add a setter that breaks the guarantee. Which combination is required?
questions.explanation: Declaring the class `final` prevents subclassing — no subclass can add setters. Declaring each field `private final` prevents reassignment after construction and blocks external access. Together they form the complete immutability guarantee. `final` methods (option A) still allow a subclass to introduce entirely new setter methods. A private constructor (option C) prevents subclassing but also blocks normal external instantiation.

options.optionText: All fields `private` and all methods declared `final`
The class declared `final` and all fields declared `private final`
All fields `private final` and a private constructor
All fields declared `static final`

questions.questionText: A Trip copy constructor contains `this.route = other.route`. After creating tripCopy from originalTrip, the caller calls `tripCopy.getRoute().setSource("Delhi")`. What is `originalTrip.getRoute().getSource()`?
questions.explanation: this.route = other.route copies the reference pointer, not the object. Both Trip variables point to the same Route in heap memory. Calling setSource("Delhi") through either reference mutates the single shared object, so reading getSource() through originalTrip also returns "Delhi".

options.optionText: The original source — the copy owns an independent Route
"Delhi" — both Trip objects reference the same Route heap object
null — the Route field was cleared during copy
A NullPointerException is thrown

questions.questionText: A Trip class overrides equals() to compare by tripId but does NOT override hashCode(). Two Trip objects with tripId "T-101" are added to a HashSet<Trip>. How many entries does the set contain?
questions.explanation: HashSet uses hashCode() to find the bucket before it calls equals(). The default hashCode() derives from memory identity — two distinct objects produce different hashes and land in separate buckets; equals() is never compared between them. Both trips are stored, giving a set size of 2.

options.optionText: 0 — the broken contract causes an exception during insertion
2 — the unoverridden hashCode produces different bucket assignments and equals() is never called
1 — HashSet calls equals() first to detect duplicates before consulting hashCode()
It depends on JVM garbage-collection timing

questions.questionText: A Driver class declares `private final long driverId`. Which statement correctly describes how this field may be assigned?
questions.explanation: A final instance field must be definitely assigned before the constructor exits (JLS §8.3.1.2). Assignment can happen at the declaration site or inside any constructor body — but exactly once across the path that executes. The compiler performs definite-assignment analysis. Instance methods cannot assign a final field after construction.

options.optionText: It must be assigned in the field declaration itself; constructor assignment is not allowed
It can be assigned repeatedly from within any instance method
It can be assigned exactly once, either in a field initializer or in any constructor of the class
It is automatically assigned the default value 0L and cannot be explicitly set

questions.questionText: Why is it impossible for `this(...)` and `super(...)` to both appear explicitly in the same constructor?
questions.explanation: The JLS mandates that both this(...) and super(...) appear as the first statement of a constructor body. A constructor body has exactly one first statement, so only one can hold that slot. When this(...) is used, the delegated master constructor handles the super() call.

options.optionText: The JVM only permits one parent-class initializer call per class hierarchy
Both must occupy the first statement of the constructor body — a structural impossibility in a single constructor
`super(...)` is implicitly invoked after `this(...)` completes, making an explicit call redundant
`this(...)` internally delegates to `super(...)`, so an explicit super call would execute it twice

questions.questionText: In the code below, what does `super(vehicleId, licensePlate, 4)` accomplish?
questions.explanation: There is only one object being constructed — the Car instance. super(vehicleId, licensePlate, 4) delegates initialization of inherited fields to Vehicle's constructor on that same object. No second Vehicle instance is created. This is standard inheritance delegation: shared fields live in the parent constructor, subclass-specific state and overrides live in the child.

options.optionText: It creates a new Vehicle instance and stores it as a hidden parent field inside Car
It invokes Vehicle's constructor to initialize the shared fields vehicleId, licensePlate, and capacity on the current Car object
It calls a static factory method on Vehicle that pre-configures four-seat defaults
It overrides Vehicle's constructor with Car-specific behaviour

questions.questionText: After executing the three statements below in order, what is Driver.totalCount?
questions.explanation: new Driver() chains to this(0L, "Anonymous", 0.0, false), which calls the four-argument master → totalCount becomes 1. new Driver(1L, "Alice") chains to the master → totalCount = 2. new Driver(2L, "Bob", 4.8, true) calls the master directly → totalCount = 3. Constructor chaining ensures the counter lives in one place and runs once per object regardless of which overload is used.

options.optionText: 1 — only the master constructor is counted
2 — the no-arg and partial constructors are excluded
3 — every construction routes through the master constructor, incrementing the counter once per object
0 — totalCount++ inside a chained constructor is not executed

questions.questionText: Consider the following statements: i. Calling of overloaded methods is decided at compile time ii. Calling of overridden methods is decided at runtime. Which of the following is correct?
questions.explanation: Overloaded method resolution is performed statically by the compiler based on parameter signatures, while overridden method invocation is dispatched dynamically by the JVM at runtime based on the actual object instance.

options.optionText: Both are correct
Both are incorrect
i is correct, ii is incorrect
i is incorrect, ii is correct

questions.questionText: Which of the following does Java not support?
questions.explanation: Java natively supports method overriding, method overloading, and static method hiding, but intentionally does not support programmer-defined operator overloading.

options.optionText: Method overriding
Method overloading
Operator overloading
Method hiding

questions.questionText: What is true about static methods? i. They can be overloaded ii. They can be overridden Which of the following is correct?
questions.explanation: Static methods belong to the class rather than an instance; they can be overloaded with different parameter signatures, but cannot be polymorphically overridden (redefining them in a subclass results in method hiding).

options.optionText: Both are correct
Both are incorrect
i is correct, ii is incorrect
i is incorrect, ii is correct

questions.questionText: Consider the following classes: If client code does `P obj = new C(); obj.display();` where `display()` prints `d1`, `d`, then calls `fun1()`, `fun()`, `sfun()` — what is the output?
questions.explanation: Fields are never polymorphic in Java; `obj.d1` and `obj.d` resolve by the *reference type* (`P`), so both read `P`'s fields (10, 100) regardless of the actual object being a `C`. `fun1()` is not overridden in `C`, so it prints `P's fun1`. `fun()` **is** overridden, and instance methods dispatch dynamically on the *actual object type* (`C`), so it prints `C's fun`. `sfun()` is `static`, so it is hidden, not overridden — static calls resolve at compile time by reference type (`P`), printing `P's sfun`.

options.optionText: Compile Time Error
10 100 P's fun1 C's fun P's sfun
100 100 P's fun1 C's fun P's sfun
10 10 P's fun1 C's fun P's sfun

questions.questionText: Consider the following about interface data-members: 1. They are final 2. They are static Which of the following is true?
questions.explanation: All fields declared in a Java interface are implicitly `public static final` constants.

options.optionText: Both are correct
Both are incorrect
i is correct, ii is incorrect
i is incorrect, ii is correct

questions.questionText: Consider the following two statements: 1. Abstract classes should necessarily have abstract methods 2. Classes having abstract methods should be abstract Which of the following is true?
questions.explanation: An abstract class is not required to declare any abstract methods (it may contain only concrete methods to prevent instantiation), but any class that contains at least one abstract method must be declared abstract.

options.optionText: Both are correct
Both are incorrect
i is correct, ii is incorrect
i is incorrect, ii is correct

questions.questionText: Which keyword is used to make a non-inheritable class in Java?
questions.explanation: Applying the `final` keyword to a class declaration prevents any other class from extending it.

options.optionText: static
abstract
final
finally

questions.questionText: Consider the following two statements: i. Runnable interface is implemented by class which will be invoked via a separate Thread ii. The name of the function to start a new Thread is run Which of the following is correct?
questions.explanation: Statement i is true; statement ii is false because the method to start a new concurrent thread is `start()`. Calling `run()` directly merely executes the method synchronously on the calling thread.

options.optionText: Both a and b are true
Only a is true
Only b is true
Both a and b are false

questions.questionText: Consider the following two statements: 1. Threads of same process can access each other's stack data 2. Threads of same process can access each other's global data Which of the following is correct?
questions.explanation: Each thread has its own private call stack and local variable storage, while global, static, and heap data is shared across all threads within the same process.

options.optionText: Both a and b are true
Only a is true
Only b is true
Both a and b are false

questions.questionText: Consider the following two statements: 1. Parallel programming requires multiple program counters 2. Concurrent programming requires time-bound CPU scheduling Which of the following is correct?
questions.explanation: Parallel execution requires multiple physical CPU cores executing instructions simultaneously (each with its own hardware Program Counter), whereas concurrency on a single core relies on time-sliced CPU scheduling and context switching.

options.optionText: Both a and b are true
Only a is true
Only b is true
Both a and b are false

questions.questionText: Consider the following two statements: i. ExecutorService.submit returns a Future object ii. The method name to receive a value from Future object is get. Which of the following is correct?
questions.explanation: `ExecutorService.submit()` returns a `Future` instance representing the pending asynchronous computation, and `.get()` blocks the calling thread until the computed value is available.

options.optionText: Both a and b are true
Only a is true
Only b is true
Both a and b are false

questions.questionText: Consider the following two statements: 1. The responsibility of the Executor is to decide how to run different tasks on different threads 2. The responsibility of class implementing Callable is to define a task to be done on a separate thread Which of the following is correct?
questions.explanation: `Executor` manages thread lifecycle, pooling, and task scheduling, while a `Callable` implementation encapsulates the specific computation and return value of the task itself.

options.optionText: Both a and b are true
Only a is true
Only b is true
Both a and b are false

questions.questionText: Consider the following two statements: 1. Executor manages the assignment of tasks to threads within the thread pool. 2. Waiting Queue holds the tasks that couldn't be assigned to threads in the thread pool. Which of the following is correct?
questions.explanation: An Executor assigns queued tasks to available worker threads in the pool, while the internal waiting queue holds tasks when all pool threads are currently busy.

options.optionText: Both a and b are true
Only a is true
Only b is true
Both a and b are false

questions.questionText: Consider the following two statements: 1. Runnable interface is used to create classes that run on a separate thread and return values to the main thread. 2. Callable interface is used to create classes that run on a separate thread and don't need to return values to the main thread. Which of the following is correct?
questions.explanation: Both statements have it backwards: `Runnable.run()` returns `void` and cannot return a value to the caller, while `Callable<V>.call()` is specifically designed to return a typed value `V`. Neither statement correctly describes its interface.

options.optionText: Both a and b are true
Only a is true
Only b is true
Both a and b are false

questions.questionText: Consider the following two statements: 1. A class implementing Callable<Integer> will have a call function that returns integer 2. To get a value from a class implementing Callable<Integer>, we can use Future<Integer> Which of the following is correct?
questions.explanation: `Callable<Integer>.call()` is declared to return `Integer`, and submitting that `Callable` to an `ExecutorService` returns a `Future<Integer>` whose `.get()` retrieves the computed value once ready.

options.optionText: Both a and b are true
Only a is true
Only b is true
Both are false

questions.questionText: What is the name of the algorithm used by Atomic Data types for thread-safety?
questions.explanation: Atomic classes (such as `AtomicInteger`) achieve lock-free thread safety using the hardware-level Compare-And-Swap (CAS) instruction.

options.optionText: Mark and Sweep
Binary Search
Compare and Swap
None of the above

questions.questionText: Which of the following statements about mutex locks in Java is true?
questions.explanation: A mutex lock enforces mutual exclusion, ensuring that only one thread can execute within a protected critical section at any given time.

options.optionText: Mutex locks are used to achieve parallel execution of threads.
Mutex locks are synonymous with atomic data types in Java.
Mutex locks are used to protect critical sections of code from concurrent access.
Mutex locks are only applicable to single-threaded programs

questions.questionText: Which of the following statements is true about the synchronized keyword?
questions.explanation: The `synchronized` keyword can be applied to instance methods (locking the instance `this`), static methods (locking the `Class` object), and standalone synchronized blocks.

options.optionText: It can only be applied to instance methods
It can be applied to both instance methods and static methods
It can only be applied to static methods
It cannot be used in a multithreaded application

questions.questionText: Which of the following is true regarding the differences between Hashtable and ConcurrentHashMap in Java?
questions.explanation: `Hashtable` synchronizes on the entire map for every operation, allowing only one thread in at a time. `ConcurrentHashMap` uses finer-grained internal locking (segment/bucket-level), letting multiple threads operate on different parts of the map concurrently.

options.optionText: Hashtable allows multiple threads to access different parts of the map at the same time, while ConcurrentHashMap does not.
ConcurrentHashMap is synchronized, while Hashtable is not.
Hashtable is synchronized, ConcurrentHashMap is not.
ConcurrentHashMap allows multiple threads to access different parts of the map at the same time, while Hashtable does not.

questions.questionText: Consider the following class: And client code creating `A obj1 = new A();` and `A obj2 = new A();`. Which pair of calls CANNOT execute concurrently?
questions.explanation: `fun1()` is `static synchronized`, so it locks the shared `Class` object (`A.class`), not any particular instance. Both `obj1.fun1()` and `obj2.fun1()` compete for that one class-level lock regardless of which instance calls it, so they cannot run concurrently. `fun2()` is an instance-level lock, so different instances (`obj1`/`obj2`) calling it are unaffected by each other.

options.optionText: obj1.fun1() and obj1.fun2()
obj1.fun1() and obj2.fun1()

Critical section of consumer should begin with acquire on producer semaphore and end with release on consumer semaphore
