questions.explanation: The specific, named scheduling-failure event is the concrete diagnostic signal — without reading it, a missing toleration looks like an unexplained stall rather than an identifiable, fixable cause.

options.optionText: A scheduling-failure event naming the untolerated taint as the specific reason — distinguishing "this Pod is correctly refusing to run somewhere it shouldn't" from a crash or generic error, which would otherwise send the FDE looking in the wrong place
A CrashLoopBackOff error indicating the container failed to start due to a code exception
Nothing — Pending Pods with a missing toleration produce no diagnostic event at all
An OOMKilled event indicating the Pod exceeded its memory limit

questions.questionText: In the scenario, `inference-sa`'s Role grants only `get`/`list`/`watch` on ConfigMaps in its own namespace. Why exactly that set, and nothing more?
questions.explanation: This is least privilege applied concretely — the grant matches the actual task (reading model version config) and nothing else, so the answer to "what could this Pod do if compromised" stays short and specific.

options.optionText: It matches the one genuine need — reading which model version is currently active — while denying everything else, including listing Secrets or reaching another namespace, so a compromise of this Pod has a small, bounded, explainable blast radius
Kubernetes RBAC does not support granting write permissions to ServiceAccounts under any circumstances
ConfigMap access is required for GPU scheduling to function at all
This scoping has no security rationale; it was chosen arbitrarily as a minimal example

questions.questionText: Why does the practice loop have you apply the default-deny NetworkPolicy first, confirming it breaks existing traffic, before adding the explicit allow rule?
questions.explanation: Confirming the deny actually takes effect is the diagnostic step that turns "I wrote a policy" into "I verified isolation" — an unverified default-deny could be silently unenforced, per Q1's CNI dependency.

options.optionText: It makes the isolation verifiable rather than assumed — confirming traffic actually breaks under default-deny proves the policy is enforced, so the later allow rule can be trusted to be the only path back in, not one of several unnoticed gaps
Kubernetes requires NetworkPolicy objects to be applied in a specific numbered order or the API server rejects them
There is no reason for this order; applying the allow rule first would produce an identical result
Breaking traffic temporarily is required to reset the CNI plugin's internal state

questions.questionText: In the scenario, why does ArgoCD revert the on-call engineer's manual `kubectl` replica-count change three minutes later?
questions.explanation: This is the concrete enforcement mechanism the lesson highlights — self-heal is what makes "Git is the source of truth" actually true rather than aspirational.

options.optionText: Self-heal continuously re-applies the state declared in Git whenever the live cluster drifts from it — a manual change that wasn't made through Git is exactly the drift self-heal is designed to correct
ArgoCD detected the change was made by an unauthorized user account and blocked it specifically for that reason
Kubernetes itself, not ArgoCD, automatically reverts any manual kubectl edit after a fixed timeout
The revert is a bug in ArgoCD's default configuration that most teams disable

questions.questionText: Given self-heal's behavior in the scenario, what is the correct way for the engineer to make the increased replica count actually persist?
questions.explanation: The fix works with the reconciliation loop rather than fighting it — once Git reflects the desired state, ArgoCD applies exactly that instead of reverting it.

options.optionText: Commit the new replica count to the manifests repo, so Git now agrees with the desired state — ArgoCD will then apply it and stop reverting it
Disable ArgoCD self-heal permanently across the entire cluster so manual kubectl edits are never reverted again
Repeat the manual kubectl edit more frequently than ArgoCD's reconciliation interval
Edit the replica count directly in ArgoCD's own internal database rather than in Kubernetes or Git

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson treat the split between an application repo and a separate GitOps manifests repo as deliberate rather than incidental?
questions.explanation: The separation is functional, not cosmetic — it scopes what ArgoCD reacts to and lets the manifests repo apply a review gate suited specifically to production deployment changes.

options.optionText: It keeps ArgoCD watching only deployment-relevant changes instead of triggering on every application-code commit, and lets the manifests repo carry its own review discipline distinct from the application code review
Kubernetes technically requires manifests and application code to live in physically separate Git hosting providers
A single combined repo would exceed GitHub's maximum file-count limit for any real application
The split exists only to satisfy a naming convention with no functional benefit

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson claim that under the GitOps pattern described, every change ArgoCD makes to the cluster traces back to a specific, reviewable Git commit rather than a CI run's transient log?
questions.explanation: Because ArgoCD's only input is the manifests repo, the repo's commit history is inherently the durable, reviewable record of every change it ever applied.

options.optionText: ArgoCD only ever applies what's declared in the manifests repo, and that repo's commit history is the durable record of every desired-state change — unlike CI logs, which can rotate out or be harder to correlate after the fact
ArgoCD writes its own separate audit log that has nothing to do with Git commit history
CI run logs are actually more durable and reliable than Git commit history for this purpose
This traceability claim only holds if the cluster has CloudTrail data events enabled

questions.questionText: How does the lesson describe what progressive delivery tooling (Argo Rollouts) adds compared to ArgoCD's default all-at-once rollout?
questions.explanation: Progressive delivery builds on the same reconciliation loop but adds gradual, health-signal-driven traffic shifting instead of switching every replica over at once.

options.optionText: It incrementally shifts traffic to a new ReplicaSet based on live health signals, catching a bad release with a small fraction of real traffic before it reaches everyone
It replaces ArgoCD's reconciliation loop with a completely different, unrelated deployment mechanism
It removes the need for a manifests repo entirely
It only applies to Lambda-based deployments, not Kubernetes Deployments

questions.questionText: How does the scenario's GitHub Actions test-suite stage connect to the FDE Foundations Git/GitHub lesson and the Backend Observability CI lesson?
questions.explanation: This is a deliberate cross-module echo — the same required-check gating discipline extends naturally into a pipeline that also handles deployment, not a new, unrelated practice.

options.optionText: It reuses the same PR-gated, required-check discipline — the test suite must pass before an image is even built, the identical "CI gates the merge" pattern established in those earlier lessons, now feeding into a GitOps deployment instead of ending at merge
There is no meaningful connection; the CI stage in this lesson is an entirely new mechanism unrelated to earlier lessons
The connection only holds if the test suite specifically includes Hypothesis property-based tests
The Git/GitHub lesson's discipline applies only to Python projects, not to a containerized service like order-management

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson call a hand-rolled provisioning script the imperative equivalent of the polymorphism lesson's pre-interface procedural code?
questions.explanation: The comparison is precise — a hand-rolled script only handles the cases its author anticipated, while Terraform's diff-based reconciliation handles the general case of "what's the difference between desired and actual state" automatically.

options.optionText: It works for the one path it was written for, but re-running it against an already-provisioned environment or reasoning about a partial failure requires the author to have manually encoded every case Terraform's plan/apply diff computes automatically
Hand-rolled scripts are technically incapable of calling any AWS API
There is no meaningful difference between a Terraform configuration and an equivalent bash script
This comparison only applies to scripts that provision RDS instances specifically

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson insist the state file is not an implementation detail to skip past?
questions.explanation: The state file is what lets Terraform reason about "what already exists" — without an accurate one, the plan/apply diff has nothing reliable to compare the configuration against.

options.optionText: It's the ground truth mapping every resource block in configuration to a specific real resource ID, and losing or corrupting it means Terraform can no longer tell what it already created — leading to duplicate resources or a plan that wants to destroy things still in use
The state file only matters for cosmetic reasons, like formatting `terraform plan`'s output
Terraform can always regenerate a lost state file automatically from the AWS account with no data loss
The state file exists purely for Terraform's internal logging and has no bearing on plan/apply behavior

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson say the state file should be treated with the same least-privilege discipline as the AWS Core lesson's IAM policies?
questions.explanation: Treating the state file as "just config" misses that it can hold real secrets in plaintext — the same access-control discipline that scopes IAM policies applies here for the same reason.

options.optionText: The state file often contains sensitive values in plaintext — a database password set via a Terraform variable ends up in the state file unless the backend encrypts at rest and the value is marked sensitive — making it a secret-adjacent asset, not just a config artifact
Terraform state files are technically stored as IAM policy documents themselves
This concern only applies when the state file is stored locally rather than in a remote backend
State files never contain any sensitive data by design, so this comparison is purely stylistic

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson compare a Terraform module's input variables and output values to interface-first OOP thinking?
questions.explanation: The module's variables/outputs are its contract — a consumer depends on that contract without needing to know how the module implements it internally, mirroring interface-based design.

options.optionText: A consuming configuration passes inputs (like a CIDR block) and gets back outputs (like subnet IDs) without needing to know the module's internal resource count or naming — the same "depend on the contract, not the implementation" pattern
Terraform modules are compiled using the same bytecode as Java interfaces
A module's internal resource structure must always be visible to any configuration that consumes it
Modules and interfaces share no meaningful conceptual similarity; the comparison is purely coincidental phrasing

questions.questionText: In the scenario, why does the FDE add the manually-created rule into the module's configuration rather than simply running `apply` to revert it?
questions.explanation: The deliberate choice matters here — a genuinely needed fix should become a reviewed, declared part of the configuration rather than being silently reverted or left as undocumented drift.

options.optionText: The manual rule fixed a genuine connectivity issue — reconciling it into configuration turns an undocumented emergency fix into a reviewed, permanent, declared part of the infrastructure instead of either silently reverting a needed fix or leaving an unreviewed change in production
Terraform configuration cannot be edited once a resource has drifted, so reconciliation is the only technically possible option
Reverting the rule would have caused the RDS instance itself to be destroyed
The rule was already present in the module's configuration before the manual change, so no action was actually needed

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson recommend separate state files per environment (dev/prod) rather than one shared state distinguishing environments with `count` or `for_each`?
questions.explanation: This is the same least-reachability, contained-blast-radius reasoning from the AWS Core lesson, reapplied to how Terraform state itself is partitioned.

options.optionText: A mistaken `apply` against the wrong state file is a small, contained mistake, whereas one shared state file lets an error touch every environment at once — the same blast-radius reasoning as scoping an IAM policy to a specific resource ARN
Terraform technically forbids using `count` or `for_each` for environment-based configuration
Separate state files are required because Terraform cannot manage more than one AWS region from a single state file
This separation has no bearing on risk; it is purely an organizational preference with no safety benefit

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson call Lambda's per-invocation billing model the "exact inverse" of the GPU inference Deployment's cost profile?
questions.explanation: The two cost models are genuinely opposite — pay-per-millisecond-of-actual-work versus pay-for-continuous-provisioned-capacity — which is exactly why matching the model to the workload's actual traffic shape matters.

options.optionText: A function invoked briefly and infrequently has genuinely no idle cost, billed only for actual execution time, whereas the GPU Deployment is provisioned and paid for continuously regardless of whether it's actively serving a request
Lambda functions are always cheaper than any container-based deployment under every workload pattern
GPU Deployments are billed per invocation in the same way Lambda functions are
This comparison only applies to functions triggered directly by API Gateway

questions.questionText: According to the lesson, what role does API Gateway play before a request ever reaches the Lambda handler?
questions.explanation: API Gateway's boundary role directly parallels what a load balancer and middleware already do for container-hosted services — just managed and configured declaratively.

options.optionText: Request/response transformation, authentication, throttling, and request validation — the same boundary-enforcement role a load balancer plus application middleware plays for a container-hosted service, but fully managed
API Gateway executes the actual business logic itself, with Lambda only used for logging
API Gateway is required only for Lambda functions triggered by SQS, not by direct HTTP requests
API Gateway has no authentication capability and must always be paired with a separate authentication service

questions.questionText: Why does the scenario's `ChargePayment` state retry only specific transient Stripe error codes rather than retrying on any failure?
questions.explanation: The distinction matters because a permanent failure retried repeatedly wastes time and obscures the real outcome — routing it to `Catch` instead reflects that no retry will change a card decline.

options.optionText: A permanently-declined charge (a card error) will never succeed no matter how many times it's retried — retrying only transient errors and routing permanent declines to a distinct failure state avoids wasted retries on an outcome that can't change
Step Functions technically only supports retrying a single named error type per state
Stripe's API rejects any request that includes retry logic of any kind
Retrying on any failure would exceed Step Functions' maximum state machine size limit

questions.questionText: Which specific constraint does the lesson name as ruling out rebuilding the GPU inference Deployment as a Lambda function?
questions.explanation: The hardware constraint is absolute — Lambda doesn't expose GPU access at all, which alone rules it out regardless of the other throughput and warm-up considerations also mentioned.

options.optionText: GPU hardware access — Lambda does not expose GPU hardware at all, independent of the workload's throughput or warm-up characteristics
Lambda functions cannot make outbound network calls to any AWS service
Lambda has no way to process any request that originates from a Kubernetes cluster
Lambda functions are limited to a maximum of one invocation per second

questions.questionText: In the practice loop, why can the FDE confirm exactly which state ran, with what input/output, without searching application logs?
questions.explanation: The execution history is a built-in feature of Step Functions itself, giving a structured record of every state transition without needing separate log correlation.

options.optionText: Step Functions maintains a complete, inspectable execution history for each run — a debugging advantage a hand-written orchestrator's scattered application logs don't provide for free
Application logs are technically disabled for any Lambda function invoked through Step Functions
This is only possible if CloudTrail data events were separately enabled for the state machine
Step Functions requires a third-party logging tool to produce any execution record at all

questions.questionText: How does the lesson's serverless-versus-container framing connect to the "match complexity to genuine need" theme from the agent-vs-workflow and WebSockets-vs-SSE lessons?
questions.explanation: This is a deliberate cross-module echo — the same discipline of naming the actual constraint before choosing a mechanism reappears here applied to compute, not agent design or real-time transport.

options.optionText: In every case, the right choice is decided by naming the specific constraint the workload actually has — throughput shape, hardware need, or connection lifetime — not by defaulting to whichever option is more modern or more familiar
These lessons share no meaningful connection; the comparison is coincidental
This theme only applies to choices between two different AI agent architectures, not infrastructure choices
The "match complexity to genuine need" theme argues that the newer technology should always be preferred by default

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson cite the SQS-triggered notification handler from the earlier Compute, Storage & Managed Services lesson as a good serverless fit?
questions.explanation: The notification handler's traffic shape — brief, infrequent invocations — is exactly the pattern where Lambda's per-invocation billing avoids paying for idle capacity a container would otherwise sit on.

options.optionText: It runs for milliseconds only occasionally, and running it as an always-on container would waste continuous compute cost sitting idle most of the time — exactly the spiky, infrequent traffic pattern serverless is suited for
SQS-triggered functions are required by AWS to run as Lambda functions and cannot be implemented any other way
The notification handler needs GPU access, making it unsuitable for a container deployment
This workload requires a long-running, stateful connection, which only Lambda can provide

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson say framing reliability as a "budget" rather than a "target" is the substantive move?
questions.explanation: The budget framing is what makes risk-taking a deliberate, quantified decision instead of an all-or-nothing target that treats every release as equally dangerous.

options.optionText: A target that's never allowed to be missed forces every release to be treated as equally risky, while a budget that's tracked and spent deliberately turns "how much risk can we take" into a concrete, decidable number
A budget and a target produce identical engineering decisions; the wording difference is purely stylistic
Budgets apply only to financial cost, not to reliability, making this framing a misnomer
A budget framing means the SLO can be silently ignored whenever convenient

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson say an FDE without an agreed SLO on a customer engagement is walking into an unstated conflict?
questions.explanation: An agreed SLO converts a recurring, informal argument about reliability-versus-velocity into a decision already made in advance by both sides.

options.optionText: Without an agreed budget, "is this incident bad enough to stop and fix, or an acceptable cost of shipping fast" gets informally re-litigated every time, instead of being answered by a number both sides already agreed to
Customers always refuse to engage with an FDE who has not first defined an SLO
SLOs are a legal requirement for any AWS-hosted production workload
Without an SLO, the OTel tracing instrumentation from Module 2 cannot function at all

questions.questionText: What does a burn-rate alert indicate that a plain "an error occurred" alert does not?
questions.explanation: Burn rate is a pace signal — it says whether the budget is being spent too fast for the window, which is a meaningfully different and more actionable signal than any single error.

options.optionText: That the error budget is being consumed faster than the measurement window can sustain — a rate-based signal, not just the fact that a single error happened
That the error budget has already reached exactly zero
That the SLO target itself needs to be permanently lowered
That a specific individual engineer is responsible for the ongoing errors

questions.questionText: In the scenario, why does the FDE use `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` on the regressed query rather than assuming the database is generically overloaded?
questions.explanation: This is a direct reuse of the Postgres-internals lesson's diagnostic discipline — evidence from the actual query plan, not an assumption about the database being generally slow.

options.optionText: It follows the same evidence-first diagnostic discipline as the Postgres-internals lesson — checking the actual query plan reveals the specific missing index causing the regression, rather than guessing at a vague, unfalsifiable cause
EXPLAIN ANALYZE is required by AWS before any RDS query can be executed in production
This step is unnecessary in the scenario; the FDE could have found the same answer faster by restarting the RDS instance
EXPLAIN ANALYZE only works for queries that already have an existing index

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson insist the postmortem's follow-up action targets the migration review process gap, not the engineer who wrote the migration?
questions.explanation: The blameless framing is a deliberate choice about what actually reduces future incidents — a culture that surfaces near-misses openly catches more problems than one that punishes whoever happened to trigger the last one.

options.optionText: Punishing the individual who triggered the incident teaches everyone else to hide near-misses instead of surfacing them, which produces a worse long-term reliability outcome than the original incident — the fix that actually prevents recurrence is closing the process gap
The engineer who wrote the migration was not actually responsible for the missing index in any way
Blameless postmortems are a purely legal requirement with no bearing on future incident rates
Naming an individual in a postmortem is technically prohibited by every major cloud provider's terms of service

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson single out toil (like manually restarting a stuck Pod repeatedly) as a specific risk to an SRE practice, even when the error budget is currently healthy?
questions.explanation: The point is about converting slack into durable improvement — spending it on repeated manual fixes instead of the actual fix means the burden never actually goes down.

options.optionText: If the slack a healthy error budget provides gets spent on repetitive manual work instead of the automation or architectural fix that would eliminate the underlying problem, the operational burden never actually decreases over time
Toil is defined as any work performed by an on-call engineer, regardless of whether it's repetitive or one-time
A healthy error budget automatically eliminates the need to address toil at all
Toil only becomes a concern once the error budget has already been fully exhausted

questions.questionText: Why does the suggested extension say the SQS-based notification pipeline's SLO needs a different SLI (queue lag) than the order-management API's SLO (request latency)?
questions.explanation: An SLI has to reflect what the specific workload's users actually experience — copying an unrelated workload's SLI onto a queue-based pipeline would measure the wrong thing entirely.

options.optionText: The notification pipeline's user-experienced behavior is how long a message waits before being delivered, not how fast a single synchronous request completes — the SLI has to measure what the workload actually does, not be copied from an unrelated workload's SLI
Queue-based systems are technically incapable of having any SLO defined for them
Request latency and queue lag are actually the same measurement expressed in different units
The notification pipeline cannot be measured using the OTel instrumentation from Module 2

questions.questionText: What is the actual purpose of this assessment, according to the lesson?
questions.explanation: This assessment is explicitly a composition check, not new content — its value is proving the module's separate lessons actually integrate, a distinct skill from executing each one in isolation.

options.optionText: Confirming that Module 4's individual tools (infrastructure-as-code, secrets management, Kubernetes networking/RBAC, GitOps, SRE discipline) compose into one deployed, diagnosable system — not testing any single new mechanism
Teaching an entirely new cloud provider not covered elsewhere in the module
Testing typing speed under a strict time limit
Determining whether the learner should use Kubernetes or a different orchestrator going forward

questions.questionText: Per the challenge brief, why does the rubric's "infrastructure correctness" category specifically check that `terraform plan` shows zero unexpected drift?
questions.explanation: A clean `terraform plan` is a direct, verifiable signal that the declared configuration and the real infrastructure agree — exactly the kind of falsifiable check the rubric is built around.

options.optionText: It's a concrete, checkable way to confirm the infrastructure was actually provisioned declaratively through Terraform rather than by hand — any manual console change would surface as drift in the plan output
Terraform plan output has no relationship to whether infrastructure was provisioned by console clicks or by Terraform itself
This check only matters for the RDS instance, not for the VPC or EKS cluster
Zero drift is impossible to achieve in practice, so this criterion is intentionally unattainable

questions.questionText: What does the rubric's "deployment & GitOps discipline" category evaluate?
questions.explanation: This directly reuses the CI/CD lesson's core claim — a bypassed pipeline (a manual `kubectl apply`) breaks the audit-trail guarantee GitOps is meant to provide, which is exactly what this rubric category checks for.

options.optionText: Whether every change that reached the cluster traces back to a Git commit in the manifests repo, or whether a manual `kubectl apply` bypassed the pipeline at any point
How many total files exist in the application repository
Whether the Docker image was built using a specific base image tag
Whether the cluster is running on EKS specifically rather than another Kubernetes distribution

questions.questionText: Why does the final rubric category require the postmortem's follow-up action to name a process gap rather than the specific action that caused the injected failure?
questions.explanation: This is a direct reuse of the SRE lesson's postmortem framing — a process-gap fix generalizes to prevent a class of failure, while naming only the specific action produces a much narrower, less durable fix.

options.optionText: This reuses the SRE lesson's blameless-postmortem discipline — naming the process gap targets what would actually prevent a recurrence, while naming the specific triggering action produces a fix that only prevents that one exact failure from happening the same way again
The specific triggering action is always impossible to identify in an injected-failure exercise
Process gaps and triggering actions are the same thing described in different words
This requirement only applies if the injected failure involved a Terraform-managed resource

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson argue that skipping a rubric item — for example, hardcoding a secret instead of using Secrets Manager — produces a "noticeably worse, less defensible" result rather than merely a less polished one?
questions.explanation: The rubric items were chosen because each maps to a real, demonstrated capability from earlier lessons in the module — skipping one is a functional loss of that capability, not a stylistic shortfall.

options.optionText: Each rubric item corresponds to a real capability the deployment loses without it — skipping Secrets Manager means losing rotation, access-controlled retrieval, and CloudTrail-visible access auditing, a functional loss, not a cosmetic one
The rubric items are arbitrary stylistic preferences with no functional consequence
Hardcoding a secret and using Secrets Manager produce functionally identical security outcomes
This concern only applies to secrets that are rotated automatically

questions.questionText: Why does the suggested extension recommend having a peer inject a second, different failure a week later and comparing diagnosis speed against the first time?
questions.explanation: Comparing diagnosis speed across two genuinely separate incidents is a concrete way to check whether the observability and audit-trail investments actually paid off, not just whether the first fix happened to go smoothly.

options.optionText: It tests whether the observability and GitOps audit trail already in place genuinely made diagnosis faster and more evidence-based the second time, rather than the first success being a one-off — a concrete, comparable measurement instead of a subjective impression
A second injected failure is required because the first one cannot actually be fixed
This comparison has no diagnostic value; it exists only to extend the assessment's total time
The second failure is guaranteed to be identical to the first, making the comparison trivial

questions.questionText: What does the pain-quantification pass of a discovery call add that a general complaint like "this process is frustrating" does not?
questions.explanation: This mirrors the problem-discovery lesson's impact line — converting dissatisfaction into a measurable figure (frequency, cost, duration) is what makes a later solution's success checkable rather than a matter of opinion.

options.optionText: A commitment from the customer to sign a contract
A concrete number — frequency, duration, or cost — that later lets a proposed solution be checked against a real bar
A guarantee that the stated pain is the true underlying need
A list of every system the company currently uses

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson insist that constraints (technical, budget, timeline, compliance) be asked explicitly during discovery rather than assumed?
questions.explanation: The lesson frames this as a cost argument: an unstated assumption that turns out wrong compounds into wasted build effort, while surfacing the same constraint in the first conversation costs almost nothing.

options.optionText: Constraints are legally required to be documented for every engagement
A constraint discovered after work has already been built around a wrong assumption is far more expensive to fix than one surfaced in the first conversation
Customers are unaware they have any constraints until directly asked
Constraints only matter for engagements involving regulated industries

questions.questionText: What distinguishes the "champion" from the "end users" in the lesson's stakeholder-mapping framework?
questions.explanation: The lesson explicitly separates these roles because they rarely coincide: the champion's advocacy and the end users' daily experience of the problem can diverge, which is exactly why both need to be heard separately.

options.optionText: The champion always has less technical knowledge than the end users
The champion advocates internally and pulled the FDE in, but may not personally use the result day to day, unlike the end users whose actual workflow the solution changes
The champion is always the same person as the economic buyer
End users always have final budget authority over the engagement

questions.questionText: In the scenario, the VP asked for "AI-powered inventory forecasting" while the planner's actual pain was a stale, manually-updated spreadsheet. What does this specifically illustrate?
questions.explanation: This is the stakeholder-mapping risk made concrete: the VP's framing ("AI forecasting") named a solution category, while the planner — who lives the process daily — surfaced the real, narrower need (data staleness), exactly why both accounts had to be gathered separately.

options.optionText: The VP was intentionally misleading the FDE
A solution-shaped request from one stakeholder can obscure a different, more specific underlying need held by the stakeholder who actually experiences the process daily
Forecasting models are never an appropriate solution for inventory problems
The planner's account should be discarded in favor of the VP's, since the VP has budget authority

questions.questionText: Why does the FDE send the written discovery brief back to all three stakeholders and ask "is this an accurate summary?" before writing any code?
questions.explanation: Confirming the brief before building is the cheapest possible point to catch a misunderstanding — a dispute caught here costs a re-read of one page, while the same dispute caught after a demo costs a rebuilt prototype.

options.optionText: It is a formality required for legal liability purposes only
It gives the customer a chance to correct a misunderstanding while the cost of being wrong is still near zero, rather than after a prototype has already been built around it
It replaces the need for any further communication during the engagement
It shifts responsibility for the final solution's success entirely onto the customer

questions.questionText: A data privacy officer was never on the original discovery call but turns out to hold a hard constraint relevant to the engagement. What does the lesson's framework suggest as the best way to have avoided discovering this late?
questions.explanation: The constraints pass is explicitly about surfacing what might otherwise stay unstated; asking who else might hold a relevant constraint is a direct extension of that discipline rather than waiting for someone uninvited to raise it after the fact.

options.optionText: Proceed with the build and address privacy concerns only if the officer objects after launch

Explicitly ask, during the constraints pass, who else in the organization might hold relevant compliance or data constraints, rather than relying on the invited stakeholders to volunteer that information
Assume compliance constraints are the economic buyer's sole responsibility to raise
Skip the constraints pass entirely for engagements without an obvious regulatory angle

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson argue that leaving non-goals implicit doesn't actually make a project's scope smaller?
questions.explanation: The lesson's specific claim is about timing and cost of the same disagreement — resolved during scoping it's cheap, discovered at a demo it looks like a failure to deliver.

options.optionText: It just moves the disagreement about what's in scope from the cheap discovery stage to the expensive demo stage, where it reads as a broken promise
Scope is determined entirely by the engineering team's available time, regardless of documentation
Non-goals sections are optional and have no measurable effect on outcomes
Implicit non-goals always expand scope rather than leaving it ambiguous

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson say an options matrix's comparison columns should come from the constraints surfaced during discovery rather than a generic template?
questions.explanation: The matrix exists to make a real trade-off visible to this customer, which only works if the columns reflect constraints that actually matter to them (data residency, maintainability by their team), not a generic checklist.

options.optionText: Generic templates are always factually incorrect
A matrix scored against dimensions irrelevant to this customer's actual constraints doesn't help the customer make the decision that matters to them
Templates take longer to fill out than custom matrices
Matrices with generic columns cannot be shown to customers under any circumstances

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson insist every risk register entry have a named owner, not just a mitigation?
questions.explanation: A mitigation without an owner is a plan nobody is responsible for executing. Naming a specific owner is what turns a documented intention into something that actually gets done.

options.optionText: Owners are required for legal compliance in every jurisdiction
A risk with no assigned owner is a risk nobody is actually accountable for closing, regardless of how good the mitigation text sounds
Naming an owner automatically reduces the risk's likelihood
Only risks with a named owner are permitted to be included in a PRD-lite

questions.questionText: Why did the hybrid (rule-based script plus LLM-assisted anomaly flagging) win over the pure time-series forecasting model in the scenario, despite scoring lower on raw forecast accuracy?
questions.explanation: This is the trade-off the matrix was designed to surface: winning on one dimension (accuracy) doesn't automatically win overall — the matrix weighs it against the customer's actual constraints, several of which the hybrid satisfied better.

options.optionText: Time-series models cannot technically be deployed in a logistics context

The matrix's columns reflected the discovery brief's actual constraints — fast time-to-value, operability by the customer's own team, and no direct ERP write access — and the hybrid scored better across those specific constraints even though it lost on accuracy alone
LLM-based approaches always outscore time-series models regardless of the dimensions used
The rule-based script was the cheapest option to build, which was the only column scored

questions.questionText: The risk register entry about accidental ERP write access is a direct technical response to which earlier artifact?
questions.explanation: The risk register entry (read-only IAM policy, verified in a startup healthcheck) is a concrete technical safeguard built specifically to prevent the exact constraint violation the finance controller flagged during discovery from ever happening silently.

options.optionText: The demo storytelling structure covered in a later lesson
The finance controller's constraint surfaced during discovery, that the system must never directly write to the ERP's inventory table
A generic industry-standard security checklist unrelated to this engagement
The PRD-lite's non-goals section alone, independent of discovery

questions.questionText: What is the shared purpose the lesson attributes to both the options matrix and the risk register, beyond documenting the FDE's own reasoning?
questions.explanation: Both artifacts exist to externalize reasoning that would otherwise live only in the FDE's head, so someone without the original context can still follow and evaluate the decision.

options.optionText: Making the scoping decision reviewable by someone who wasn't in the room — a customer's IT director or a second FDE picking up the engagement later — so they can see why the approach was chosen, not just that it was
Satisfying a mandatory audit requirement present in every FDE engagement
Replacing the need for the discovery brief entirely
Guaranteeing that the chosen approach will succeed without further validation

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson hold customer-facing written status updates to a different standard of precision than an internal Slack message to another engineer?
questions.explanation: The distinction is about correction cost and audience distance — internal imprecision gets caught and fixed quickly by a peer with full context; customer-facing imprecision persists as the stakeholder's understanding of reality.

options.optionText: Customers are contractually forbidden from asking follow-up questions
An internal message is quickly correctable if imprecise, while a customer-facing update, written to a stakeholder not in the room daily, becomes in practice the record the customer holds the FDE to
Slack messages cannot contain technical detail, unlike status updates
There is no meaningful difference; the same precision standard applies to both

questions.questionText: Which of the following two status sentences does the lesson consider the better practice, and why?
questions.explanation: The lesson's certainty-language discipline specifically favors sentences a stakeholder can act on correctly, which requires stating what evidence currently supports the claim rather than a vague overall impression.

options.optionText: "It's basically working" — because it is shorter and easier for a customer to read
"Validated against 20 real emails, three edge cases still open" — because it tells the reader exactly what has been checked versus what remains unverified
Both sentences are equally acceptable in any status update
"It's basically working" — because vague language avoids setting expectations the FDE might not meet

questions.questionText: According to the lesson, when does collapsing "done" and "prototyped, not yet validated" into casual language like "it's working" typically cost the most trust?
questions.explanation: The lesson's claim is about timing of discovery — imprecise status language doesn't cost trust immediately, it costs trust later when the actual state of the work becomes visible at a high-stakes moment like a demo.

options.optionText: When the gap becomes visible at the worst possible time, usually during a demo or a go-live, rather than being caught earlier through precise status language
The distinction never actually matters to a customer relationship
Immediately, the moment the imprecise sentence is written, regardless of what happens afterward
Only if the customer explicitly asks for a legal definition of "done"

questions.questionText: In the scenario, why did the FDE surface the cost-field redaction requirement in the status update rather than quietly building the fix and mentioning it only once resolved?
questions.explanation: Because the requirement fell outside the originally scoped non-goals, it is a genuine scope decision — extra time versus a rollout restriction — that only the customer can make, which is exactly why it belongs in a status update with options, not a silent fix.

options.optionText: Company policy requires every technical decision to be pre-approved by the customer

The redaction requirement was not covered by the original PRD-lite's non-goals, meaning it represents new scope requiring a customer decision (extra build time or a rollout restriction), not something the FDE could unilaterally resolve
The FDE lacked the technical skill to build the redaction feature without customer input
Warehouse staff had already discovered the cost field on their own

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson argue that a PRD-lite's non-goals and a risk register's named risks "only stay useful" if status updates keep referring back to them honestly?
questions.explanation: The discipline established in scoping only holds if ongoing status reporting stays honestly anchored to it — otherwise, optimistic reporting can drift away from the documented scope and risks without anyone noticing until it matters.

options.optionText: Early scope and risk discipline can quietly erode into optimistic status reporting over time if status updates stop being checked against those original documents
Risk registers automatically update themselves based on status update content
Non-goals sections expire after the first status update is sent
Status updates and risk registers serve entirely unrelated purposes with no meaningful connection

questions.questionText: If the redaction requirement had been discovered one day before a scheduled customer demo instead of during a routine weekly update, what should change about how it is communicated, per the lesson's principles?
questions.explanation: The lesson's principle of surfacing bad news early and honestly applies with even more urgency close to a high-visibility moment like a demo — the cost of the customer discovering the gap live is much higher than an early, direct heads-up.

options.optionText: Nothing should change; the same weekly-cadence email is always sufficient regardless of timing

The blocker should be surfaced immediately and directly, likely outside the normal weekly cadence, since the cost of the customer discovering it live during the demo is far higher than the cost of an early, direct heads-up
The blocker should be omitted from the demo entirely and addressed only if a stakeholder happens to notice
The demo should be presented as if the redaction feature is already complete to avoid disrupting the schedule

questions.questionText: What does the lesson say a demo generating zero questions from affected stakeholders is more likely a sign of?
questions.explanation: The lesson explicitly reframes pushback as a sign of engagement, not failure — silence from people whose daily workflow the tool affects is a weaker signal of quality than genuine, specific questions.

options.optionText: The work is flawless and needs no further validation
The stakeholders were not engaged enough to spot the gaps, rather than proof the work has none
The demo was too short to cover meaningful content
The audience already fully agreed with every decision before the demo began

questions.questionText: Which two categories of pushback does the lesson say come up in nearly every technical demo?
questions.explanation: The lesson names accuracy skepticism ("how do I know this is right?") and edge-case gaps ("what about this case?") as the two categories worth preparing for before nearly any demo.

options.optionText: Budget disputes and timeline disputes
Accuracy skepticism and edge-case gaps
Branding concerns and naming conventions
Licensing questions and vendor comparisons

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson say responding "yes, it'll definitely handle that too" to an untested edge case creates a debt the FDE cannot pay?
questions.explanation: The specific risk is that the stakeholder treats an unvalidated verbal claim as a real commitment, creating an expectation the FDE has no actual evidence to support meeting.

options.optionText: The claim was never validated, yet the stakeholder will remember it as a commitment the FDE made, creating an obligation that outpaces what is actually known
Stakeholders never remember specific claims made verbally during a demo
Over-promising is only a problem if the untested case later succeeds
This phrasing is technically a lie regardless of whether the case is eventually handled correctly

questions.questionText: What are the three components of the lesson's recommended pattern for responding to live pushback?
questions.explanation: This is the lesson's explicit three-part pattern, illustrated directly in the new-SKU scenario response, and it holds up regardless of the eventual answer because it never claims more than was known at the time.

options.optionText: Specific acknowledgment of what was asked, a statement of what current evidence shows and doesn't show, and a concrete, checkable follow-up
An apology, a promise, and a change of subject
A generic "good question," a restatement of the original demo, and a request to move on
A technical explanation of the system architecture, a disclaimer, and a thank-you

questions.questionText: Why did the FDE's response to the warehouse planner's new-SKU question land well in the scenario, specifically?
questions.explanation: Because the gap was already named in a document the stakeholders had seen, the live answer reinforced consistency between what was scoped and what was demoed, rather than revealing a previously hidden limitation.

options.optionText: The FDE promised the new-SKU case would be fixed by the following week

The response matched what was already documented in the PRD-lite's non-goals that both the planner and VP had already reviewed, so it confirmed existing scope rather than surprising anyone with a new gap
The FDE avoided answering the question directly and moved on to the next demo item
The FDE claimed the system already handled new SKUs correctly

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson suggest sending a formal follow-up email scoping the new-SKU cold-start case as a named item, rather than leaving the demo-floor response as the final word?
questions.explanation: This ties the demo lesson's live-pushback pattern back to the stakeholder-communication lesson's written-artifact discipline — a concrete follow-up promised verbally becomes durable and checkable once it's also written down.

options.optionText: Verbal commitments made during a demo are legally binding without written confirmation

It converts a spoken, in-the-moment answer into the same kind of written, checkable artifact established in the stakeholder-communication lesson, giving both sides a durable record of the concrete follow-up promised
Follow-up emails are required only when a stakeholder explicitly requests one
It replaces the need for the original PRD-lite's non-goals section

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson insist that fallback behavior for a failed or timed-out LLM call be decided during scoping rather than improvised the first time it happens in front of a customer?
questions.explanation: Planning the fallback in advance, as part of scoping, means the response to a real failure is a known, tested behavior rather than a decision made under pressure in front of the customer at the worst possible moment.

options.optionText: A deliberately chosen fallback (cached response, honest degraded message, queued retry) can be validated and communicated in advance, while an improvised response under live pressure risks a worse outcome than any of the planned options
LLM API failures are so rare that fallback behavior is rarely relevant in practice
Customers never notice a failed LLM call if no fallback is defined
Improvised fallback behavior is always technically superior to a planned one

questions.questionText: What is the correct process for handling a vendor's model deprecation notice on a production LLM feature, according to the lesson?
questions.explanation: The lesson frames deprecation handling as an ordinary dependency-upgrade process: validate the replacement before switching, and schedule the change deliberately before the hard retirement deadline rather than reacting to a sudden failure.

options.optionText: Wait until the model is retired and switch to whatever replacement is default at that point

Track the notice, re-run the feature's evaluation suite against the replacement model version, and schedule the cutover before the retirement date — the same discipline as dependency-upgrade management in ordinary software
Ignore deprecation notices, since providers never actually retire models that are already in production use
Immediately switch to the replacement model the day the notice is received, without re-running evaluation

questions.questionText: The lesson describes output drift that can occur "even without a version bump." What does this refer to?
questions.explanation: The lesson's specific claim is that a model's outputs can drift even when the FDE has changed nothing and the version identifier looks unchanged, which is exactly why passive monitoring, not just deployment discipline, is needed to catch it.

options.optionText: A model's behavior on a given prompt can shift subtly over time due to a provider's continuous updates behind a stable-seeming interface, or ordinary sampling variance, without any code change on the FDE's side
Drift only happens when a customer manually edits a prompt template
This is a theoretical risk with no observed real-world cause
Output drift is caused exclusively by network latency between the FDE's service and the model provider

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson argue an LLM call should get the same structured logging and tracing discipline as any other service-to-service call, rather than a special exemption?
questions.explanation: The lesson explicitly connects this to the earlier observability module's discipline — an LLM call has the same failure modes (latency, errors, silent behavior change) as any dependency call, so exempting it from tracing just reintroduces the blind spot that discipline was built to close.

options.optionText: LLM providers require structured logging as a contractual condition of API access

An LLM call is a backend dependency call like any other, and treating it as exempt from observability just recreates the same blind spots that structured logging and tracing exist to eliminate for every other dependency
Structured logging is only useful for debugging network-layer issues, which don't apply to LLM calls
LLM calls are inherently more reliable than database calls, so less monitoring is needed

questions.questionText: According to the lesson, what does the FDE-role lesson's "enable" step require for an LLM feature specifically, beyond a working demo?
questions.explanation: The lesson makes this concrete: without real observability into individual call outcomes, the customer's team cannot actually operate or troubleshoot the feature themselves, which is exactly what genuine enablement requires.

options.optionText: The customer's own team needs visibility, in their own monitoring, into what a specific failed or degraded LLM call actually did — the same operational transparency expected of any other production dependency
The customer's team only needs a document describing how the feature works in general terms
Enabling an LLM feature is not meaningfully different from enabling any feature with no external dependency at all
Enablement is complete once the feature passes its initial demo successfully

questions.questionText: In the scenario, why did the summarization feature's Monday-morning failures go unnoticed until they became a customer complaint?
questions.explanation: The combination of silently swallowing the error and having no observability into LLM call outcomes meant the failure produced no internal signal — exactly the gap the lesson's structured-logging discipline is meant to close.

options.optionText: The vendor's API was completely down during that window, with no partial functionality

The code swallowed 429 responses into an empty summary rather than surfacing them as a defined error, and there was no structured logging or dashboard signal that would have made the failures visible before a customer noticed
The feature had never been tested against any real ticket data before go-live
The customer's support lead was unaware the feature used an LLM at all

questions.questionText: What is the key property a lightweight, automated drift-detection check needs in order to catch a shift like the scenario's tone-and-length change without relying on a customer to notice first?
questions.explanation: A useful drift check needs to run continuously against a stable, representative sample so a shift shows up as a measurable signal over time — a one-time check or reliance on manual customer reports both fail to catch a slow, ongoing drift automatically.

options.optionText: It must run against a small, fixed set of representative prompts on a recurring schedule and compare outputs (e.g. by length or similarity) over time, rather than only being checked ad hoc when someone happens to look
It must re-validate every possible customer input the feature could ever receive, exhaustively, before each release
It only needs to run once, immediately after the feature first goes live
It must rely entirely on the customer manually reporting perceived changes in tone

questions.questionText: What three categories of inputs does the lesson say a well-constructed golden test set should include?
questions.explanation: The lesson explicitly names these three categories as covering the feature's core cases, its known edge cases, and adversarial inputs — a golden set missing any one of these leaves a real class of regression uncaught.

options.optionText: Only representative, everyday inputs — edge cases and adversarial inputs are handled separately
Representative core cases, known edge cases, and adversarial inputs
Only adversarial inputs, since representative cases rarely reveal regressions
A random sample of unlabeled production traffic with no expected-behavior criteria

questions.questionText: Why is the same golden test set useful for detecting a regression caused by a vendor upgrading the underlying model, not just for detecting regressions from your own prompt edits?
questions.explanation: Pinning a dated identifier means model changes only happen at a moment the FDE chooses, which is exactly the moment the golden set can be run against the candidate version before it goes live — the same re-run discipline as the earlier deprecation-handling process.

options.optionText: Because you pin an exact, dated model identifier, a model-side change only reaches production at a deliberate version bump you control, and running the golden set against the candidate new version before switching reveals whether it still meets the same behavior bar
Vendor-side model upgrades never actually change output behavior, so this scenario is purely theoretical
The golden set automatically re-runs itself whenever the vendor updates any model, with no action needed from the FDE
Golden test sets can only detect regressions caused by prompt edits, never vendor-side changes

questions.questionText: How does this lesson's red-teaming practice differ from the injection-defense mechanism covered in the earlier advanced-prompting-and-safety lesson?
questions.explanation: The earlier lesson covered the general injection mechanism and layered defenses; this lesson is specifically about the operational discipline of testing a given shipping prompt against its own concrete attack surface before it reaches a customer, which two different prompts require differently even though the underlying risk mechanism is the same.

options.optionText: This lesson claims privilege separation and instruction hierarchy are no longer necessary once red-teaming is in place

This lesson adds the FDE operational practice of writing a dedicated, concrete set of adversarial test inputs targeting a specific prompt's own actual attack surface (its real fields, its real tool access) before shipping it, rather than relying on the general defense mechanisms alone
Red-teaming replaces the need for deterministic output validation entirely
The earlier lesson and this one describe an identical practice with no meaningful difference

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson describe a prompt padded with instructions or examples that don't measurably improve the golden set's pass rate as "pure waste multiplied across production request volume"?
questions.explanation: Because prompt tokens are billed and add latency on every call, not just once, unnecessary length is a recurring cost that compounds with request volume — the lesson's specific reason to favor the shortest prompt that still clears the golden set's bar.

options.optionText: Extra prompt content is free at low volume but becomes expensive only above a fixed daily request threshold

Every token in a prompt is billed and adds latency on every single call, so unnecessary content that adds no measurable benefit is a real, recurring cost that scales directly with request volume, unlike a one-time cost
Longer prompts always produce lower-quality output regardless of content
Token costs only apply to the model's output, not to the prompt itself

questions.questionText: In the scenario, why did the updated prompt fail the golden test set's adversarial case, specifically?
questions.explanation: The regression was specifically caused by the new instruction's wording undermining the earlier instruction-hierarchy phrasing that had previously kept the injection attempt from succeeding — exactly the kind of small-edit-causes-hidden-break the golden set exists to catch.

options.optionText: The updated prompt was too short to include the necessary recall-flagging instruction

The new recall-flagging instruction's wording accidentally weakened the existing instruction-hierarchy language, allowing the injected "ignore prior instructions" case to succeed where it previously failed
The golden test set had never included any adversarial cases before this change
The model provider deprecated the pinned model version at the same time as the prompt change

questions.questionText: Why was blocking the merge, rather than shipping the recall-flagging change and monitoring for issues afterward, the correct response in the scenario?
questions.explanation: Catching a real injection regression in a controlled test run, before it reaches production traffic, is precisely the value an eval gate provides — shipping first and monitoring afterward would have left the vulnerability exploitable in the meantime.

options.optionText: The regression was a real, reproducible injection vulnerability caught in testing before any customer or attacker could exploit it in production — exactly the outcome an eval gate is designed to guarantee
Blocking merges is always required by company policy regardless of what the golden set shows
Shipping the change with monitoring would have been strictly faster with no meaningful downside
The FDE had no way to fix the underlying wording issue, so blocking was the only option

questions.questionText: Why does a second adversarial test case targeting system-prompt disclosure need to be a separately designed case, rather than assuming the "ignore prior instructions" case already covers it?
questions.explanation: Red-teaming a prompt's actual attack surface means considering distinct attack goals separately — an instruction-override attempt and a system-prompt-extraction attempt exploit the same architectural weakness differently, so each needs its own concrete test case to be reliably caught.

options.optionText: Different injection attempts target different parts of a prompt's attack surface (altering behavior versus extracting hidden instructions), so a test case that catches one doesn't necessarily catch the other — each concrete attack vector needs its own designed case
System-prompt disclosure is not actually a real risk for customer-facing LLM features
A single adversarial test case is always sufficient to cover every possible injection attempt against a given prompt
This risk only applies to agents with tool-calling access, never to a plain summarization prompt

questions.questionText: Why does a production ingestion pipeline need a confidence signal from its OCR step, rather than always ingesting whatever text OCR produced?
questions.explanation: Garbled OCR text still gets embedded and indexed like any other chunk, but its content is wrong, which is a silent failure mode; a confidence threshold routes suspect pages to human review instead of ingesting them as if they were clean.

options.optionText: OCR always fails completely or succeeds completely, so a confidence signal is unnecessary

OCR quality on real customer scans varies, and silently ingesting low-confidence, garbled text produces chunks that appear normal but embed and retrieve incorrectly, so low-confidence pages should be flagged for review instead
Confidence signals are only useful for detecting duplicate documents
OCR confidence has no relationship to retrieval quality

questions.questionText: A naive parser flattens a table into one run of plain text. Why does this specifically damage a query asking for "the Q3 number for the EMEA region"?
questions.explanation: A table's meaning depends on which row and column a value belongs to; collapsing that structure into undifferentiated text loses exactly the relationship a structured query depends on, which is why table-aware parsing (e.g. preserving markdown table structure) matters.

options.optionText: Flattened tables cannot be embedded by any embedding model
Flattening destroys the row/column structure that connects "Q3" and "EMEA" to their specific intersecting value, so the information the query needs is no longer recoverable from the chunk
This only affects keyword search, not vector search
Flattened tables are always split into a separate chunk automatically

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson say a pipeline that only supports a full reindex becomes operationally unusable at real document counts?
questions.explanation: The cost is compounding: every document, changed or not, gets re-embedded on every full reindex, which is wasteful at scale and creates an inconsistent window during the rebuild — the exact problems incremental re-ingestion is designed to avoid.

options.optionText: Vector databases have a hard limit on the total number of reindex operations they can ever perform

A full reindex re-parses, re-chunks, and re-embeds every document from scratch every time, which is slow, costs a billed embedding call per document regardless of whether it changed, and creates a window reflecting neither the old nor new state cleanly
Full reindexing is only a problem for documents under 1,000 words
Incremental and full reindexing produce identical index states, so the distinction doesn't matter operationally

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson describe a RAG system confidently citing a superseded, uncorrected document version as worse than having no RAG system at all?
questions.explanation: The specific harm is epistemic: a wrong answer delivered with the same confident tone as a correct one gives the user no reason to question it, whereas no system at all at least doesn't create false confidence in stale information.

options.optionText: A missing RAG system always produces more accurate answers than any RAG system
The stale citation looks authoritative and confident while being factually wrong, which is more damaging than an obvious absence of an answer, since the user has no signal to distrust it
Stale citations only occur when the embedding model itself is outdated
This problem cannot occur if chunking is done correctly

questions.questionText: In the manufacturing customer scenario, why does the pipeline pull the `role:hr` tag directly from SharePoint's own permission API rather than hardcoding it per document?
questions.explanation: Sourcing the tag from the actual permission system, rather than a hardcoded guess, means it stays correct as the source system's real access rules change over time, avoiding silent drift between the index's metadata and the truth.

options.optionText: SharePoint's permission API is required by law for all RAG systems

A hardcoded tag drifts out of sync the moment the source system's actual permissions change, while pulling from the real permission system keeps the tag accurate to the document's true current access rules
Hardcoding tags is technically impossible in a production ingestion pipeline
The tag only needs to be accurate at the moment of the very first ingestion

questions.questionText: What role does a per-document change signal (a last-modified timestamp, content hash, or webhook) play in the ingestion pipeline described in this lesson?
questions.explanation: The change signal is the mechanism that makes incremental sync possible at all — without a reliable way to detect which documents changed, the pipeline has no basis for skipping unchanged documents during a sync.

options.optionText: It determines which embedding model to use for a given document
It lets incremental re-ingestion identify exactly which documents actually changed, so only those are re-parsed, re-chunked, and re-embedded instead of the entire corpus
It is only used to generate the access-control tag
It replaces the need for OCR confidence checking

questions.questionText: A source document is deleted from the customer's system entirely. What should a correctly designed incremental ingestion pipeline do?
questions.explanation: An orphaned chunk from a deleted source is a direct analog to the stale-citation problem — it can still surface in retrieval and be presented as current, so deletion needs to propagate into the index promptly, not wait for a full reindex cycle.

options.optionText: Leave the document's existing chunks in the index indefinitely, since deletion is rare
Detect the deletion and remove the document's chunks from the index, so they cannot still be retrieved and cited after the source no longer exists
Mark the document's chunks as low-priority but keep them retrievable
Wait until the next scheduled full reindex to remove the chunks

questions.questionText: A system retrieves a restricted chunk, includes it in the prompt sent to the model, but only hides it from the citation list shown to the unauthorized user in the UI. Why does the lesson say this does not actually enforce access control?
questions.explanation: Enforcement has to happen before the model sees the content, not after, at display time — once a restricted chunk is in the prompt, the model can reflect its content in the answer regardless of what the citation UI later chooses to show or hide.

options.optionText: Citation UIs are always displayed to every user regardless of permissions

The model already read the restricted chunk's content when generating its answer, so the restricted information can leak into the response text itself even if the citation UI hides the source — the boundary was never enforced upstream
This approach is equivalent in effect to a correctly implemented pre-filter
Hiding a citation always prevents the underlying information from influencing the answer

questions.questionText: According to the lesson, when should an FDE prefer a dual-system hybrid search approach (two separate systems merged in application code) over a single system with native dense-plus-keyword support?
questions.explanation: The lesson frames native combination as operationally simpler and the default, with the customer's existing infrastructure being the concrete reason to deviate — for example, extending an already-running Elasticsearch deployment rather than adding an entirely separate system.

options.optionText: Always — dual-system approaches are strictly superior in every deployment

When the customer's existing infrastructure already has a strong preference, such as an existing investment in a search system that can be extended, rather than defaulting to a second, separate vector store
Never — dual-system hybrid search is never a valid production choice
Only when the customer's document set is smaller than 100 documents

questions.questionText: A query uses the abbreviation "L4," but source documents spell out "Level 4 Individual Contributor" and never use "L4." Why does the lesson say hybrid search alone does not reliably fix this?
questions.explanation: Hybrid search combines two retrieval methods, but both still depend on some form of lexical or semantic overlap between query and document; an undocumented internal abbreviation defeats both unless something (query rewriting) bridges the vocabulary gap first.

options.optionText: Hybrid search only functions correctly on numeric queries

Neither the dense embedding nor the keyword/BM25 component can match "L4" against "Level 4 Individual Contributor" without an explicit mapping, since the exact term doesn't appear in both forms in both places — the gap is a vocabulary mismatch, not a retrieval-method limitation
BM25 always outperforms dense retrieval on abbreviations by default
This problem only occurs with single-word queries

questions.questionText: The lesson connects building an accurate query-rewriting glossary back to a skill from earlier in this module. Which skill, and why does it matter for the glossary's accuracy?
questions.explanation: An accurate glossary depends on correctly capturing how the customer's own staff actually talk about their work — exactly the kind of vocabulary that surfaces during a well-run discovery conversation, not something an FDE can accurately guess from outside.

options.optionText: Demo storytelling skills, because the glossary is presented to the customer as part of the final demo

Discovery-call skills — the glossary's term mappings need to be accurate to the customer's real internal vocabulary, and that vocabulary surfaces through the same structured discovery conversations used to gather requirements, not through guessing
Status-update writing skills, because the glossary is documented in a weekly status email
Risk register skills, because each glossary term is treated as a named risk

questions.questionText: In the scenario, the engineer's compound question about torque spec and HR travel policy was answered correctly for one part and appropriately declined for the other. What specifically made this possible?
questions.explanation: Because the pre-filter removed the HR chunk from the candidate set before ranking, the model had no restricted content in its context at all, which is why it could answer the engineering part correctly and correctly decline the HR part rather than fabricating from content it never received.

options.optionText: The model was trained specifically on this customer's HR policies
The access-control pre-filter excluded the HR-restricted chunk from the candidate set before the model ever saw it, so the model could only draw on the unrestricted engineering chunk for its answer
The query-rewriting step detected the question was compound and split it automatically
Hybrid search naturally excludes any HR-related content from all queries

questions.questionText: In the scenario, plant-floor staff use "twelve-mil" as shorthand for "M12," which the embedding model doesn't reliably associate with the documented term. What fixes this without re-writing the source documents or the embedding model?
questions.explanation: Query rewriting closes the vocabulary gap at query time, which is cheaper and more targeted than re-embedding an entire document set, and it fixes the specific term mismatch rather than a general retrieval-quality lever like model size or chunk count.

options.optionText: Re-embedding every document with a larger embedding model
A query-rewriting step that expands "twelve-mil" to "M12" using a glossary built from real plant-floor vocabulary, applied before the query reaches retrieval
Switching from hybrid search to dense-only search
Increasing the number of chunks retrieved per query

questions.questionText: Why might document-level access-control tagging be insufficient for a single document that mixes a restricted section (e.g. a salary table) with unrestricted general content?
questions.explanation: A single access-control tag applied to an entire mixed document forces an all-or-nothing choice that either over-restricts or under-restricts; chunk-level tagging at ingestion (the previous lesson's mechanism) is what makes fine-grained enforcement possible.

options.optionText: Document-level tagging always correctly protects every section of a mixed document

Tagging the whole document as restricted excludes unrestricted content unnecessarily, while tagging it as unrestricted exposes the restricted section — only chunk-level tagging (applied per section during ingestion) allows the unrestricted parts to remain retrievable while the restricted section stays protected
Chunk-level tagging is never necessary once hybrid search is in place
This problem is specific to scanned PDFs and doesn't apply to other formats

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson say an eval dataset an FDE writes entirely alone, without customer SME input, tends to be a weaker signal of real-world quality?
questions.explanation: The specific risk is representativeness, not validity — an FDE alone tends to write questions that don't reflect the actual distribution and phrasing of real user queries, which real SME input or real usage logs correct for.

options.optionText: RAGAS cannot score any dataset the FDE writes without customer sign-off
It tends to be easier and more evenly distributed across topics than real usage, which clusters around high-frequency intents and phrasing an FDE would not think to write
FDE-written questions are always factually incorrect
Eval datasets must contain at least 1,000 questions to be valid

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson say a moving (unversioned, frequently-changed) eval dataset makes month-over-month RAGAS score comparison meaningless?
questions.explanation: A stable yardstick is what makes a score comparison meaningful — if the eval set itself changes, a score movement could reflect the new question mix rather than any real change in system quality.

options.optionText: RAGAS scores are only valid for exactly 30 days after computation
If the questions being scored change between two measurements, you cannot tell whether a score difference came from a real system change or simply from scoring a different set of questions
Versioned datasets always produce higher scores than unversioned ones
RAGAS requires a minimum dataset size that only versioned datasets can guarantee

questions.questionText: Which changes does the lesson say should trigger a full RAGAS eval-gate run before merging?
questions.explanation: The lesson names a broad set of change types spanning both retrieval and generation layers as gate triggers — the common thread is anything that could plausibly move a RAGAS metric, not a narrow or manually-flagged subset.

options.optionText: Only changes to the customer-facing UI, since backend changes cannot affect RAGAS scores
Any change that can affect retrieval or generation quality — chunking strategy, prompt edits, reranking model swaps, or embedding model upgrades
Only changes explicitly labeled "RAG update" in the commit message
Changes are never gated; RAGAS is run only once, before initial launch

questions.questionText: Why does the lesson recommend a smaller, automated LLM-as-judge for continuously scoring sampled production traffic, rather than full human review of every live query?
questions.explanation: The practical constraint is scale — continuous, ongoing scoring of a meaningful sample of production traffic is only sustainable with automation, since human review of every query is not operationally viable at real volume.
