questions.explanation: `time.monotonic() - ts < 10` evaluates true at 4 seconds elapsed, so the function returns the write region, implementing read-your-writes for that session within the window.

options.optionText: To `eu-west-1`, since 4 seconds is within the 10-second sticky window
To the nearest healthy region by latency, ignoring the recent write
To `us-east-1` unconditionally, regardless of the write
The function raises an error because 4 seconds is not a valid input

questions.questionText: The team proposes applying read-your-writes routing to the submission-history list "to be safe." Why does the FDE push back?
questions.explanation: The lesson's central discipline is that a stronger guarantee is a cost, applied only where the underlying invariant requires it — "to be safe" is not sufficient justification when the specific consequence of staleness on this read is genuinely negligible.

options.optionText: Read-your-writes routing is technically impossible to implement for list-type reads

No business invariant on the submission-history list depends on sub-second freshness — applying the stronger guarantee would add real, permanent latency cost on every page load for every customer, paid for a safety margin nothing on that read actually needs
The submission-history list is already strongly consistent by default, making the proposal redundant but harmless
The FDE agrees with the proposal but defers the decision to a later phase

questions.questionText: Per the trade-off table, why does the premium rate display use eventual consistency with a short TTL rather than session or strong consistency?
questions.explanation: The table explicitly ties this row to Lesson 8's CDN caching strategy — a low-consequence staleness tolerance in exchange for the largest latency win among the four rows.

options.optionText: Prices never change at PolicyVault, so any consistency guarantee would be equivalent

A price shown up to 60 seconds stale is an acceptable, low-consequence trade-off in exchange for the lowest latency of the four operations — this ties directly to the edge-caching strategy from Lesson 8
Strong consistency is technically impossible to apply to catalog data
The premium rate display is on the same code path as the bind confirmation read and inherits its guarantee automatically

questions.questionText: Per the Suggested Extension, a "binding authority nearly exhausted" warning banner sourced from live bind-capacity counts is added. What is the correct way to classify its consistency need using this lesson's framework?
questions.explanation: This is the lesson's actual method, applied to a new case: name the concrete cost of each direction of error, then place the operation on the spectrum based on that comparison — not a default rule based on the data's general category.

options.optionText: Always choose the strongest available guarantee for any operation involving remaining capacity, since capacity is a business-critical concept

Name the specific consequence of both an overly strong guarantee (unnecessary latency on every quote page) and an overly weak one (a broker completes a bind the warning failed to flag as already over capacity), and place the operation on the strong-to-eventual spectrum based on which consequence is more costly to the business
Classification is unnecessary for warning banners, since they are advisory and not authoritative
Apply the same guarantee as the quote worksheet read automatically, since both involve per-line state

questions.questionText: A high-throughput telemetry gateway initializes its shared ConnectionPool lazily using double-checked locking, but omits the volatile modifier on the private static instance field. Under multi-threaded stress tests, worker threads intermittently encounter NullPointerExceptions or corrupt states immediately after pool initialization. What JVM mechanism causes this defect?
questions.explanation: Instantiating an object involves memory allocation, constructor execution, and assigning the reference to the variable. Without the volatile keyword establishing a happens-before memory barrier, instruction reordering can publish the reference before internal fields are populated. A concurrent thread executing the first unsynchronized null check observes a non-null reference and attempts to use the uninitialized object. Option A is incorrect because stale reads would simply cause threads to enter the synchronized block and retrieve the initialized instance; Option C is incorrect because monitor release happens strictly at block exit; Option D misapplies the semantics of final fields, which protect field publication within an object rather than the variable holding the singleton reference itself.

options.optionText: The CPU hardware caches fail to synchronize cache lines, causing reader threads to observe a permanently stale null reference indefinitely.

The compiler and CPU are free to reorder instructions during instantiation—allocating memory and assigning the reference before constructor execution completes—allowing other threads to observe a non-null reference pointing to a partially constructed object.
Double-checked locking without volatile causes the inner synchronized block to release its monitor before constructor execution finishes.
The Java Memory Model requires the final modifier on the singleton class definition to publish object references safely across threads.

questions.questionText: A distributed session cache manager is implemented as a thread-safe Singleton with a private constructor and double-checked locking. When session tokens are transmitted across nodes via standard Java object serialization, developers discover that multiple distinct session manager instances exist in memory, causing session state divergence. What causes this Singleton breakdown, and how is it natively avoided in modern Java?
questions.explanation: Java deserialization creates a new instance via reflection without invoking any constructor or static factory method, violating the Singleton constraint unless readResolve() is defined. An enum Singleton solves this definitively because the JVM explicitly guarantees that enum constants cannot be instantiated more than once, even across serialization or reflective attacks. Option B is incorrect because cloning and deserialization are distinct mechanisms; Option C does not prevent new instance allocation during readObject(); Option D wipes field data but still yields a duplicate object instance.

options.optionText: Standard serialization skips private constructors and getInstance() entirely by reconstructing objects reflectively from byte streams; implementing the Singleton as an enum natively guarantees instance uniqueness and serialization safety per the JVM specification.
The class failed to implement Cloneable; overriding clone() to return the existing instance prevents duplicate creation during deserialization.
Double-checked locking only protects static methods; synchronizing all instance methods prevents multiple instances from being reconstructed.
Instance variables were not marked transient; declaring all state transient forces deserialization to bind to the existing singleton reference.

questions.questionText: An order management service creates an immutable PaymentRequest domain entity using a Builder. The entity contains required scalar fields and a List<MetadataTag> tags. The caller populates an ArrayList, calls paymentRequestBuilder.setTags(tags).build(), and later executes tags.clear() in a cleanup routine. In production, the built PaymentRequest unexpectedly has an empty tags collection during authorization. Where did the Builder implementation fail?
questions.explanation: True immutability requires defensive copying of mutable collection references during construction. If the Builder simply assigns this.tags = builder.tags, the internal domain entity and the outside caller share the exact same list reference on the heap, allowing post-construction external mutations to corrupt domain invariants. Option A is incorrect because records also store shallow references without automatic defensive copying; Option C is incorrect because collections are standard in Builders; Option D is incorrect because volatile manages reference visibility, not mutation of elements inside a collection.

options.optionText: The PaymentRequest class was not declared as a Java record, which automatically deep-freezes collections.

The build() method assigned the caller's tags collection reference directly instead of making an unmodifiable defensive copy (e.g., List.copyOf(this.tags) or new ArrayList<>(this.tags)), leaving internal state coupled to external mutation.
The Builder pattern requires collections to be passed as immutable streams rather than List implementations.
The tags field should have been declared volatile to prevent external threads from modifying the underlying elements.

questions.questionText: A banking application introduces a TransactionSpec class with extensive validation rules (account verification, currency checks, and positive balance limits) encapsulated inside TransactionSpecBuilder.build(). An engineer bypasses these rules in an integration test by directly calling new TransactionSpec("ACC-1", -500.0, null), injecting invalid state into the database. How must the class structure be fixed to prevent this bypass?
questions.explanation: A core requirement of the Builder pattern is making the target class constructor private. This guarantees that all instantiation attempts must pass through the Builder, where validation logic and invariant checks are enforced prior to object creation. Leaving the constructor public or package-private provides an uncontrolled backdoor. Option B relies on external framework runtime interception rather than language-level encapsulation; Option C permits unauthorized instantiation from any class within the same package or subclasses; Option D complicates inheritance without securing construction.

options.optionText: Declare the TransactionSpec constructor private, ensuring instances can only be instantiated through the nested static TransactionSpecBuilder.
Annotate the constructor with @Valid and configure a runtime reflection interceptor to enforce validation.
Move TransactionSpec into a separate package and declare the constructor protected.
Declare TransactionSpec as an abstract class and subclass it inside the Builder.

questions.questionText: A cloud provisioning engine caches VirtualMachineTemplate prototypes in a ConcurrentHashMap registry. When a new VM is provisioned, the engine fetches the prototype via registry.get("standard-linux") and invokes clone(). A provisioned VM instance adds an IP route to its cloned networkRoutes list, but engineers observe that all subsequent VMs provisioned from the registry suddenly contain this custom route. What is the root cause?
questions.explanation: This is the canonical shallow copy trap in the Prototype pattern. When an object with mutable collection fields is shallow-cloned, only the collection reference is copied. Consequently, the prototype in the registry and the newly cloned instance share the exact same list on the heap. Mutating the clone's routes pollutes the prototype template. The solution is a deep copy, creating a fresh collection with duplicated route entities inside clone(). Option B is incorrect because ConcurrentHashMap returns references without altering modifiability; Option C would cause the clone to throw UnsupportedOperationException rather than allowing independent routes; Option D conflates hash code equality with object reference cloning.

options.optionText: The clone() implementation performed a shallow copy by copying the networkRoutes list reference rather than instantiating a new independent collection populated with cloned route objects.
The prototype's clone() method was called while another thread was executing registry.put(), causing ConcurrentHashMap to return an unmodifiable view.
The prototype template in the registry should have been wrapped with Collections.unmodifiableList() upon registration to prevent mutations on the clone from modifying the original template.
The class implemented Cloneable but failed to override equals() and hashCode(), causing the collection to treat the clone and the prototype as the identical hash bucket key.

questions.questionText: An AI orchestration service uses an AIServiceClientFactory with a static getClient(String provider) method containing a switch statement (OPENAI -> new OpenAiClient(), ANTHROPIC -> new AnthropicClient(), etc.). Every time a new LLM provider is integrated, the factory source file must be edited, recompiled, and redeployed, causing merge conflicts. How should this factory be refactored to satisfy the Open/Closed Principle?
questions.explanation: A static factory with switch/if-else branching centralizes object creation but violates the Open/Closed Principle because adding new types requires modifying existing, tested code. A registry-backed factory maintains a map of factory suppliers (Map<String, Supplier<T>>) and exposes a register(name, supplier) method. New providers self-register during application bootstrapping (or via Java ServiceLoader), leaving the factory closed for modification but open for extension. Option A adds boilerplate class hierarchies without solving dynamic registration; Option C introduces fragile reflection and eliminates compile-time safety; Option D caches instances without addressing the OCP violation.

options.optionText: Convert the factory into an Abstract Factory with a separate interface and implementation factory for every individual provider.

Convert the factory to a registry-backed factory holding a Map<String, Supplier<AIServiceClient>>, allowing new provider modules to register their constructor lambda during startup without altering the factory class.
Use dynamic reflection inside the switch statement to look up classes matching the provider string at runtime.
Wrap the switch statement in a Singleton to ensure only one instance of each provider client is ever created.

questions.questionText: During a 90-minute machine coding interview for an in-memory vehicle management system, a candidate spends the first 35 minutes designing a distributed sharded PostgreSQL schema, Kafka partition topics, and Redis cache clusters. The interviewer stops the candidate and notes a critical pacing failure. What fundamental Step 0 principle did the candidate violate?
questions.explanation: Machine coding rounds evaluate an engineer's ability to translate ambiguous requirements into clean, production-grade, object-oriented code running on a single JVM. Spending time on distributed databases, messaging queues, or microservice infrastructure mistakes an LLD round for an HLD system architecture interview, burning critical time and guaranteeing failure to deliver a working vertical slice. Option A is a secondary testing concern; Options C and D reinforce the misconception that database persistence or heavy infrastructure is required before demonstrating core in-memory domain models.

options.optionText: The candidate failed to write unit tests before drawing the database schema diagrams.

The candidate conflated High-Level Design (HLD) with Low-Level Design (LLD); LLD evaluates in-memory object modeling, separation of concerns, and clean code execution rather than distributed infrastructure plumbing.
The candidate should have designed database tables with JPA annotations first, as interview rubrics require automated schema generation before in-memory services can be tested.
The candidate should have used an embedded in-memory database like H2 rather than external infrastructure to satisfy the persistence requirement quickly.

questions.questionText: An engineer models a Vehicle class hierarchy where a VehicleManager class contains giant procedural methods with 500-line if-else chains checking vehicleType == "ELECTRIC" or vehicleType == "FUEL", while Vehicle and its subclasses are passive data containers with only getters and setters. Why is this considered an architectural failure in an LLD evaluation?
questions.explanation: Relegating entities to passive data bags while concentrating all behavior in bloated procedural "Manager" or "Helper" services is the hallmark of the Anemic Domain Model. It recreates procedural C-style programming in Java syntax, violating encapsulation, Single Responsibility, and Open/Closed principles. Real OOP requires domain models to govern their own internal invariants (e.g. vehicle.recharge()), while application services orchestrate dependencies. Option B describes a real symptom of anemic models but fails to identify the core architectural anti-pattern; Option C promotes another procedural anti-pattern; Option D is factually incorrect regarding Java compilation.

options.optionText: It violates the Anemic Domain Model anti-pattern and OOP fundamentals: business rules and state transitions should be encapsulated inside rich domain entities, while service classes coordinate multi-entity workflows.

Placing stateful business rules in service classes requires making domain model fields public or adding unconstrained public setters, breaking encapsulation and allowing external classes to bypass invariants.
Business logic should reside entirely in utility classes with static methods to maximize code reuse across disparate packages.
Using manager classes creates circular classpath dependencies that prevent the Java compiler from resolving subclass types.

questions.questionText: A ride-hailing design problem asks you to support FuelVehicle and ElectricVehicle with distinct refuel() and recharge() operations. A candidate considers creating subclasses for every combination: ElectricCar, FuelCar, ElectricBike, FuelBike, HybridSedan, and HybridSUV. What design principle directly addresses this combinatorial explosion?
questions.explanation: Inheritance hierarchies model "is-a" relationships but quickly cause combinatorial class explosions when applied across orthogonal dimensions (propulsion type vs chassis type). Favoring composition and fine-grained interfaces (Interface Segregation Principle) allows a HybridVehicle to compose an ElectricEngine and a CombustionEngine, implementing both Rechargeable and Refuelable without creating duplicate leaf classes. Option B is an irrelevant behavioral pattern; Option C introduces an unmaintainable flag-ridden monolith; Option D exacerbates inheritance coupling.

options.optionText: Favor object composition and behavioral interfaces (e.g., Refuelable, Rechargeable) over deep class inheritance hierarchies to mix and match capabilities flexibly.
Apply the Memento pattern to save the state of each vehicle variant before refueling.
Merge all vehicle types into a single concrete Vehicle class with optional boolean flags (isElectric, isHybrid).
Use abstract class inheritance with package-private protected fields to allow subclasses full access.

questions.questionText: When designing a system like a Parking Lot or Task Planner, how does an experienced engineer proactively identify extensibility points during the first 15 minutes of problem analysis?
questions.explanation: Anticipating extension points is a key senior engineering skill in machine coding. By identifying business policies subject to change (pricing strategies, allocation algorithms, matching heuristics) and declaring clean interfaces (e.g., FeeCalculationStrategy), the core service logic remains closed for modification while accommodating new variations easily. Option B creates rigid, inheritance-coupled base classes; Option C represents premature infrastructure over-engineering; Option D sacrifices type safety and compile-time verification.

options.optionText: By isolating algorithms that are likely to vary or change (e.g., fee calculation, spot allocation, task prioritization) and abstracting them behind Strategy interfaces before implementing concrete classes.
By implementing the Template Method pattern across all classes with abstract hook methods for every prospective operation.
By wrapping every entity in a generic repository and building a multi-layered event bus architecture before writing the core domain models.
By declaring all method parameters as Object or Map<String, Object> to allow arbitrary data payloads without modifying method signatures.

questions.questionText: In an in-memory repository implementation for an LLD problem, an engineer uses a ConcurrentHashMap<String, User> to store entities. When registering a new user, the code executes: if (!users.containsKey(id)) { users.put(id, user); }. Under concurrent requests with identical IDs, duplicate accounts are intermittently created. Why did ConcurrentHashMap fail to prevent this race condition?
questions.explanation: A common concurrency misconception is assuming that using a thread-safe collection makes multi-step sequences atomic. In check-then-act (if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, v)), two threads can both evaluate containsKey(k) as false simultaneously, and both proceed to put(). Concurrent collections provide atomic compound primitives such as putIfAbsent() or computeIfAbsent() specifically to eliminate this race condition. Option A misattributes the flaw to memory barrier latency; Option C is false because writes are internally synchronized per bucket; Option D confuses lock striping behavior with lack of operation atomicity.

options.optionText: ConcurrentHashMap requires a volatile read barrier, so checking containsKey() inside an if statement flushes CPU cache registers too slowly.

Individual methods like containsKey() and put() are thread-safe in isolation, but compound check-then-act sequences are not atomic; the operation must use putIfAbsent() or computeIfAbsent() to be atomic.
ConcurrentHashMap only synchronizes read operations; write operations must be enclosed in an explicit ReentrantLock.
ConcurrentHashMap uses bucket locks, so concurrent writes to different keys within the same segment will block each other unless an explicit ReentrantLock is used.

questions.questionText: At the end of an LLD interview, what role does the Main driver class play in determining whether a candidate passes the evaluation?
questions.explanation: A working driver script in Main is non-negotiable in machine coding rounds. An elegant abstract class hierarchy that cannot compile or demonstrate an end-to-end execution path fails the round. A comprehensive Main class instantiates repositories, registers strategies into services, and runs through the complete happy path and key edge cases, proving the system is complete and functional. Option A is completely false under modern evaluation criteria; Option C is inaccurate because interviewers prioritize a clean executable driver over extensive mock-based unit tests when time is tight; Option D is an anti-pattern that slows down evaluation compared to deterministic scripted scenarios.

options.optionText: It is merely a formality; evaluators grade solely on class diagrams and whether interfaces are present, regardless of whether code runs.

It demonstrates working execution by orchestrating a realistic end-to-end user story, demonstrating that dependencies are wired cleanly, business invariants hold, and exceptions are handled without crashes.
It must contain automated unit tests with 90%+ code coverage using JUnit and Mockito rather than running procedural scenario scripts.
It should expose an interactive command-line REPL that reads user commands from System.in in an infinite loop, as hardcoded test scenarios are disqualified.

questions.questionText: When generalizing an N x N TicTacToe game to support an arbitrary number of players, why does the game engine enforce the strict constraint that the number of players must be at most N - 1?
questions.explanation: To win an N x N board, a player must fill an entire row, column, or diagonal of length N with their unique symbol. If there are N players and each makes one reasonable placement, every row, column, and diagonal will contain at least two different symbols, making a winning line of size N mathematically impossible and turning the game into a guaranteed stalemate. Restricting players to at most N - 1 preserves the possibility of victory. Option B is incorrect because N players take N moves, which is far fewer than the N^2 cells on the board; Option C misapplies the pigeonhole principle; Option D is false because turn order in sequential games is inherently asymmetric.

options.optionText: Having N or more players with distinct symbols guarantees that no single player can ever complete an unbroken line of length N across rows, columns, or diagonals, mathematically forcing every game into an unwinnable gridlock.
Allowing N players would guarantee an immediate draw after the first round because every cell would be occupied before anyone can take a second turn.
The pigeonhole principle dictates that with N players, at least one player will be starved of turns if the game ends in under N moves.
Game theory mandates N - 1 players so that every player has an equal number of turns regardless of who plays first.

questions.questionText: An engineer is implementing the Undo feature in TicTacToe. Two approaches are proposed: Approach 1 clones the entire Board object on every move and pushes it to a stack. Approach 2 pushes a Move object (containing the target Cell and the Player) onto a Deque<Move>. Why is Approach 2 architecturally superior?
questions.explanation: Storing full snapshots of an N x N grid on every turn consumes O(N^2) heap allocations per move, generating substantial GC pressure on large boards. Storing only the delta—a lightweight Move(cell, player) on a Deque<Move>—operates in O(1) time and memory. An undo simply pops the top Move, sets cell.setCellState(EMPTY), removes the player symbol, decrements the turn counter, and reverses the win-checker count maps. Option B is irrelevant as turn-based games are sequential; Option C is incorrect because equals() can be implemented for value equality; Option D misapplies LSP.

options.optionText: Approach 1 incurs O(N^2) memory allocation and garbage collection overhead per move, while Approach 2 operates in O(1) space per move and enables clean undo by simply clearing the cell and rolling back the player index.
Approach 2 allows the Undo command to be executed asynchronously across multiple thread pools.
Approach 1 breaks reference equality, causing equals() checks between board states and active GUI listeners to fail.
Approach 1 violates the Liskov Substitution Principle because Board is a mutable entity.

questions.questionText: In a naive N x N TicTacToe implementation, the game engine checks for a winner after each move by scanning all N rows, N columns, and 2 diagonals, resulting in O(N^2) checks per turn. How does an optimal design achieve O(1) time complexity for win-condition checking?
questions.explanation: Instead of re-scanning the entire grid, an optimized win checker maintains Map<Symbol, Integer> arrays for each row and column, plus two counters for the main and anti-diagonals. When player P places a symbol at (r, c), the engine simply increments rowCounts[r][P], colCounts[c][P], and (if applicable) diagCounts[P]. If any counter reaches N, player P wins. This evaluation takes O(1) operations independent of board size. Option B still performs O(N^2) work, just distributed; Option C is impossible because state space grows exponentially (3^(N^2)); Option D fails because 64-bit masks cannot represent boards larger than 8x8.

options.optionText: By maintaining count maps for each row, column, main diagonal, and anti-diagonal tracking symbol frequencies; after a move at (r, c), only the counters for row r, column c, and applicable diagonals are incremented and checked against N in O(1) time.
By running the board scan in a parallel Stream utilizing ForkJoinPool.
By pre-computing all possible winning board states in a static HashSet at application startup.
By using bitwise XOR masks on 64-bit Long integers, which natively works for boards of any size up to 100x100.

questions.questionText: When constructing the Game object in TicTacToe, which pattern and validation strategy should be used to guarantee that a game cannot be started in an invalid state?
questions.explanation: Game setup involves multiple interlocking constraints: board dimension must be valid, player count must match N - 1, each player must have a unique character symbol, and rules on bot participation must be enforced. A Builder pattern with a private Game constructor centralizes all validation inside build(). If any invariant fails, an InvalidGameException is thrown before the Game object is created. Option B allows invalid intermediate states; Option C prevents running multiple games; Option D delays validation until runtime during gameplay.

options.optionText: Use a GameBuilder whose build() method validates that board dimension N >= 3, player count equals N - 1, player symbols are unique, and at most one Bot player exists, before instantiating Game.
Use a Prototype pattern to clone a default game and mutate player symbols after game launch.
Use the Singleton pattern so only one Game instance exists in the JVM, validating state inside getInstance().
Allow the Game constructor to accept null parameters and validate players dynamically as they make their first move.

questions.questionText: A TicTacToe system needs to support Bot players with variable difficulty levels (e.g. EasyBot selects random available cells, MediumBot blocks opponent wins, HardBot uses minimax). How should bot decision-making be designed to satisfy the Open/Closed Principle?
questions.explanation: Decoupling move-generation algorithms from the Bot entity using the Strategy pattern allows new playing strategies (e.g. heuristic, minimax, Monte Carlo) to be added without modifying the Bot class or existing strategy code. Bot simply holds a BotPlayingStrategy reference and delegates makeMove() to it. Option A violates OCP by forcing modifications to Bot for every new algorithm; Option C tightly couples bot identity to inheritance; Option D misplaces gameplay logic inside a data cell.

options.optionText: Add an if-else chain inside Bot.makeMove() checking botDifficulty == EASY, MEDIUM, or HARD.
Define a BotPlayingStrategy interface with makeMove(Board board) and inject concrete implementations (EasyBotPlayingStrategy, HardBotPlayingStrategy) into Bot instances via Strategy pattern.
Subclass Bot into EasyBot, MediumBot, and HardBot, with each subclass overriding the private field cellState.
Use the Template Method pattern inside Cell to execute bot moves directly on the board.

questions.questionText: The product owner requests a custom game variant where, in addition to standard rows, columns, and diagonals, a player can also win by occupying all four corners of the board. How should the win-checking architecture be designed to accommodate this and future rule variations without modifying the core Game class?
questions.explanation: Applying the Strategy pattern to victory conditions isolates win-evaluation logic behind a WinningStrategy interface. The Game engine simply iterates over its configured List<WinningStrategy> after each move. Adding "Four Corners", "Diamond", or "Block" win rules requires authoring a new WinningStrategy implementation and registering it in the GameBuilder, without touching the Game loop or Board class. Option B violates OCP; Option C misapplies Adapter where no interface incompatibility exists; Option D duplicates game-loop orchestration code.

options.optionText: Define a WinningStrategy interface with checkWinner(Board board, Move move) and maintain a List<WinningStrategy> in Game, allowing RowWinningStrategy, ColWinningStrategy, and FourCornersWinningStrategy to be plugged in.
Hardcode a boolean checkFourCorners() method inside the Board class.
Use an Adapter pattern to adapt the Board class into a FourCornersBoard.
Subclass Game into FourCornersGame and override the entire play() game loop.

questions.questionText: In a layered backend design (Controller → Service → Repository), what is the Repository layer's job?
questions.explanation: A Repository's sole job is persistence (save/find/list). Resource-assignment logic (C) belongs in a Service using a Strategy, DTO conversion (B) belongs at the Controller boundary, and business-rule validation (D) belongs in the Service layer. Mixing any of these into the Repository breaks the separation the layered architecture exists to provide.

options.optionText: Saving and fetching data — nothing about business rules
Converting request DTOs into model objects
Deciding which resource (e.g. a parking spot) to assign to a request
Validating business rules, like rejecting an invalid input type

questions.explanation: Without a bound, `T` is erased to `Object`, and `Object` has no `getId()`/`setId()` methods, so the method body wouldn't compile. The bound is what gives the generic class compile-time access to `BaseModel`'s methods on every `T`. Option A is backwards (a bound narrows what `T` can be, it doesn't widen storage); C is false (unbounded generics are valid Java); D confuses compile-time type-checking with runtime performance.

options.optionText: It lets the repository store multiple unrelated types at once
Without it, `item.getId()` wouldn't compile, since plain `Object` has no `getId()` method
It is required syntax for all Java generic classes
It makes the compiled code run faster at execution time

questions.explanation: `nextId` starts at 1. `save(g1)` reads `nextId` (1), assigns it to `g1`, then post-increments `nextId` to 2. `save(g2)` reads `nextId` (2), assigns it to `g2`, then increments to 3. So `g1.getId()==1` and `g2.getId()==2`, printing `1, 2`.

The code is logically and syntactically fine (A, B, C are all false claims about this specific snippet); the real problem is architectural: storage lookup and business logic sit directly in the Controller, which should be a thin layer delegating to a Service and Repository.

options.optionText: The gate-type check compares against `GateType.EXIT` instead of `GateType.ENTRY`, which is a logic bug
`IssueTicketResponseDTO` is never returned, so this code doesn't compile
`InvalidGateException` needs to be declared in a `throws` clause for this to compile

`fetchGate()` is a storage lookup and `buildTicket()` contains real business logic (spot assignment, ticket creation), but both are implemented directly inside the Controller instead of a Repository/Service

questions.explanation: The validation lives in the Service, not the Controller, so every caller of `TicketService.issueTicket()` gets it for free. This is precisely why business logic belongs in the Service layer: it becomes a single enforced rule regardless of how many Controllers call into it.

options.optionText: Yes — because the check lives inside `TicketService`, any caller of the Service automatically gets the same validation, regardless of which Controller invoked it
No — the check lives in the Controller layer, so `AdminController` would need to reimplement it
No — validation only runs when a DTO object is passed in, and `AdminController` might use different DTOs
Yes, but only if `AdminController` also extends `TicketController`

questions.explanation: The filter keeps only `SUCCESS` payments, so only Payment1's 200 counts. `200 >= 500` is false, so the bill's status is untouched (the `if` block never runs) — it stays whatever it already was, not explicitly set to "unpaid."

options.optionText: totalPaid = 500; bill is marked PAID
totalPaid = 200; bill stays whatever it was before (not PAID)
totalPaid = 300; bill is marked PAID
totalPaid = 500; bill stays unpaid because one payment failed

questions.explanation: Without the `SUCCESS` filter, a `FAILED` payment's amount still gets summed, so a bill can cross the paid threshold and get marked `PAID` (freeing the spot) purely from failed payment attempts — a real correctness and revenue bug, not a compile error (A is false) or a doubling/undercounting bug (B, D are false).

options.optionText: It won't compile, since `mapToInt` requires an `IntStream` as its argument
It silently doubles the amount charged to the customer
A bill could be marked PAID (and its spot freed) even though an online payment attempt actually FAILED, since failed payments now count toward the total
Cash payments would stop being counted entirely

questions.questionText: In multithreaded code, what is a "critical section"?
questions.explanation: This is the standard definition: a critical section is the specific region of code touching shared mutable state that requires mutual exclusion. A, B, and C describe unrelated concepts (exception declarations, object construction, DTO mapping) with no inherent connection to concurrency.

options.optionText: Any method that is allowed to throw a checked exception
The part of a method that only constructs new objects (no shared state)
The part of a Controller responsible for converting a model into a response DTO
A piece of code, operating on shared data, that must never be executing simultaneously in more than one thread at a time

questions.explanation: This is the canonical check-then-act race condition: with no synchronization, both threads can read `EMPTY` before either writes `OCCUPIED`, so both pass the check and both return `true` — a double claim on one physical spot. The JVM provides no automatic blocking (B is false), writes don't "cancel out" (C is false), and no exception is thrown by this code (D is false).

options.optionText: Both threads see EMPTY at their read, and both proceed to set the status and return `true` — the spot gets "claimed" twice
Only one thread's `if` check passes; the JVM automatically blocks the second thread's read until the first thread finishes
The final status ends up back at EMPTY, since the two writes cancel out
A `ConcurrentModificationException` is thrown, and neither thread returns `true`

questions.explanation: A `synchronized` block only excludes threads that lock on the *same* object instance. Since `lock` is instantiated fresh inside the method on every call, two concurrent invocations each get their own private lock object and never actually contend — the synchronization is a no-op in practice. A is false (the lock object identity is exactly what matters); C is nonsensical; D is false (`synchronized` works with any object reference, no such requirement exists).

options.optionText: Yes — any `synchronized` block prevents concurrent access, regardless of which object is used as the lock
No — `lock` is a brand-new object on every call, so each thread synchronizes on a DIFFERENT object and never actually blocks the other
Yes, but only the first two times the method is called
No — this code fails to compile, since `synchronized` requires a `static final` lock object

questions.explanation: `final` only means the field reference can't be reassigned after construction; it says nothing about sharing across instances. Each `new SpotAllotter()` gets its own `lock` object, so two separate instances mean two separate locks — no mutual exclusion between them. A and B misunderstand what `final` and instance fields actually do; D is simply false (synchronized blocks work correctly with multiple threads when the lock object is genuinely shared).

options.optionText: Yes — `lock` is declared `final`, so it's automatically shared across all instances
Yes — Java merges fields with the same name across different instances of a class
No — each `SpotAllotter` instance has its own separate `lock` object, so two different instances mean two different locks that never block each other
No — `synchronized` blocks stop working once more than one thread is involved, regardless of instances

questions.questionText: A test is written to prove that two concurrent requests for the same single resource can't both succeed. Version 1 spins up two threads that both call a method on the exact same request object, just with two different thread names. Version 2 spins up two threads that call the method using two separate, independently-constructed request objects (e.g., two different `Gate` instances) representing two different real-world entry points, competing for the same one resource. Which version more faithfully proves that a real-world "two independent callers, one shared resource" bug is actually fixed?
questions.explanation: Real concurrent requests come from independent callers (different gates, different users) each with their own request object, not from one shared object accessed by two threads with different names. Version 2's use of two genuinely distinct `Gate` instances is what makes the test faithful to the actual production scenario; Version 1 tests something related but not identical. A and C invert this reasoning; B is false since object identity is exactly the variable that determines test fidelity here.

options.optionText: Version 1 — using the same object for both threads is closer to how concurrent requests actually arrive
Neither — thread names and object identity have no effect on whether a race condition is proven
Version 1 — it uses fewer objects, so it's a simpler and therefore stronger test
Version 2 — it recreates the real scenario of two distinct, independent callers competing for one resource, rather than one object being accessed by two threads in the abstract

questions.explanation: Locking per vehicle-type is the wrong granularity because one physical spot can be claimed under two different type keys (a spot supporting both CAR and TRUCK can be locked via either), so two threads requesting different types never contend for the same lock even though they're racing for the same underlying resource — reintroducing the exact double-claim bug locking was meant to fix. B, C, and D are all false claims about `ConcurrentHashMap`'s real, well-defined behavior.

options.optionText: The two threads lock on different `VehicleType` keys (CAR vs TRUCK), so they never block each other — both can read and claim the SAME physical spot object, causing a double assignment
`ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent` throws an exception when called concurrently from two threads
`getLockFor()` returns `null` the first time a new `VehicleType` is seen
The code fails to compile, since `Object` cannot be used as a `ConcurrentHashMap` value type

questions.explanation: Locking on `spot` itself means both threads contend for the same lock object; one acquires it first, sees `EMPTY`, claims it, and releases the lock. The second thread then acquires the lock, but by that point re-reads `status` as `OCCUPIED` (not stale), so it correctly returns `false`. This is exactly the correct, deterministic behavior a mutual-exclusion lock should guarantee — not a race (A), not a deadlock (`synchronized` blocks waiting threads, it doesn't deadlock two threads over one lock — C is false), and not JVM-dependent (D is false).

options.optionText: Both threads return `true`, since both read EMPTY before either one writes
Exactly one thread returns `true` and sets the status to OCCUPIED; the other thread enters the lock afterward, sees OCCUPIED (not its earlier assumption), and returns `false`
Both threads deadlock, since they both try to `synchronize` on `spot` at the same time
The result is undefined and could differ depending on the JVM version

This class's `tryClaim()` still calls `getLockFor(requestedType)`, so it still has Q14's exact double-claim bug, regardless of what was discussed elsewhere. A and B both wrongly treat a description as equivalent to an implementation; D misdiagnoses the bug (`ConcurrentHashMap` itself is thread-safe — the bug is lock granularity, not the map's thread-safety).

options.optionText: Yes — since a correct version has been described elsewhere, the bug is effectively already fixed
Yes — per-vehicle-type locking is safe as long as `ConcurrentHashMap` is used

No — the class shown here still uses the flawed per-vehicle-type locking strategy in its actual code; describing a correct fix elsewhere doesn't change what this class does at runtime, so the fix still needs to be implemented and verified with a real concurrency test on this class
No — the real problem is that `ConcurrentHashMap` isn't thread-safe for this use case

questions.questionText: In a movie ticketing system like BookMyShow, physical seats in an auditorium (e.g., Row A, Seat 12) have a SeatType (SILVER, GOLD, RECLINER). Why does a well-designed domain model separate Seat from ShowSeat instead of storing the availability status directly on the Seat entity?
questions.explanation: An auditorium's physical seating topology (Seat) rarely changes: rows, numbers, and physical chair configurations are constant. However, seat availability, lock states, and pricing vary for every distinct Show (e.g. weekend vs weekday rates). Mutating status directly on Seat would corrupt availability across concurrent or future shows in the same auditorium. ShowSeat acts as the temporal associative entity binding a specific Show to a Seat with dynamic state (AVAILABLE, LOCKED, BOOKED). While Option D points out the exact real-world collision defect, Option A provides the complete architectural definition. Option B confuses screens with shows; Option C incorrectly claims table-level locking is required.

options.optionText: Physical seats are layout templates that remain immutable across shows, whereas availability and pricing are ephemeral and show-specific; ShowSeat is an associative projection binding Seat, Show, pricing, and dynamic status (AVAILABLE, LOCKED, BOOKED).

Physical Seat entities represent immutable theater infrastructure, whereas availability changes per show; embedding status in Seat would prevent the venue from running concurrent shows across different screens.
Updating availability directly on Seat would require taking a table-level write lock on the entire auditorium layout during peak booking hours.

Storing availability directly on Seat would mean updating the status for a 6:00 PM show would overwrite and corrupt the availability status for the 9:00 PM show scheduled in the same auditorium on the same date.

questions.questionText: During a flash sale for a blockbuster movie, thousands of users select the same seats simultaneously. The system introduces a SeatLock mechanism. Why is a time-bounded temporary SeatLock placed before initiating payment, rather than directly updating ShowSeat to BOOKED inside a long database transaction?
questions.explanation: A cardinal rule of high-scale transaction design is never to hold open database transactions or database locks across external network calls. Payment authorization takes anywhere from 30 seconds to several minutes while a customer enters OTPs or scans UPI codes. Holding DB row locks for that duration would immediately exhaust the database connection pool, starving the entire platform. A SeatLock provides a lightweight, time-bounded lease (e.g. 5–10 minutes) verified by the application service, releasing DB connections immediately. Option B is incorrect because read queries do not block on uncommitted locks under read-committed isolation; Option C misapplies 2PC where asynchronous callbacks are standard; Option D identifies an operational headache but misses the fatal connection-exhaustion outage.

options.optionText: Payment gateway processing involves asynchronous network round-trips taking several minutes; holding an open database transaction with pessimistic row locks across external HTTP payment calls exhausts connection pools and causes cascading outages.
Updating ShowSeat to BOOKED immediately would prevent other users from viewing the real-time seating map until the first user completes checkout.
Marking seats BOOKED early requires implementing a two-phase commit (2PC) protocol across the database and third-party bank APIs, which causes frequent distributed deadlocks.
Directly setting status to BOOKED risks phantom inventory loss if the user's browser crashes, as uncompleted bookings cannot be distinguished from confirmed reservations without manual audits.

questions.questionText: A customer attempts to reserve four adjacent seats (A1, A2, A3, A4). When the SeatLockService attempts to acquire locks, it successfully locks A1, A2, and A3, but discovers that A4 was locked by another user 50 milliseconds earlier. What is the required behavior of the lock manager?
questions.explanation: Batch resource acquisition must strictly guarantee atomicity. If a multi-seat reservation cannot acquire every requested seat, any partially acquired locks must be immediately and cleanly released. Holding partial locks causes severe resource starvation, bad customer experience (being forced to purchase disjoint subsets), and potential deadlocks if another user contends for the reverse subset. Option B and D force partial reservations onto customers unexpectedly; Option C blocks HTTP worker threads, leading to thread exhaustion.

options.optionText: Lock acquisition must be all-or-nothing: the service must release the locks on A1, A2, and A3 immediately and throw a SeatUnavailableException to prevent partial reservations and deadlocks.
Retain locks on A1, A2, and A3 and prompt the user to pay for three tickets while waiting for A4 to unlock.
Place the customer in a synchronized queue waiting on A4's monitor lock, blocking the request thread until A4 is released.
Commit the reservation for A1, A2, and A3, and return a partial booking response so the customer can proceed to pay for the three seats.

questions.questionText: When using an in-memory lock store backed by ConcurrentHashMap<String, SeatLock>, why is a background cleanup daemon using ScheduledExecutorService necessary?
questions.explanation: In-memory data structures lack the native Time-To-Live (TTL) expiration mechanisms provided by distributed caches like Redis. If a user reserves seats and abandons the browser tab, the lock remains in the map. Without a periodic eviction process (such as a ScheduledExecutorService sweeping expired locks every 30 seconds), orphaned locks would permanently render those seats unavailable to all other customers. While Options B, C, and D are valid contributing factors, Option A identifies the primary functional necessity.

options.optionText: If a user closes their browser tab or crashes after acquiring a lock without completing payment, the orphaned lock would block that seat indefinitely unless periodically purged upon expiration.
ConcurrentHashMap memory scales with entry count; without eviction, old completed locks accumulate until the JVM runs out of heap space (OutOfMemoryError).
A passive expiration check during subsequent lock acquisitions is insufficient because unpopular movie shows with zero subsequent traffic would leave expired locks in memory indefinitely.
Relying on client-side JavaScript unload beacons to release locks fails whenever users experience sudden browser crashes, operating system reboots, or network disconnects.

questions.questionText: In the Booking finite state machine, a Booking moves from PENDING to CONFIRMED upon successful payment. Consider the edge case where a payment authorization succeeds at the bank, but the webhook delivery is delayed by network lag and arrives 2 minutes after the seat lock TTL expired (and the seats were released to another user). How must PaymentService handle this webhook?
questions.explanation: Late payment callbacks following lock expiration are a critical production failure mode in ticketing and inventory systems. If seats have been reclaimed or re-booked, the system must never forcibly double-allocate the inventory. Instead, detecting that the associated Booking is already EXPIRED must trigger a compensating transaction: recording the late payment, logging the anomaly, and scheduling an automatic refund to the customer. Option B creates manual review overhead and compromises seat allocation integrity; Option C abandons the user in limbo; Option D silently drops revenue reconciliation, leading to untracked customer credit card charges.

options.optionText: The service must observe that the Booking transitioned to EXPIRED, reject the confirmation, and trigger an automated compensatory refund workflow rather than creating an illegal double-booking.
Reopen the seat lock retroactively and mark the second booking as pending review in an administrative dashboard.
Acknowledge the webhook with HTTP 200 OK and record the payment against the user's account without allocating seats, requiring manual customer support intervention.
Attempt an optimistic lock update on the ShowSeat row; if the update fails due to a version mismatch, silently ignore the webhook callback.

questions.questionText: A payment aggregator experiences transient network timeouts and retries sending the payment webhook callback three times for the same successful transaction. How must the booking system defend against issuing duplicate tickets or corrupted states?
questions.explanation: Payment webhooks are distributed network events that adhere to "at-least-once" delivery semantics, making retries inevitable. The receiver must implement idempotency: storing the unique payment transaction reference or idempotency key in a transaction repository. If a subsequent webhook arrives with an already-processed key, the handler skips side-effects (ticket generation, inventory updates) and immediately acknowledges with HTTP 200 OK. Option B is ineffective because legitimate retries can arrive after the throttle window; Option C fails across distributed multi-pod deployments; Option D risks updating timestamps without verifying idempotency against specific payment references.

options.optionText: Enforce webhook idempotency by inspecting an idempotencyKey or payment transaction ID: if the transaction is already recorded as SUCCESS, return an immediate HTTP 200 OK without re-executing booking confirmation logic.
Rely on the payment gateway's rate limiter to throttle duplicate webhook deliveries within a 60-second sliding window.
Synchronize the entire webhook controller method using synchronized (this), serializing incoming webhook traffic across all server instances.
Check whether a ticket already exists for the show; if so, update the ticket's updatedAt timestamp and return HTTP 200 OK.

questions.questionText: In Splitwise, an Expense entity models a financial transaction across users. Why does Expense decompose into a collection of fine-grained Split entities rather than directly updating user account balances during expense creation?
questions.explanation: Financial systems require strict auditability, reversibility, and mathematical verification. An Expense decomposes into Split objects (each representing one user's exact owed portion) so the system can validate the fundamental invariant: totalAmount == sum(splits). Direct mutations without an itemized split ledger prevent auditability, error rollback, expense editing, and verification. Option B highlights transaction risks but misses the domain audit requirement; Option C treats ledger history as an afterthought; Option D promotes an unnormalized schema anti-pattern.

options.optionText: Decomposing an expense into Split records creates an immutable audit trail and isolates the core domain invariant: the sum of individual split amounts must equal the total expense amount down to the exact cent.
Directly updating mutable balance fields on User objects avoids allocating temporary objects, but leaves no transactional record if a later operation in the batch fails.
Maintaining split records is only necessary when generating monthly PDF statements; real-time expense creation can simply update a single shared net balance map.
Storing individual Split objects causes excessive relational join overhead that degrades query performance compared to storing an aggregated balance string on the group record.

questions.questionText: A developer uses double or float data types for monetary balances in Splitwise. After several hundred split operations, users notice balances like $33.000000000000004 or off-by-a-penny errors in their balances. What is the fundamental technical reason for this bug, and what is the standard fix?
questions.explanation: IEEE-754 floating point numbers represent values in binary fractions. Common decimal fractions like 0.1 or 0.01 have repeating binary representations, causing silent precision loss during repeated additions and subtractions. In financial domains, all monetary calculations must use BigDecimal with explicit scale (typically 2 decimal places) and an explicit rounding mode (such as RoundingMode.HALF_UP) to preserve mathematical exactness. Option B is incorrect because overflow to Infinity requires values exceeding 10^308; Option C describes a valid alternative architecture (integer cents) but misidentifies the root cause of floating point imprecision; Option D confuses rounding modes with binary representation error.

options.optionText: Binary floating-point types (IEEE-754) cannot represent base-10 fractions (like 0.1) exactly, accumulating rounding errors; financial ledgers must use BigDecimal with an explicit scale and RoundingMode.
The double data type has an insufficient dynamic range and overflows to Infinity when calculating cumulative balances across multiple months.
The balance calculation should be performed using integer arithmetic representing total cents (long cents), but developers mistakenly cast intermediate division steps back to double.
The issue occurs because the standard Java Math.round() method always rounds toward positive infinity rather than utilizing bankers rounding (HALF_EVEN).

questions.questionText: When splitting a $100.00 restaurant bill equally among three friends using EqualSplitStrategy, dividing 100.00 by 3 yields 33.3333... per person. Truncating to 2 decimal places yields $33.33 each, leaving an unallocated $0.01 remainder. How does a production EqualSplitStrategy handle this remainder to preserve monetary conservation?
questions.explanation: In financial ledgers, the invariant sum(splits) == totalAmount is non-negotiable; money cannot be created or destroyed by division. For uneven divisions (e.g. $100 among 3 users = $33.33, $33.33, $33.33 + $0.01 remainder), production implementations deterministically allocate the remainder cent to either the payer or the first participant (yielding $33.34, $33.33, $33.33). Option B violates monetary conservation; Option C prevents standard equal splits; Option D arbitrarily inflates the debt beyond the total expense.

options.optionText: The strategy deterministically allocates the remainder penny to the paying user (or the first participant), ensuring that sum(splits) == totalAmount strictly holds.
The strategy discards the remaining cent as unrecoverable rounding loss.
The strategy throws an ArithmeticException and rejects the entire expense.
The strategy charges an extra penny to all three users to round up to $100.02.

questions.questionText: In PercentageSplitStrategy, participants specify percentage shares (e.g. User A: 40%, User B: 30%, User C: 30%). What validation invariant must execute before computing individual split amounts, and how are rounding discrepancies resolved?
questions.explanation: Percentage splits require two levels of validation: first, the input percentage shares must sum to exactly 100.00% (throwing InvalidExpenseException otherwise). Second, because percentage multiplication on arbitrary totals can produce fractional cents (e.g. $73.50 * 33.33%), individual rounded amounts can sum to $73.49 or $73.51. The strategy calculates delta = totalAmount - sum(computedSplits) and applies delta to the last participant, preserving exact mathematical equality. Option B is an arbitrary business restriction not found in accounting standards; Option C violates exact settlement precision; Option D silently masks invalid user input.

options.optionText: Validate that the sum of all percentages equals exactly 100.00%; when multiplying percentages yields fractional cents, adjust the final participant's split by the rounding delta so the total matches exactly.
Validate that no single participant's share exceeds 50.00% to prevent unilateral veto power in group expense settlements.
Truncate all calculated participant shares to whole integer dollar amounts, accumulating unallocated fractions into a group tip jar.
Automatically scale each participant's entered percentage proportionately so they sum to 100%, without alerting the user to the invalid input.

questions.questionText: In a shared apartment with 5 roommates, dozens of pairwise expenses are recorded. If balances are maintained solely as a directed pairwise graph (e.g. A owes B $10, B owes C $15, C owes A $20), what problem arises as the number of transactions grows, and how does Net Balance calculation resolve it?
questions.explanation: Direct pairwise ledgers create complex networks of mutual obligations (O(N^2) edges) with redundant cycles (e.g., A owes B, B owes C, C owes A). When roommates want to settle up, tracking and executing dozens of peer-to-peer payments is chaotic. Calculating individual net balances (NetBalance = TotalPaid - TotalOwed) decouples users from the specific historical web of transactions, reducing the problem to a simple bipartite matching of net debtors and net creditors. Option B confuses graph data structures with object reference loops; Option C states a social trade-off rather than an architectural mechanism; Option D overstates database transaction overhead.

options.optionText: Pairwise graphs become dense and contain redundant circular debt chains; computing each user's Net Balance (TotalPaid - TotalOwed) collapses mutual obligations into a single scalar value per user, identifying net creditors and net debtors.
Pairwise graphs cannot be serialized to JSON because circular payment references cause infinite recursion errors in REST controllers.
Net balance calculation obscures the original bilateral trust relationships, forcing users to pay people they may not know or interact with directly.
Maintaining pairwise ledgers requires executing O(N) distributed database transactions whenever a single user leaves a group.

questions.questionText: How does the greedy Two-Heap (PriorityQueue) Debt Simplification algorithm minimize cash-flow transactions across a group of users?
questions.explanation: The classic cash-flow minimization problem is solved using a greedy two-heap approach. Debtor nodes are stored in a max-heap based on magnitude of debt, and creditor nodes in a max-heap based on credit. At each iteration, the largest debtor pays the largest creditor min(debt, credit). At least one party is completely settled and eliminated from their heap, while the other party's reduced balance is re-inserted if non-zero. This reduces an O(N^2) tangle of transactions to at most N - 1 optimal settlement payments. Option B eliminates cycles but does not minimize non-cyclic transaction counts; Option C is unnecessarily complex and typically used for currency arbitrage; Option D introduces a central bottle-neck and counterparty credit risk.

options.optionText: Maintain a max-heap of debtors (ordered by absolute debt) and a max-heap of creditors (ordered by credit); iteratively match the largest debtor with the largest creditor for min(debt, credit), completely settling at least one party per step in at most N - 1 transactions.
Perform depth-first search (DFS) cycle cancellation on the pairwise graph, eliminating all circular paths until the graph is a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG).
Model the debt network as a min-cost max-flow problem and execute the Bellman-Ford algorithm to compute global equilibrium.
Have every debtor send their owed balance directly to the group creator, who then redistributes the funds to creditors in separate payments.

questions.questionText: In the Hotel Management System machine-coding lab, the architecture is layered into Controller, Service, and Repository. What is the explicit responsibility boundary of the Controller layer?
questions.explanation: In layered architectures, the Controller is strictly an entry adapter: it handles transport-level concerns, converts incoming payloads into request DTOs, performs basic parameter validation, and invokes the appropriate domain service method. It must never contain business logic (pricing, date validation) or direct persistence storage access. Option B belongs to Repository; Option C belongs to Service; Option D belongs to transaction management / service boundaries.

options.optionText: Translating external request payloads into internal DTOs, validating request syntax, delegating business orchestration to the Service, and formatting response DTOs or HTTP status codes.
Executing database queries and holding ConcurrentHashMap storage instances directly.
Calculating room pricing multipliers and mutating room availability flags.
Managing database transaction commit and rollback routines.

questions.questionText: When modeling the Room entity in a Hotel Management System, why should a Room have an immutable base RoomType (e.g. DELUXE, SUITE) and base price, while booking date intervals are maintained in a separate Reservation entity?
questions.explanation: A Room is a physical inventory asset with fixed attributes (room number, floor, room type). Booking a room is a temporal event valid over an interval [checkIn, checkOut]. If Room stored checkIn and checkOut directly, it could only hold one reservation at a time, making it impossible to book the room for future dates. Decoupling Reservation into a separate entity linking Room, Customer, and DateRange allows a room to have many non-overlapping reservations over time. Options B, C, and D describe practical complications, but Option A identifies the core domain modeling failure.

options.optionText: Rooms represent persistent physical assets, while reservations represent temporal customer agreements; storing booking dates on Room would prevent multiple bookings across different non-overlapping date ranges.
Adding booking dates to Room violates the Single Responsibility Principle by forcing physical maintenance schedules and customer reservations to share the same fields.
It would require adding a new column to the Room database table for every prospective booking, causing schema instability.
Directly mutating booking dates on Room creates write contention on the Room row, preventing concurrent search queries on adjacent dates.

questions.questionText: The Hotel Management System lab progresses across four incremental stages (Stage 1: Room Inventory CRUD, Stage 2: Availability Search & Filtering, Stage 3: Date-Range Booking, Stage 4: Checkout & Bill Generation). Why is building incrementally in this sequence critical for machine coding success?
questions.explanation: Machine coding interviewers intentionally structure requirements in incremental stages to observe how a candidate models foundations. Starting with core entity CRUD (Stage 1) establishes clean repositories and controllers; adding search (Stage 2) tests query filters; adding reservations (Stage 3) introduces stateful domain invariants; adding billing (Stage 4) tests extensibility. Each stage produces a runnable milestone. Option B is technically meaningless for Java compilation; Option C inverts natural domain dependencies; Option D describes the consequence of failing to work incrementally, but Option A captures the primary benefit.

options.optionText: Each stage builds directly on the clean domain contracts of prior stages, ensuring that a working, testable application exists at every checkpoint while managing cognitive load.
Writing all four stages in parallel allows the compiler to optimize cross-package method calls more effectively.
Designing billing logic before inventory modeling ensures financial constraints dictate the entity relationships.
Attempting to build billing and search before core room management creates ungrounded abstractions that must be heavily refactored once domain constraints become clear.

questions.questionText: When validating whether a Room is available for a requested date range [reqCheckIn, reqCheckOut], an engineer checks against existing reservations [resCheckIn, resCheckOut]. What is the exact mathematical condition indicating an illegal overlapping booking?
questions.explanation: Two continuous intervals [A, B] and [C, D] overlap if and only if A < D and B > C. In booking domains, a requested range overlaps with an existing reservation whenever the requested check-in is before the existing check-out, and the requested check-out is after the existing check-in. Option B only detects identical intervals (failing on partial overlaps); Option C is the condition for NON-overlapping intervals; Option D ignores the start dates entirely.

options.optionText: reqCheckIn < resCheckOut && reqCheckOut > resCheckIn
reqCheckIn.equals(resCheckIn) && reqCheckOut.equals(resCheckOut)
reqCheckIn >= resCheckOut || reqCheckOut <= resCheckIn
reqCheckOut.isAfter(resCheckOut)

questions.questionText: In the booking service, when a customer attempts to book an already-occupied room, a candidate considers returning null from bookRoom() and letting the Controller check for null. Why is throwing a custom domain exception (e.g., RoomNotAvailableException) superior?
questions.explanation: Returning null for domain failures is an anti-pattern: it leaves callers guessing why an operation failed (was the room non-existent, already booked, or did a database error occur?) and frequently causes NullPointerExceptions downstream. Strongly-typed domain exceptions (RoomNotAvailableException, InvalidDateRangeException) encapsulate error context and enable global exception handlers (or controllers) to return structured error messages and appropriate HTTP status codes (e.g. 409 Conflict). Option B is false because Optional does not force serialization; Option C is incorrect because transactions only rollback on exceptions; Option D describes boolean returns rather than null returns.

options.optionText: Returning null creates an ambiguous contract that easily causes NullPointerExceptions if callers forget null checks, whereas typed domain exceptions force explicit handling, carry structured error details (conflicting dates), and map cleanly to HTTP 409 Conflict.
Returning null forces the method signature to return Optional<Room>, which imposes serialization overhead in REST controllers.
Returning null triggers an automatic rollback of the entire database transaction even if the error is caught by an enclosing try-catch block.
Returning a boolean flag (e.g. false) requires passing mutable output parameters to retrieve failure reasons, cluttering method signatures.

questions.questionText: A hotel booking engine must calculate room prices dynamically based on room type, seasonal peak surcharges, and customer loyalty tier discounts. How should this calculation be designed to prevent bloating BookingService with nested if-else logic?
questions.explanation: Applying the Strategy pattern decouples price calculation formulas from the BookingService. The service simply delegates price computation to an injected PricingStrategy. New promotional campaigns, holiday multipliers, or loyalty discount algorithms can be introduced by creating new strategy implementations without altering existing reservation logic. Option B introduces security risks and execution overhead; Option C violates OCP and pollutes entity models; Option D misapplies the State pattern to a calculation algorithm.

options.optionText: Define a PricingStrategy interface with calculatePrice(Room room, LocalDate checkIn, LocalDate checkOut, User user) and inject concrete strategies (StandardPricingStrategy, SurgePricingStrategy, LoyaltyPricingStrategy) via Strategy pattern.
Store dynamic pricing scripts as JavaScript strings in a database column and execute them using Java Nashorn.
Hardcode all pricing percentages as static final integers inside the Room domain entity.
Use the State pattern where every price change requires transitioning the Hotel into a new State object.

questions.questionText: An enterprise PaymentProcessingService directly instantiates StripeClient via new StripeClient(apiKey) inside its constructor. When writing unit tests and onboarding a secondary provider (AdyenClient), the engineering team faces tight coupling and an inability to run fast, hermetic mock tests in CI without live network calls. How does Spring's Inversion of Control (IoC) container and dependency injection resolve this architectural rigidity?
questions.explanation: Inversion of Control delegates dependency creation and lifecycle management to the container. By programming to an interface (PaymentGateway) and receiving it via constructor injection, PaymentProcessingService is decoupled from concrete vendor implementations. In production, Spring injects the configured vendor bean; in unit tests, test suites can pass mockito mocks or fake implementations directly without booting Spring or touching network sockets. Option B confuses dependency injection with mock proxying; Option C relies on brittle low-level network interception rather than clean polymorphism; Option D uses mutable global state, which introduces severe multi-threading test pollution.

options.optionText: It replaces concrete instantiation by having PaymentProcessingService declare a dependency on a generic PaymentGateway interface injected via its constructor, allowing Spring to inject production beans at runtime and lightweight test stubs in unit tests.
It automatically wraps StripeClient in a bytecode proxy that intercepts HTTP calls and redirects them to a local SQLite database during Maven test goals.
It configures an aspect-oriented programming (AOP) pointcut on all outgoing socket connections to automatically redirect traffic to wiremock stubs.
It forces PaymentProcessingService to declare its client fields as public static so unit tests can overwrite the reference prior to each test case.

questions.questionText: A senior architect mandates removing all @Autowired annotations from private fields across the microservices codebase in favor of constructor injection with private final fields. What primary engineering benefits justify this architectural mandate?
questions.explanation: Constructor injection ensures that an object cannot be constructed in an invalid or partially initialized state, allows fields to be marked final for thread-safety and immutability, and makes required dependencies explicit in the public API. Crucially, it allows plain unit tests to instantiate the class with mock dependencies via new MyService(mockRepo) without requiring slow reflection or Spring context bootstrapping. Option B describes fabricated runtime errors; Option C and D identify real drawbacks of field injection, but Option A synthesizes the complete architectural justification.

options.optionText: Constructor injection enforces immutability, guarantees that dependencies cannot be null after instantiation, prevents partial initialization bugs, and allows clean unit testing without needing reflection or Spring's test runner.
Field injection bypasses security manager permissions, causing ClassCircularityError exceptions in containerized Linux deployments.
Field injection hides dependencies, making it easy for a class to accumulate too many responsibilities without violating visible constructor parameter thresholds.
Field injection prevents fields from being declared final, leaving dependencies mutable post-construction and allowing reflection-based re-assignment.

questions.questionText: A trading platform service requires a pre-computed cache of currency exchange matrices loaded from an external treasury vault service at startup before the application starts accepting HTTP traffic. If the vault is unreachable or returns invalid matrices, the microservice must fail to start and crash immediately. Which Spring bean lifecycle mechanism is most appropriate to implement this startup validation and initialization?
questions.explanation: The @PostConstruct annotation (or InitializingBean) defines initialization logic that runs immediately after the container has injected all required dependencies and configured the bean, but before the application publishes endpoints or processes requests. Throwing an exception here halts the ApplicationContext startup, preventing traffic from reaching an unready service (fail-fast principle). Option B logs errors without failing fast, allowing invalid instances to serve traffic; Option C introduces a race window where requests encounter uninitialized state; Option D runs before Spring injects configuration properties, preventing dynamic credential injection.

options.optionText: Annotate an initialization method with @PostConstruct (or implement InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet()), which executes after all dependencies are injected but before the bean is exposed to requests, throwing an exception to abort application context startup.
Inject an ApplicationListener<ContextRefreshedEvent> bean, but catch and log all vault exceptions to allow partial boot.
Use a @Scheduled(fixedDelay = 60000) background task that polls the vault every minute, leaving matrices null until the first run completes.
Place the vault loading logic inside a static initializer block (static { ... }) on the service class so it runs during classloading.

questions.questionText: An e-commerce service integrates with Twilio for SMS notifications in production and staging, but developers running the system locally in Docker or minikube need a lightweight LoggingNotificationService that prints messages to stdout without hitting paid third-party APIs. How should Spring's configuration classes be structured to cleanly swap these beans based on configuration?
questions.explanation: Spring Boot's @ConditionalOnProperty allows bean registration to be conditional on externalized configuration properties (application.yml or environment variables). By combining havingValue and matchIfMissing = true, the application defaults to the lightweight mock for local runs while switching to the production implementation when the property is set. Option B introduces tight coupling and violates open-closed principles; Option C leads to ConflictingBeanDefinitionException because two @Primary beans cannot coexist; Option D works but is coarse-grained and less flexible than feature-specific property flags.

options.optionText: Define two @Bean methods in a @Configuration class, decorating TwilioNotificationService with @ConditionalOnProperty(name = "notification.provider", havingValue = "twilio") and the fallback with @ConditionalOnProperty(name = "notification.provider", havingValue = "mock", matchIfMissing = true).
Use an if/else block inside every service class that checks System.getProperty("ENV") before instantiating the HTTP client.
Annotate both beans with @Primary, relying on bean definition override settings in application.properties to select the active bean.
Use Spring profiles (@Profile("production") vs @Profile("local")), though this tightly couples bean presence to entire environment profiles rather than feature-specific configuration flags.

questions.questionText: A developer implements an InvoiceExportTask annotated with @Scope("prototype") because it holds mutable customer export state and a counter. They inject this prototype bean directly via @Autowired into a standard @Service bean (which uses the default singleton scope).
