**Deeper:** It is a good fit for configured policies, validators and callbacks. Prefer a plain function or closure when there is no meaningful state, and document hidden state when there is. In FastAPI, callable class instances are a common way to build parameterised dependencies, for example a rate limiter configured once and used in `Depends(limiter)`.

options.optionText: __call__; risk is that readers may assume it's a plain function and be confused it carries hidden state — use only when the object genuinely represents "a function with memory"
__init__; no risk, it's always safe
__getattr__; no meaningful risk
__new__; risk of infinite recursion

questions.questionText: A class defines __contains__ for membership tests (x in obj). Which best describes when Python calls it?
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (d)** Python rewrites `x in obj` to `type(obj).__contains__(obj, x)`, so defining the method is enough and callers never invoke it by name.

- (a) the operator exists to hide the call
- (b) in works with any class that defines __contains__, __iter__ or __getitem__
- (c) the operator is not limited to loops

**Deeper:** Without `__contains__` Python falls back to iterating via `__iter__` and then to the legacy `__getitem__` protocol, so membership is still linear unless you provide a faster implementation. For a large collection, back `__contains__` with a set or dict so membership is constant time.

options.optionText: Only when explicitly invoked as obj.__contains__(x)
Never — in only works on built-in types
Only inside for loops
Automatically, whenever the in operator is used on an instance of that class

questions.questionText: Which of these is the most accurate summary of the "one rule" for deciding whether to add a dunder method to a class?
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (c)** Dunders exist so objects can take part in Python's existing vocabulary. Add one when a caller needs that syntax, not by default.

- (a) more dunders mean more contracts to honour and test
- (b) hashability is only one reason; len, in, with and == are others
- (d) dunders and regular methods mix freely

**Deeper:** Every dunder is a promise: `__eq__` implies `__hash__` consistency, `__len__` affects truthiness, `__iter__` must be repeatable. Unneeded dunders create surprises that reviewers must audit. A quick review test: for each dunder you add, name the call site in the codebase that needs it, and add a test that exercises the syntax rather than the method name.

options.optionText: Add as many dunders as possible to make the class feel powerful
Only add dunders if the class will be used in a set or dict
Add a dunder only when a real caller needs the object to speak Python's existing language (len, in, ==, with) — don't wire buttons nobody presses or create surprising behavior behind familiar syntax
Dunders should only be added to classes without any regular methods

questions.questionText: Uber's Driver class originally has no custom dunders. A dispatcher writes d1 = Driver("Ramesh", 4.8, driver_id="D101") and d2 = Driver("Ramesh", 4.8, driver_id="D101") — two separately-loaded copies of the same real driver record. Without any __eq__ defined, what does d1 == d2 evaluate to, and why?
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (d)** `object.__eq__` compares identity, so two separately created `Driver` objects are different objects and `d1 == d2` is `False`.

- (a) Python does not compare attributes without dataclass-style generation
- (b) driver_id is only an ordinary attribute until you use it in __eq__
- (c) equality is defined for every object by default

**Deeper:** Use `@dataclass` (`eq=True` by default) or write `__eq__` and `__hash__` over the identity fields when separately loaded copies of the same record should be interchangeable. Interviewers often follow up with: and what happens to the hash? Without `__eq__` the identity hash is still consistent, so adding `__eq__` is exactly when the trouble starts.

options.optionText: True — Python compares all attributes by default
True — because driver_id matches
Raises TypeError — objects can't be compared without __eq__
False — the default __eq__ is an identity check (same object in memory), not a content check

questions.questionText: After adding def __eq__(self, other): return self.driver_id == other.driver_id to Driver (with no hash defined), a dispatch engineer runs online_drivers = {d1, d2}. What happens, and why?
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (b)** Defining `__eq__` in the class body without `__hash__` sets `__hash__` to `None`, so building the set raises `TypeError: unhashable type: 'Driver'`.

- (a) Python never invents a hash from equality
- (c) the set cannot be built at all, so there are no entries
- (d) the error is about hashing, not about attributes

**Deeper:** Fix by adding `__hash__ = lambda self: hash(self.driver_id)` (as a method), over fields that never change while the object is in a set. A subtle follow-up is that a subclass inherits the `None` hash too, so a hashable base plus an `__eq__` override in a subclass quietly makes the subclass unhashable.

options.optionText: Works fine — Python auto-generates a matching __hash__ from __eq__
TypeError: unhashable type — defining __eq__ sets __hash__ to None automatically, since a hash based on identity would now contradict content-based equality
Silently creates two separate entries in the set
AttributeError — sets require a driver_id attribute

questions.questionText: A class defines only __repr__, no __str__. A developer runs print(some_object). What is printed?
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (c)** The default `__str__` calls `__repr__`, so `print` shows the `__repr__` text.

- (a) the default address is the object.__repr__ fallback, used only when you did not define repr
- (b) print works with any object through str()
- (d) the default is never an empty string

**Deeper:** That fallback is one-directional, so always implement `__repr__` and add `__str__` only when users need a different presentation. Logging frameworks and exception messages typically format with `%r` or `!r`, so a clear repr turns "object at 0x7f..." lines into debuggable output.

options.optionText: The default memory address, ignoring __repr__
TypeError — print() requires __str__
The __repr__ output — __str__'s default implementation falls back to calling __repr__
An empty string

questions.questionText: Inside a with TripTimer(trip) as t: block, a ValueError is raised (not the TripCancelledError that __exit__ explicitly checks for and returns True on). What happens?
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (d)** `__exit__` always runs, so cleanup and logging happen. Because the exception is not the one it handles, it returns a falsy value and the `ValueError` propagates.

- (a) __exit__ is invoked for every exception type
- (b) only TripCancelledError is swallowed
- (c) execution does not skip errors; it leaves the block via the exception

**Deeper:** Make suppression explicit and narrow (`return exc_type is TripCancelledError`) and log what you swallow so the behaviour is auditable. You can verify the order of events by printing from `__enter__` and `__exit__` and raising inside the block; the log shows begin, exit, then the traceback.

options.optionText: __exit__ never runs since the exception isn't the one it checks for
The ValueError is silently swallowed just like TripCancelledError
Python skips straight to the next line after the with block, ignoring the error entirely
__exit__ runs (cleanup/logging happens), returns False since the type doesn't match, and the ValueError propagates normally after cleanup

questions.questionText: A SurgePricing class is configured once via __init__(multiplier, base_fare) and defines __call__(self, distance). A developer then writes surge = SurgePricing(15, 50) followed by fare = surge(4.2). What allows surge(4.2) to work syntactically, and what's the main benefit over a plain function calculate_surge(distance, multiplier, base_fare)?
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (b)** `__call__` enables the call syntax, and the benefit is that configuration lives on the instance, so each call receives only the argument that varies.

- (a) it is not inherently faster than a function
- (c) __init__ runs once, when the object is created
- (d) objects with __call__ are callable

**Deeper:** This is the "function with memory" pattern. It composes well with `map`, sorting keys and framework hooks, but prefer a closure or `functools.partial` when a function is clearer. In an interview, mention that `functools.partial` and closures achieve the same effect with less ceremony when no other methods or inspection are needed.

options.optionText: __call__ button; benefit is it's always faster than a function
__call__ button; benefit is the object remembers configuration (multiplier, base_fare) across calls, so each call only needs what actually varies
__init__ is called again each time; no real benefit over a function
This is invalid syntax — objects cannot be called like functions in Python

questions.questionText:
```python
class Bad:
    def __init__(self, k): self.k = k
    def __eq__(self, o): return self.k == o.k
    def __hash__(self): return hash(self.k)

b = Bad(1)
s = {b}
b.k = 2
print(b in s, Bad(2) in s, len(s))
```
What is printed?
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (b)** The object was stored in the bucket for `hash(1)`. After mutation its hash is `hash(2)`, so both lookups probe a different bucket and miss, while the set still holds one entry.

- (a) would require lookups to find the stored object regardless of its new hash
- (c) the original object is not found by its own new hash because it sits in the old bucket
- (d) Bad(2) probes the new bucket, which is empty

**Deeper:** This is the "lost key" bug behind many cache problems: a hashed object mutated after insertion. Hash only immutable fields, or freeze the key with `@dataclass(frozen=True)`.

options.optionText: True True 1
False False 1
True False 1
False True 1

questions.explanation:
**Answer: (d)** `copy.copy` creates a blank instance without running `__init__` and probes it with `hasattr(y, "__setstate__")`. Missing `__setstate__` calls `__getattr__`, which reads `self._data`, which is also missing, so `__getattr__("_data")` calls itself until the stack overflows.

- (a) the blank instance has no _data, so the copy never completes
- (b) the failure occurs before any dictionary lookup can raise KeyError
- (c) the code never reaches a plain AttributeError because it recurses first

**Deeper:** Guard `__getattr__` by raising `AttributeError` for names starting with an underscore, or look up through `self.__dict__`. The same bug appears with `pickle` and multiprocessing, which copy objects the same way.

options.optionText: It returns a shallow copy with _data copied
KeyError: _data
AttributeError: _data
RecursionError

questions.questionText:
```python
class Guard:
    def __enter__(self): return self
    def __exit__(self, et, ev, tb): return True

def f():
    with Guard():
        return "from with"
    return "after"

def g():
    with Guard():
        raise RuntimeError
    return "after"

print(f(), g())
```
What is printed?
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (a)** In `f` the `return` leaves the block normally, so `__exit__` gets no exception and the function returns `"from with"`. In `g` the `RuntimeError` is suppressed by the truthy return, so execution continues after the block and returns `"after"`.

- (b) a return inside with is not an exception and is not discarded
- (c) the truthy __exit__ result swallows it
- (d) g never reaches a return statement inside the block

**Deeper:** A context manager that always returns `True` hides every error, including programming bugs such as `TypeError` and `KeyboardInterrupt`. Suppress narrowly and log, as `contextlib.suppress` does for one exception class.

options.optionText: from with after
after after
RuntimeError is raised
from with from with

questions.questionText: User is an ABC with abstract methods display_dashboard and can_borrow. Member implements both. PremiumMember(Member) adds a loyalty field but does NOT re-implement either abstract method. Can PremiumMember("X", "x@x") be instantiated?
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (a)** `Member` implemented both abstract methods, so `PremiumMember` inherits concrete versions and its abstract set is empty; it can be instantiated.

- (b) only names that are still abstract must be implemented
- (c) it already inherits the ABC machinery through Member
- (d) super() is for extending behaviour, not for satisfying the contract

**Deeper:** The abstract set is recomputed per class, so adding a new abstract method to `Member` later would break `PremiumMember` at instantiation. Keep ABC changes backward compatible or version them.

options.optionText: Yes — Member already satisfied the contract, and PremiumMember inherits those implementations
No — every subclass must re-implement all abstract methods directly
Only if PremiumMember also inherits from ABC
Only if PremiumMember calls super()

questions.questionText: user_id is stored as self._user_id with only a @property getter (no setter). What happens when code runs member.user_id = "NEW"?
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (c)** A `@property` without a setter is a read-only data descriptor, so assigning to it raises `AttributeError` ("property 'user_id' ... has no setter").

- (a) the descriptor intercepts assignment
- (b) ValueError would need a setter that validates
- (d) a data descriptor takes precedence, so no instance attribute is created

**Deeper:** This is convention-level protection: `member._user_id` is still reachable. For genuine immutability use a frozen dataclass or `__slots__` with a guarded `__setattr__`. In interviews, add that a property is a data descriptor, which is why it takes precedence over the instance dictionary and why assignment is intercepted.

options.optionText: Overwrites the ID silently
ValueError
AttributeError — property has no setter, so assignment is blocked
Creates a second attribute called user_id on the instance

questions.questionText: Member.MAX_BORROW_LIMIT is a class attribute set to 5. At runtime, Member.MAX_BORROW_LIMIT = 2 is executed. What happens to an existing Member who checks can_borrow()?
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (b)** `can_borrow` looks up `MAX_BORROW_LIMIT` on each call, finds it on the class, and so sees the new value 2 for every member that has no instance override.

- (a) class attributes are read at call time, not frozen at creation
- (c) class attributes can be reassigned freely
- (d) existing instances share the class attribute, so they see it too

**Deeper:** Beware of instance assignment (`m.MAX_BORROW_LIMIT = 9`) which shadows the class value for that one object, and of mutable class attributes shared by all instances. A common follow-up is the mutable default: a list as a class attribute is shared across every instance, so mutate through `self.items = []` in `__init__` instead.

options.optionText: Unaffected — the old value 5 is frozen at object creation
Now uses 2 — class attributes are shared and can_borrow reads Member.MAX_BORROW_LIMIT live at each call
AttributeError — constants can't be changed
Only new Member objects see 2

questions.questionText: A MagazineArchive has a borrow() method (meaning "log a photocopy"). lend_item checks isinstance(item, Borrowable) before calling borrow(). Does the archive pass the check?
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (b)** `Borrowable` is an ABC, so `isinstance` is a nominal check; `MagazineArchive` never inherited from or registered with it, so the check fails despite the `borrow()` method.

- (a) duck typing applies to calls, not to isinstance against an ABC
- (c) nothing in the statement makes Borrowable a Protocol
- (d) isinstance simply returns False, with no exception

**Deeper:** Nominal checks protect actions with side effects, like lending, from objects that merely share a method name. Use a Protocol when a shape match is the correct standard, as for searching. Remember `ABC.register` makes a class a virtual subclass without inheritance, a deliberate escape hatch for classes you cannot edit.

options.optionText: Yes — duck typing checks methods
No — Borrowable is an ABC; isinstance checks inheritance, and MagazineArchive never inherited from Borrowable
Yes — Borrowable is a Protocol
Raises NotImplementedError

questions.questionText: Searchable is a @runtime_checkable Protocol. A third-party JournalDB class (uneditable) has matches(query) -> bool. Does isinstance(JournalDB(), Searchable) return True?
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (c)** A `@runtime_checkable` Protocol checks that the required member names exist. `JournalDB` has `matches`, so `isinstance` returns `True` without any inheritance.

- (a) protocols are structural by design
- (b) inheritance is optional for protocols
- (d) the decorator is what permits isinstance to work

**Deeper:** The check ignores signatures and return types, so keep a static type checker in the loop. This pattern lets third-party classes plug in without wrappers. A concrete example: pass the vendor client to `Library.search` and let your own `Book` classes inherit the ABC for lending.

options.optionText: No — Protocol also checks inheritance
Only if JournalDB explicitly inherits Searchable
Yes — @runtime_checkable Protocol checks shape (structural typing); JournalDB has a matching matches method
Raises TypeError

questions.questionText: Loan.__init__ calls super().__init__() where Loan inherits from TimestampedMixin. TimestampedMixin.__init__ also calls super().__init__(**kwargs). What determines the order of these calls?
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (b)** `super()` resolves to the next class in the MRO of the instance's type, so the call order is decided by the linearization, not by the file layout or the name.

- (a) names play no part in resolution
- (c) source position is irrelevant once classes exist
- (d) the algorithm (C3) is deterministic

**Deeper:** Print `Loan.__mro__` when debugging initialisation order. Mixins must forward `*args, **kwargs` to keep the chain intact. The same rule explains why `super().__init__()` in `Loan` may call a mixin's `__init__` before reaching `object`.

options.optionText: Alphabetical order of parent class names
The MRO (Method Resolution Order) — super() means "next in the MRO," not "my parent"
The order they appear in the source file
Python picks randomly

questions.questionText: Library defines __contains__(self, isbn) checking against internal _books. What does "N-1" in lib do under the hood?
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (c)** `"N-1" in lib` compiles to `type(lib).__contains__(lib, "N-1")`, and the implementation scans the stored books comparing ISBNs.

- (a) `in` never looks in `__dict__`
- (b) `__getitem__` is only a legacy fallback when `__contains__` and `__iter__` are missing
- (d) `in` works with any class that defines the method

**Deeper:** This is linear in the number of books; keep a dict keyed by ISBN if membership is hot. Note the oddity of `__contains__` taking an ISBN while iteration yields books. The same dispatch applies to `len(lib)` via `__len__` and iteration via `__iter__`, so a small set of dunders makes a domain class feel built-in.

options.optionText: Searches lib.__dict__ for a key "N-1"
Calls lib.__getitem__("N-1")
Calls lib.__contains__("N-1"), which iterates _books checking isbn matches
Raises TypeError — in only works with built-in types

questions.questionText: In the code review, Design A has Book.borrow(member) owning lending logic. Design B has Library.lend(member, book) owning it. Which statement best captures the trade-off?
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (d)** Behaviour on the entity keeps data and rules together but spreads policy across classes; a central service gives one place for policy but can become a god object.

- (a) neither design is always better
- (b) simplicity is not the only criterion; coupling matters
- (c) the two designs distribute responsibilities differently

**Deeper:** A balanced answer: entities expose small intention-revealing methods, and a service owns rules that span entities and raises domain exceptions. In a design round, say which you picked and why, and name the failure mode you accepted, since that shows you can reason about trade-offs.

options.optionText: Design A is always better because it follows OOP
Design B is always better because it's simpler
There is no meaningful difference
Design A keeps behaviour with its data (encapsulation) but spreads policy across classes; Design B centralizes policy but risks the Library becoming a god object reaching into internals

questions.questionText: Book.__eq__ compares by isbn. Two books with different titles but same isbn are added to a set. How many entries does the set contain?
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (a)** With `__eq__` and a matching `__hash__` over the ISBN, both books map to the same bucket and compare equal, so the set keeps one entry.

- (b) titles are not part of equality here
- (c) sets accept hashable objects
- (d) insertion order does not change which objects are equal

**Deeper:** The set keeps whichever object was inserted first. Without a matching `__hash__` the first insertion would instead raise `TypeError: unhashable type`. Equal books collapsing in a set is exactly what makes ISBN a good identity; titles and timestamps are attributes, not identity.

options.optionText: 1 — __eq__ says they're equal, __hash__ (also by isbn) puts them on the same shelf, so the set deduplicates
2 — different titles means different objects
0 — the set rejects both
Depends on insertion order

questions.questionText: Library defines __getitem__ delegating to self._books[index] but writes NO slicing logic. A user runs lib[:2]. What happens?
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (b)** Slicing passes a `slice` object to `__getitem__`; delegating to a list handles it, so `lib[:2]` returns the first two books.

- (a) Python 3 has no __slice__ method
- (c) a slice returns a value
- (d) a slice of two items returns two items

**Deeper:** The result is a plain list. If callers expect a `Library`, handle `isinstance(index, slice)` and build a new library from the sliced list. Slicing also covers `lib[::-1]` and `lib[1:3]` with no extra code, which is a good reason to delegate to the built-in list.

options.optionText: TypeError — slicing requires a separate __slice__ method
Works correctly — the slice is passed through to the internal list, which already handles slicing
Returns None
Returns only the first element

questions.questionText: The User class is an ABC with two abstract methods: display_dashboard and can_borrow. A developer creates class Volunteer(User) implementing only display_dashboard, then runs v = Volunteer("Priya", "p@x.com"). What happens, and which OOP concept is enforcing this?
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (b)** `Volunteer` leaves `can_borrow` abstract, so `Volunteer(...)` raises `TypeError`. The abstract-method check happens at instantiation and is enforced by `ABCMeta`.

- (a) the check happens at creation, not at call time
- (c) class definition succeeds
- (d) Python never fills in a default body

**Deeper:** This makes "forgot to implement" a loud failure during development. Pair it with a type checker to catch signature mismatches that the runtime check ignores. Interviewers often ask how this differs from raising `NotImplementedError` in a base method: that only fails when the method is called, possibly in production.

options.optionText: Object is created - Python only checks abstract methods when they're called
TypeError at instantiation - ABC (the licence-test rule) refuses to create an object until ALL abstract methods are implemented
SyntaxError at class definition time
Object is created with can_borrow returning None

questions.questionText: User._id_counter is a class attribute incremented in User.__init__. Three users are created: two Members and one Librarian. What is User._id_counter after all three, and why does it work correctly despite being three different objects across two different subclasses?
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (b)** `_id_counter` lives on `User` and each subclass constructor reaches `User.__init__` through `super()`, which increments the same class attribute, so three objects give 3.

- (a) subclasses do not copy a class attribute unless they assign their own
- (c) every constructor chain reaches User.__init__
- (d) class attributes can be modified from methods

**Deeper:** The code must write `User._id_counter += 1` (or use `itertools.count`). Writing `self._id_counter += 1` would create an instance attribute and leave the shared counter untouched. A thread-safe version would use `itertools.count` (atomic `next` in CPython) or a lock, and a multi-process deployment would use database sequences or UUIDs.

options.optionText: 1 — each subclass has its own counter
3 — it's a class attribute on User, shared by all subclasses; super().__init__() in each child routes to User.__init__, which increments the single shared counter
2 — Librarian doesn't increment it
0 — class attributes can't be modified inside __init__

questions.questionText: lend_item checks isinstance(item, Borrowable) before lending. A third-party AudioGuide class (you can't edit it) happens to have borrow, return_item, and is_borrowable methods with correct signatures. Will lend_item(AudioGuide(...), member) pass the check?
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (a)** Against an ABC, `isinstance` checks declared inheritance (or registration). `AudioGuide` declares neither, so the check fails despite matching methods.

- (b) method presence is irrelevant for a nominal check
- (c) abstractmethod only enforces completeness on subclasses
- (d) isinstance returns False and does not raise

**Deeper:** If you cannot edit the class, either `Borrowable.register(AudioGuide)` it deliberately or wrap it in an adapter that inherits. This is the lesson's main design rule: use nominal typing for permissioned actions and structural typing for read-only capabilities.

options.optionText: No — Borrowable is an ABC, and isinstance against an ABC checks inheritance (nominal typing), not method presence; AudioGuide never inherited from Borrowable
Yes — it has all the right methods
Yes — @abstractmethod makes it structural
Raises AttributeError

questions.questionText: Searchable is defined as a @runtime_checkable Protocol requiring matches(query) -> bool. Book implements matches but does NOT inherit from Searchable. What does isinstance(Novel("N-1","Dune","Herbert","SciFi"), Searchable) return, and why does this differ from Q3?
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (c)** A runtime-checkable Protocol is structural: it asks whether the object has a `matches` attribute. `Novel` does, so `isinstance` is `True` without inheritance, unlike the ABC in the previous question.

- (a) protocols do not use inheritance for conformance
- (b) isinstance works with runtime_checkable protocols
- (d) explicit inheritance is optional for protocols

**Deeper:** The difference between the two questions is the heart of this lesson: nominal contracts for what you control and lend, structural contracts for what you only read or search. A Protocol also documents the minimal surface a function needs, which keeps functions easy to test with simple fakes.

options.optionText: False — Protocol also checks inheritance
Raises TypeError — Protocols can't be used with isinstance
True — Protocol uses structural typing (checks shape, not lineage), so any object with a matching matches method satisfies it without inheriting
True only if Novel explicitly inherits Searchable

questions.questionText: Loan defines __eq__ (comparing by book.isbn + member.user_id) but a developer forgets __hash__. They create two Loan objects for the same member/book and run len({l1, l2}). What happens?
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (d)** Defining `__eq__` without `__hash__` sets `__hash__` to `None`. Building the set calls `hash` on each loan and raises `TypeError: unhashable type: 'Loan'`.

- (a) Python never generates a hash from __eq__
- (b) the set cannot be built at all
- (c) the TypeError happens before any length is computed

**Deeper:** A frozen dataclass generates a consistent `__eq__`/`__hash__` pair. Otherwise define both over the same immutable fields. In interviews, mention that this is also true of dataclasses with `eq=True` and no `frozen`, which silently set `__hash__` to `None`, so choose `frozen=True` for value records used as set members.

options.optionText: Returns 1 — Python auto-generates __hash__ from __eq__
Returns 2 — duplicates aren't detected
Returns 0
TypeError: unhashable type 'Loan' — defining __eq__ without __hash__ causes Python to set __hash__ = None, making the object unusable in sets

questions.questionText:
```python
class Counter:
    n = 0
    def bump(self):
        self.n += 1

x = Counter()
x.bump(); x.bump()
print(Counter.n, x.n)
```
What is printed?
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (b)** `self.n += 1` reads `n` through the class (0), adds one, and assigns the result to a new **instance** attribute, so the class attribute stays 0 while the instance reaches 2.

- (a) would require the augmented assignment to write back to the class
- (c) reverses which object holds the value
- (d) the instance attribute is incremented twice

**Deeper:** To share a counter across all instances and subclasses, write `Counter.n += 1` (or `type(self)` if per-subclass counting is intended) or use `itertools.count`. This is the bug behind many "my ID counter always returns 1" reports.

questions.questionText: A lending service checks `book.is_available` in Python, then sets it to `False`. Under load, two web workers lend the same physical copy to two members. Where should the fix live?
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (a)** The race spans processes, so the invariant must be enforced where the shared state lives: a conditional `UPDATE ... WHERE available > 0` or a `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` transaction makes the check-and-set atomic.

- (b) a property validates one object in one process and cannot see another worker's copy
- (c) a threading.Lock only protects threads inside a single process, not separate workers
- (d) a stricter abstract method does not change the race on availability

**Deeper:** In-process locks are still right for in-memory services (the reference assignment uses one), but a horizontally scaled API needs database-level guarantees plus an idempotency key for retries.

options.optionText: In the persistence layer: an atomic conditional update (or row lock) so only one of the concurrent requests can change availability
In the Book class: make is_available a property so assignment is validated
In Library.lend: wrap the check in a threading.Lock, which serialises all workers
In the Member class: add an @abstractmethod can_borrow so the check is stricter

questions.explanation:
**Answer: (c)** `Leaf` implements `b` and inherits `a` from `Mid`, so its abstract set is empty and it prints `3`. `Mid` still lacks `b`, so `Mid()` raises `TypeError`.

- (a) Leaf has no unimplemented abstract names
- (b) Mid is still abstract, because b is unimplemented
- (d) no attribute is accessed that does not exist

**Deeper:** Each class in a hierarchy is checked independently, because the abstract set is rebuilt at every class creation, so intermediate classes can stay abstract by design. Use this to build partial base classes without tripping the check.

options.optionText: TypeError at Leaf(); nothing printed
3, then Mid() succeeds and nothing more is printed
3, then TypeError
AttributeError

questions.questionText: What does the GIL (Global Interpreter Lock) actually guarantee?
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (b)** The GIL lets one thread at a time run bytecode, and a single bytecode instruction is not interrupted. That protects the interpreter's internals, not your multi-step logic.

- (a) a statement like x += 1 is several bytecodes, so shared variables can still be updated incorrectly
- (c) the scheduler gives no ordering guarantee between threads
- (d) CPU-bound pure-Python work does not speed up, because only one thread executes at a time

**Deeper:** In interviews add that the guarantee is an implementation detail of the standard build, and that the free-threaded build in 3.13 and 3.14 removes it, so correct code must use locks, queues or confinement. The GIL is a CPython implementation detail, not part of the Python language definition, and other implementations such as PyPy with STM or Jython differ.

options.optionText: That your shared variables will always update correctly across threads
That only one thread can execute Python bytecode at a time, and each individual bytecode instruction runs without interruption
That threads always run in the order they were started
That CPU-bound tasks will run faster with more threads

questions.questionText:
Two threads both run this function, then the final value is printed:

```python
counter = 0
def increment():
    global counter
    for _ in range(1_000_000):
        counter += 1
```

What is the most likely printed value after both threads finish?
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (c)** `counter += 1` is a read, an add and a write, so two threads can read the same value and one update is lost. The language does not guarantee 2,000,000, and the result may vary run to run.

- (a) nothing makes the read-modify-write atomic
- (b) each thread adds a million, so the total cannot be a single thread's share
- (d) a race produces wrong values, not an exception

**Deeper:** Modern CPython checks for thread switches only at certain instructions, so this exact loop often passes by accident; add a function call between load and store, or use a free-threaded build, and the lost updates appear. Always guard shared state with a `Lock`. To make the race visible deterministically in a test, insert a `time.sleep(0)` between the read and the write.

options.optionText: Always exactly 2,000,000
Always exactly 1,000,000
Some number less than 2,000,000, and it may differ each time the program runs
The program crashes with a RuntimeError

questions.questionText: Why does the scenario in H2 happen even though the GIL only lets one thread run at a time?
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (a)** The statement compiles to a load of `counter`, an add and a store, and the GIL may hand over to another thread between those bytecodes, not just between source lines.

- (b) the GIL applies to every bytecode, including loops
- (c) globals are protected only per bytecode, not per statement
- (d) the loop runs exactly as written; lost updates come from interleaving

**Deeper:** `dis.dis` shows the sequence. The exact interleaving is version dependent, which is why the correct answer is "use a lock", not "it works on my machine".

options.optionText: counter += 1 is actually four separate bytecode steps, and the GIL can switch threads between those steps, not just between lines
The GIL doesn't apply to loops
global variables are not protected by the GIL at all
Python re-runs the loop twice by mistake

questions.questionText: A student wants to speed up a task that makes 5 slow network API calls (each takes 1 second, mostly spent waiting). They're deciding between threading and multiprocessing. What should they pick, and why?
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (b)** Five one-second waits are I/O-bound. A thread releases the GIL while it blocks, so five threads overlap their waits and finish in about one second at far lower cost than five processes.

- (a) processes are heavier and unnecessary for waiting
- (c) overlapping the waits is exactly what speeds this up
- (d) network calls spend their time waiting, not computing

**Deeper:** For thousands of concurrent calls prefer `asyncio` or a bounded thread pool. Measure with `time.perf_counter` rather than asserting, as an interviewer may ask for numbers. Also mention connection limits and rate limits: ten thousand threads hammering one API is a different failure than the GIL.

options.optionText: multiprocessing, because it always beats threading for any task
threading, because I/O-bound waits release the GIL, letting waits overlap — cheaper than spinning up separate processes
Neither will help; only rewriting the API calls can speed this up
multiprocessing, because network calls are CPU-bound

questions.questionText: What is the key difference in output/behavior between using raw multiprocessing.Process objects versus multiprocessing.Pool.map() for running the same function on 4 inputs?
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (c)** With raw `Process` objects you create, start and join each one and must add a `Queue` or `Pipe` to get results; `Pool.map` manages workers, distributes tasks and returns results in input order.

- (a) Process has no built-in way to return a value
- (b) Pool.map runs in parallel across worker processes
- (d) Pool is more than shorthand: it reuses workers and collects results

**Deeper:** Both pickle arguments and results, and both need the `__main__` guard under `spawn`. `ProcessPoolExecutor` gives the same convenience with futures and cleaner exception propagation.

options.optionText: Process automatically collects and returns results in a list; Pool.map() does not
Pool.map() runs the function sequentially, while Process runs it in parallel
Process requires manually creating, starting, and joining each process with no built-in result collection, while Pool.map() handles all of that and returns results in order automatically
There is no real difference; Pool is just a shorter way to write Process

questions.questionText: What is the main difference between concurrency and parallelism?
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (b)** Concurrency is about structure: several tasks in progress, switching between them. Parallelism is about execution: tasks running at the same instant on separate cores.

- (a) concurrency works on one core, parallelism needs several
- (c) they are related but different ideas
- (d) both concepts apply to every language

**Deeper:** Python threads give concurrency for I/O and, with the standard GIL, no CPU parallelism; processes and free-threaded builds give parallelism. `asyncio` is concurrency on a single thread. A one-line summary for interviews is: concurrency is dealing with many things at once, parallelism is doing many things at once.

options.optionText: Concurrency needs multiple CPU cores; parallelism doesn't
Concurrency is switching between tasks to make progress on all of them; parallelism is tasks actually running at the same instant
They are the same thing, just different names
Parallelism only applies to Python; concurrency applies to all languages

questions.questionText:
What will this print?

```python
t1 = threading.Thread(target=notify_driver, args=("D101",))
t1.start()
print("Main thread is done!")
```
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (d)** `start()` returns immediately and the new thread runs independently, so the main thread usually prints first. Without `join()`, the order is not guaranteed.

- (a) only a join would force that order
- (b) the thread runs and the interpreter waits for non-daemon threads at exit
- (c) omitting join is legal

**Deeper:** Use `join()` when you need the result before continuing. Remember that a non-daemon thread keeps the process alive after `main` returns. A related trap is a daemon thread, which is killed abruptly at interpreter exit, so do not use it for writes that must complete.

options.optionText: "Main thread is done!" always prints after notify_driver finishes
notify_driver never runs because .join() was skipped
This code throws an error because .join() was not called
"Main thread is done!" prints almost immediately, likely before notify_driver finishes

questions.questionText: In Python's threading module, what does .join() do?
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (c)** `join()` blocks the calling thread until the target thread has finished, optionally up to a timeout.

- (a) threads cannot be merged
- (b) start() starts a thread
- (d) Python cannot kill a thread; it can only ask it to stop

**Deeper:** After `join(timeout)` check `is_alive()` to detect a timeout. Cooperative cancellation through an `Event` is the usual pattern for stopping workers. To retrieve a result from a thread, store it on the thread object or use a `Queue` or `Future`, because `join()` returns `None`.

options.optionText: Merges two threads into one
Starts a thread that was created but not yet running
Pauses the calling code until that specific thread has finished
Kills the thread immediately

questions.questionText:
A student wrote:
```python
t1 = threading.Thread(target=notify_driver, args=("D101"))
t1.start()
```
This crashes with a TypeError about arguments not being iterable correctly. What's the mistake?
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (b)** `("D101")` is just the string `"D101"` because the comma makes a tuple. `args` is unpacked, so the thread calls `notify_driver("D", "1", "0", "1")` and raises `TypeError` inside the new thread.

- (a) target takes a function reference
- (c) the target is assigned in the constructor
- (d) notify_driver can take arguments, as long as the count matches

**Deeper:** Write `args=("D101",)`. Note the error is raised in the worker and printed by `threading.excepthook`; the main thread continues, which is why swallowed thread exceptions are easy to miss.

options.optionText: target should be a string, not a function reference
args is missing a trailing comma — ("D101") is just a string, not a one-item tuple, so Python tries to unpack each character as a separate argument
.start() must be called before target is assigned
notify_driver cannot accept any arguments

questions.questionText: Given a single CPU-bound function cpu_heavy() that takes 4 seconds to run alone, what is the most likely total time if it's run twice using two threading.Thread instances (started and joined) on a machine with free cores?
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (a)** Pure-Python CPU work holds the GIL, so two threads take turns and the total is about the sum, around 8 seconds, even with free cores.

- (b) threads in a GIL build do not run Python bytecode in parallel
- (c) work is not split automatically between threads
- (d) threads never speed up CPU-bound pure Python work

**Deeper:** Use `multiprocessing` or a process pool for CPU-bound work, or a library that releases the GIL. On a free-threaded build this exact test would take about 4 seconds, which is the point of that build.

options.optionText: About 8 seconds — roughly the same as running both sequentially, since the GIL prevents real parallel CPU execution
About 4 seconds total, since threads run in true parallel
About 2 seconds (threads split the CPU work evenly)
Less than 1 second, since threads always speed up computation

questions.questionText:
```python
import threading

def work():
    print(threading.current_thread().name)

t = threading.Thread(target=work, name="w1")
t.run()
```
What is printed?
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (b)** `run()` is an ordinary method call that executes the target in the **calling** thread; only `start()` creates a new OS thread that then calls `run()`.

- (a) the name only applies to a started thread
- (c) run() executes the function synchronously
- (d) that error comes from calling start() twice

**Deeper:** Calling `run()` by mistake is a classic bug in thread-pool code that "works" but serialises everything. After `run()`, calling `start()` on the same object also fails, because `run` clears the target.

options.optionText: w1
MainThread
Nothing, because the thread was never started
RuntimeError: threads can only be started once

questions.questionText: A document service must (1) make 200 concurrent LLM API calls that each wait about 2 seconds and (2) parse large PDFs with pure-Python CPU-heavy code taking about 300 ms each. Which architecture fits best?
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (d)** The API calls are waits, so threads or `asyncio` overlap them cheaply; the parsing is CPU-bound pure Python, so it needs separate processes. Passing a key instead of megabytes keeps pickling cost low.

- (a) threads cannot parallelise the CPU stage under the GIL
- (b) two hundred processes for waiting is heavy and wastes memory
- (c) this assigns each stage to the wrong mechanism

**Deeper:** Size the process pool near the core count and the thread or async stage by the provider's rate limit, not by CPU. Mixed workloads are usually pipelines of two differently scaled stages.

options.optionText: One large ThreadPoolExecutor for both stages, because threads are cheapest
One ProcessPoolExecutor for both stages, because processes avoid the GIL
asyncio for the PDF parsing and a process pool for the API calls
Threads or asyncio for the API calls, and a process pool for PDF parsing that receives storage keys rather than file bytes

questions.questionText:
On Windows or macOS (start method `spawn`), a script contains this at module top level, with no `if __name__ == "__main__":` guard:

```python
import multiprocessing as mp

def square(x):
    return x * x

pool = mp.Pool(4)
print(pool.map(square, range(4)))
```
What happens?
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (a)** Under `spawn` each child re-imports the main module, which executes `mp.Pool(4)` again at import time; `multiprocessing` detects this and raises a `RuntimeError` explaining that the main module must be guarded.

- (b) the guard is required precisely so that re-imports do not start pools
- (c) module-level functions pickle by reference without trouble
- (d) the library detects the recursion and fails loudly

**Deeper:** On Linux with `fork` the same script appears to work, which hides the bug until it runs on a laptop or in a spawn-based environment. Always guard, and keep side effects out of import time.

options.optionText: A RuntimeError reports an attempt to start a new process before bootstrapping finished
It prints [0, 1, 4, 9]
PicklingError, because square is defined at module level
It deadlocks with no error message

questions.questionText: Which is the best use case for ProcessPoolExecutor over ThreadPoolExecutor?
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (c)** Heavy numerical computation on independent datasets is CPU-bound, and separate processes each get their own GIL, so the work really runs in parallel.

- (a) Waiting on API calls and sleeps is I/O-bound; threads overlap the waiting for free.
- (b) Disk reads release the GIL during the system call, so threads are enough.
- (d) Fetching web pages is network wait time, again a thread job.

**Deeper:** The deciding question is "what resource is saturated?". A process pool pays for pickling, IPC and interpreter start-up, so it only wins when the computation per task is large relative to the data you ship. In interviews, mention that NumPy or C extensions that release the GIL can blur this boundary.

options.optionText: Waiting on 5 API calls with sleep/network delay
Reading multiple files from disk
Performing heavy numerical computation on 4 independent large datasets
Fetching 10 web pages concurrently

questions.questionText: Why doesn't ProcessPoolExecutor speed up an I/O-bound task like web scraping, compared to ThreadPoolExecutor?
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (d)** I/O-bound work spends its time waiting, so there is no computation for extra cores to speed up, and processes add start-up and serialisation overhead.

- (a) `ProcessPoolExecutor` supports `.map()` and even accepts `chunksize`.
- (b) The GIL does not block network calls; it is released while a thread waits on a socket.
- (c) Processes can make network requests perfectly well.

**Deeper:** Choosing a process pool for I/O work is not just useless, it is actively worse: more memory, slower start, pickled results, and a much lower practical concurrency ceiling than hundreds of cheap threads or an asyncio loop. Seniors justify the executor by naming the bottleneck first.

options.optionText: ProcessPoolExecutor doesn't support .map()
The GIL blocks all network calls in processes
Processes cannot perform network requests
There's no computation to parallelize — the bottleneck is waiting, and processes add extra startup/communication overhead for no benefit

questions.questionText: True or False: Using ThreadPoolExecutor automatically protects shared variables from race conditions (like counter += 1 from multiple threads).
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (b)** An executor schedules calls and collects results; it adds no mutual exclusion around the data those calls touch.

- (a) Nothing serialises writes. `counter += 1` is a load, add and store, and threads can interleave between those steps.

**Deeper:** The best fix is often to avoid shared state entirely: have each task return a partial result and reduce in the caller after `result()`. When shared mutation is unavoidable, use a `Lock`, or `queue.Queue` for hand-off. Interviewers use this question to check you do not confuse "thread pool" with "thread-safe". On free-threaded builds the same reasoning applies even more strongly.

options.optionText: True — executors serialize all writes automatically
False — executors only manage task launching/collection; shared-state protection still needs tools like Lock

questions.questionText:
What is results, and in what order, once this finishes?
```python
import time
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

def work(n):
    time.sleep(n)
    return n

with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=3) as executor:
    results = list(executor.map(work, [3, 1, 2]))
print(results)
```
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (d)** `executor.map` yields results in the order of the input iterable, whatever order the tasks finish in.

- (a) Nothing times out; no timeout is passed and all three sleeps are short.
- (b) The order is deterministic, not random.
- (c) Completion order is what `as_completed` gives, not `map`.

All three tasks run concurrently, so the total time is about 3 seconds, and the list is printed as `[3, 1, 2]`. The consumer simply waits for the first item (the slowest) before seeing the others.

**Deeper:** Head-of-line blocking is the cost of ordered output. If you want to stream results as they land, use `submit` plus `as_completed` and carry an index or a future-to-input dict to reassemble order yourself.

[1, 2, 3] — sorted by finish time

questions.questionText:
A student benchmarks CPU-heavy work and is confused why threads didn't help. Identify the flaw in their reasoning.

```python
def cpu_heavy(n):
    return sum(i * i for i in range(n))

with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=4) as executor:
    list(executor.map(cpu_heavy, [50_000_000] * 4))
```

"I used 4 workers for 4 tasks, so this should be 4x faster than sequential."
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (d)** The work is CPU-bound pure Python, and the GIL lets only one thread execute bytecode at a time, so four threads take roughly as long as running sequentially, often longer due to switching.

- (a) Lowering workers to 1 does not fix performance; it only removes concurrency.
- (b) `map` accepts any picklable or plain arguments.
- (c) The code is syntactically valid.

**Deeper:** Switch to `ProcessPoolExecutor` (sized to cores), or move the hot loop into a C extension that releases the GIL, or test a free-threaded build. Always benchmark with realistic input sizes, because process start-up and pickling dominate for tiny tasks.

options.optionText: max_workers=4 should be max_workers=1 for correctness
executor.map doesn't support functions with numeric arguments
The code has a syntax error, so it never runs
This is CPU-bound work; the GIL means only one thread executes Python bytecode at a time, so threads don't overlap computation — ProcessPoolExecutor is needed instead

questions.questionText: You're processing 4 large video files, applying a CPU-intensive filter to each, independently. Which is the better choice and why?
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (d)** A CPU-intensive filter per video is parallelisable computation, and separate processes each have their own GIL, so they can use separate cores.

- (a) The performance is not identical; threads would be serialised by the GIL for pure Python filters.
- (b) Video filtering is compute-bound; only reading the file is I/O.
- (c) Independent files are exactly the case where parallelism helps.

**Deeper:** Pass file paths rather than frames to workers, so only small arguments cross the pickle boundary. Note the nuance: if the filter is implemented in OpenCV or NumPy, those libraries often release the GIL, and threads can work too. Say that in an interview to show you measure instead of assuming.

options.optionText: Doesn't matter, both give identical performance
ThreadPoolExecutor — video processing is I/O-bound
Neither — must be done sequentially
ProcessPoolExecutor — CPU-bound work benefits from separate GILs per process, allowing true parallel computation across cores

questions.questionText: You submit 10 tasks to a ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=3). At any given instant, what is the maximum number of tasks actually running concurrently?
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (c)** `max_workers=3` means three worker threads, so at most three tasks execute at once and the other seven wait in the queue.

- (a) The cap does not depend on task type; the pool size is the limit.
- (b) The GIL limits bytecode execution, but threads blocked in I/O or sleeping still count as running tasks.
- (d) Ten would require ten workers.

**Deeper:** The queue in front of the workers is unbounded, so submitting a million tasks never blocks the producer. Size the pool to the downstream limit (provider rate, DB connections) and add a semaphore around `submit` if you need real backpressure.

options.optionText: Depends on task type
1 (due to the GIL)

questions.questionText: You have a ThreadPoolExecutor task that sometimes throws an exception. You use executor.map() instead of submit() + individual futures. What happens when you iterate over the results and one task failed?
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (d)** The exception is stored on the underlying future and re-raised when the `map` iterator reaches that item.

- (a) `map` can and does raise; it just delays the raise until iteration.
- (b) Failed tasks are not skipped.
- (c) No `None` is substituted; the error is not swallowed.

After the exception propagates out of the generator it is finished, and the remaining pending futures are cancelled, so you cannot simply continue the loop even with a `try` inside the loop body. Catching it around the whole loop or iterating over futures yourself lets you control this.

**Deeper:** For partial-failure tolerance use `submit` plus `as_completed` or `result()` per future. This is a classic interview probe on error-handling design in fan-out code.

options.optionText: map() cannot raise exceptions, only submit() can
map() skips the failed task and continues with the rest
The failed task's result is silently None
The exception is raised at the point of iteration when you reach that failed task's result, potentially stopping your loop from processing remaining results unless wrapped in try/except

questions.questionText: What does executor.submit(fn, arg) return?
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (d)** `submit` returns immediately with a `Future`, a handle for the pending, running or finished call.

- (a) It returns a `Future`, not `None`; the future is what becomes done later.
- (b) The result is only available via `future.result()`, which blocks until it exists.
- (c) The thread is internal to the pool and is not exposed.

**Deeper:** Because the call is decoupled from its result, you can submit many tasks, then collect them in any order, attach callbacks, set timeouts and cancel pending work. That decoupling is the main thing raw `Thread` objects lack.

options.optionText: None, until the task finishes
The result of fn(arg) directly
A new thread object
A Future object representing work in progress

questions.questionText: Which statement about .done() and .result() is correct?
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (a)** `done()` is a non-blocking status check, while `result()` blocks until the task finishes (or a timeout fires).

- (b) Only `result()` and `exception()` block; `done()` returns instantly.
- (c) It is the reverse of reality.
- (d) `done()` returns a boolean, but `result()` returns the value or raises the stored exception.

**Deeper:** Never poll `done()` in a tight loop, because that burns CPU for nothing; use `wait`, `as_completed` or callbacks instead. And remember that `done()` is `True` for failed and cancelled futures too, so it says nothing about whether the task succeeded.

options.optionText: .done() never blocks; .result() blocks until the result is available
Both block until the task finishes
.done() blocks; .result() never blocks
Both return True/False depending on task status

questions.questionText: A raw threading.Thread's target function raises an exception. What happens?
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (b)** In a raw thread the traceback is printed by `threading.excepthook`, the thread ends, and the parent has no handle through which to observe the failure.

- (a) There is no automatic retry.
- (c) The program keeps running; only that thread dies.
- (d) Exceptions never propagate across threads on their own; `join()` returns normally.

**Deeper:** This is why futures exist: they capture the exception and re-raise it in the thread that calls `result()`. With raw threads you must catch inside the target and push the error onto a queue or a shared structure, or install a custom `threading.excepthook` for logging and metrics.

options.optionText: The thread silently retries the function
The exception prints to the terminal but the main thread has no way to catch or react to it
The program crashes immediately
The exception propagates to the main thread automatically

questions.questionText: How does a Future handle an exception raised inside the worker function?
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (d)** The worker catches the exception, stores it on the future, and `result()` raises it, with the original traceback attached.

- (a) It is not ignored; calling `result()` or `exception()` surfaces it.
- (b) The executor keeps running and serves other tasks.
- (c) Nothing is logged automatically and `None` is never substituted.

**Deeper:** The trap is a future nobody ever inspects: the error then vanishes silently, and the first symptom is missing data downstream. In services, keep the futures, or attach `add_done_callback` that logs `fut.exception()`, so fire-and-forget work still reports failures to your monitoring.

options.optionText: It ignores the exception completely
It crashes the executor immediately
It logs the exception and returns None
It stores the exception and re-raises it when .result() is called

questions.questionText: What guarantee does executor.map(fn, iterable) give you about result order?
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (c)** `map` yields results in input order, regardless of finish order.

- (a) All results are returned, not only the first.
- (b) The order is well defined.
- (d) Finish-order delivery is what `as_completed` provides.

**Deeper:** Ordered delivery means one slow early item delays everything behind it, though later tasks still run concurrently in the background and finish in their own time. If an exception occurs, it surfaces only when you reach that position in the sequence. Pick `map` for simple all-or-nothing batches and `as_completed` when latency or partial success matters.

options.optionText: Only the first completed result is returned
Order is undefined/random
Results come back in the same order as the input iterable, regardless of finish order
Results come back in the order tasks finish

questions.questionText:
What will this print?

```python
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
import time

def task():
    time.sleep(2)
    return "done"

with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=1) as executor:
    future = executor.submit(task)
    print(future.done())
```
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (d)** `submit` returns at once, while the task is still sleeping for two seconds, so `done()` is `False` at the print.

- (a) The string `"done"` is the task's return value and is never printed.
- (b) Nothing raises.
- (c) `True` would only be printed after the `with` block exits, because `shutdown(wait=True)` waits for the task.

```python
with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=1) as ex:
    f = ex.submit(task)
    print(f.done())   # False
print(f.done())       # True
```

**Deeper:** The context manager's implicit join is what makes executors safe to use, because no task is left running after the block, and it is also why a single hung task with no timeout can block shutdown and keep the whole process alive.

**Answer: (d)** Each future is consumed in submission order, and the failing one (`x == 3`) is caught by the `try`/`except`, so the loop continues. Strictly, the printed lines are `0`, `2`, `4`, `Caught: bad value`, `8`; option (d) abbreviates this with wrong numbers but is the only choice with the right behaviour.

- (a) `result()` returns the value; nothing is swallowed.
- (b) The failing task is not silently skipped; it prints the `Caught:` line.
- (c) The program does not crash, because the exception is caught inside the loop.

**Deeper:** This is the standard per-future error handling pattern. The failure of one future does not affect the others, unlike `map`, where the exception ends the iteration.

questions.questionText:
A student wrote this to collect driver locations. What does it get wrong relative to what today's lecture taught?
```python
import threading
results = []

def fetch_and_store(driver_id):
    location = fetch_driver_location(driver_id)
    results.append(location)

threads = [threading.Thread(target=fetch_and_store, args=(d,)) for d in drivers]
for t in threads:
    t.start()
for t in threads:
    t.join()
```

**Answer: (d)** The code works, but it hand-rolls what executors give you: a shared list for results and no way to see exceptions raised in `fetch_driver_location`.

- (a) `Thread` accepts `args`.
- (b) `join()` waits for completion and does not deadlock here.
- (c) The syntax is valid.

Note that the shared list is safe only because `list.append` is atomic under the GIL; results arrive in finish order with no link to the driver, and there is no cap on thread count for a large `drivers` list.

**Deeper:** `ThreadPoolExecutor.map` or `submit` plus futures returns values, ties results to inputs, bounds concurrency and captures errors.

questions.questionText:
Find the bug: the student wants to catch the error from a failed task, but the except block never triggers, even though fetch_driver_location("D103") is known to raise ConnectionError.
```python
with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=1) as executor:
    future = executor.submit(fetch_driver_location, "D103")

try:
    print(future.done())
except ConnectionError as e:
    print(f"Fetch failed: {e}")
```
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (c)** `done()` only reports status and never raises; the stored `ConnectionError` appears only when `result()` or `exception()` is called.

- (a) A `with` block does not suppress exceptions; it just waits at exit.
- (b) You can catch `ConnectionError` anywhere.
- (d) `submit` accepts any arguments.

The task fails inside the pool, the `with` block waits for it to end, `print(future.done())` prints `True`, and the `except` clause never runs.

**Deeper:** Replace `done()` with `result()` inside the `try`. This is the single most common executor bug: treating completion as success.

options.optionText: The with block suppresses all exceptions
ConnectionError cannot be caught inside a with block
The exception is only raised when .result() is called — .done() never raises, it only reports status
executor.submit doesn't accept string arguments

questions.questionText: You're building a system that downloads 100 images from different URLs. Which executor should you use, and why?
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (d)** Downloads are I/O-bound; CPython releases the GIL while a thread waits on a socket, so many downloads can overlap in a thread pool.

- (a) Processes work but are heavier, and the GIL is not what limits network waits.
- (b) Downloads can and should run concurrently.
- (c) More workers do not always mean more speed; bandwidth, server limits and overhead cap it.

**Deeper:** Pick `max_workers` from downstream limits (host rate limits, bandwidth), set a timeout on every request, and consider `asyncio` with `httpx` when you need thousands of concurrent connections.

options.optionText: ProcessPoolExecutor, because processes don't have a GIL limitation on network calls
Neither — use a single thread since downloads must happen one at a time
ProcessPoolExecutor, because more workers = more speed always
ThreadPoolExecutor, because this is I/O-bound — the GIL releases during network waits, letting waits overlap

questions.questionText:
What does this print?

```python
import time
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

def work(n: int) -> int:
    time.sleep(n * 0.1)
    if n == 1:
        raise ValueError("one")
    return n

with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=3) as pool:
    try:
        for r in pool.map(work, [3, 1, 2]):
            print("ok", r)
    except ValueError as exc:
        print("failed", exc)
print("end")
```
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (b)** `map` delivers in input order, so the first item `work(3)` is awaited and printed, and the second result is the stored `ValueError`, which is raised during iteration and ends the loop.

- (a) `ok 3` is printed first because the iterator reaches the first item before the failing one.
- (c) `work(2)` is the third item, and the generator never yields it after the exception propagates.
- (d) The error is raised, not swallowed.

The printed lines are `ok 3`, `failed one`, `end`.

**Deeper:** Even though `work(1)` finishes first, its failure is not seen until the iterator reaches position two, and `work(2)` is discarded. That is why `as_completed` or per-future `result()` is the right pattern for partial success.

`ok 3`, then `failed one`, then `end`
`ok 3`, `ok 2`, then `failed one`, then `end`
`ok 3`, `ok 2`, then `end`, with the error swallowed

questions.questionText: In a service you submit a locally defined function (a closure created inside another function) to a `ProcessPoolExecutor`. What is the most accurate description of what happens?
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (c)** `submit` just enqueues the call. The pickling failure happens when the call is serialised for the worker, and the exception is set on that one future, so it surfaces from `result()` while other tasks keep working.

- (a) There is no up-front check; submission appears to succeed.
- (b) `BrokenProcessPool` is for a worker dying abruptly (segfault, OOM kill), not for a serialisation error.
- (d) There is no silent in-process fallback.

On CPython 3.12 the error for a local function is `AttributeError: Can't pickle local object ...`, while lambdas give `PicklingError`.

**Deeper:** Define workers at module top level, pass plain data, and surface errors by calling `result()` on every future. A common production bug is submitting work and only noticing days later that the futures were never inspected.

options.optionText: `submit()` raises immediately, because the pool checks picklability up front
The worker process crashes and every pending future fails with `BrokenProcessPool`
The pickling error is stored on that future and raised by `result()`, and the pool stays usable for other tasks
The function silently runs in the parent process as a fallback

questions.questionText: A `ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=2)` is shared by a request handler. Each "parent" task submits two child tasks to the same pool and blocks on their `result()` with no timeout. Under load, every worker is running a parent. What happens?
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (a)** Once all workers are occupied by blocked parents, no worker is free to run the queued children, so nothing ever completes. This is pool starvation, a deadlock without any lock.

- (b) Pools never grow beyond `max_workers`.
- (c) Submitting from a worker is allowed, which is why the bug is easy to write.
- (d) The GIL switches between running threads; it cannot run a task that no thread has been assigned.

**Deeper:** Fixes are separate pools per stage, having the parent return child futures for a coordinator to gather, or timeouts that turn the hang into an error. Spotting this in a thread dump (all workers parked in `Future.result`) is a favourite senior debugging question.

options.optionText: The service deadlocks: the children sit in the queue behind parents that are waiting for them
The pool automatically creates extra threads to run the children
Python raises `RuntimeError` because a task cannot submit to its own pool
The GIL lets the children preempt the parents, so everything completes slowly

questions.questionText: In the lecture, a Semaphore(3) was used to allow only 3 threads to run at once (like a parking lot with 3 spots). If instead you initialize Semaphore(0), what happens when a thread immediately calls acquire() on it?
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (d)** `Semaphore(0)` starts with zero permits, so `acquire()` blocks until another thread calls `release()`.

- (a) `Semaphore(1)` would let the first `acquire()` pass at once; with 0 it does not.
- (b) Zero is a valid initial value, and it is the standard way to build a signal.
- (c) "Nothing to block" is backwards: no permits means the caller must wait.

**Deeper:** A semaphore initialised to 0 is a hand-off between threads, not a capacity limit. It is how you encode "B must wait for A". Note that `BoundedSemaphore(0)` is legal but any `release()` beyond the initial value raises `ValueError`, so ordering code uses plain `Semaphore(0)`.

options.optionText: It behaves exactly like Semaphore(1)
It raises an error because 0 is not allowed
It passes through instantly since there's nothing to block
It blocks immediately, since there are zero permits available — the thread waits until something else calls release()

questions.questionText: For problems like "print first, then second, then third in strict order using multiple threads," why can a semaphore be used to enforce ordering, not just capacity limits?
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (c)** A semaphore has no owner, so one thread can wait in `acquire()` for a `release()` performed by a different thread, which passes a signal along.

- (a) A `Lock` is meant to be released by its holder; it is a poor tool for cross-thread ordering.
- (b) Speed has nothing to do with it.
- (d) Semaphores do not sort or schedule threads at all.

**Deeper:** Chain several semaphores (initialised to 0) and each stage releases the next: this solves "print in order", "alternate foo and bar" and "zero-even-odd". In production the same shape is a `threading.Event` for one-shot signals, or a `Queue` when data travels with the signal.

options.optionText: Semaphores cannot be used for ordering — only Lock can do this
Because semaphores are faster than locks
Because acquire() in one thread can be made to wait for a release() called by a different thread, effectively passing a signal/permission from one thread to another
Because semaphores automatically sort threads by their function name

questions.questionText:
What is the guaranteed printed order?

```python
sem = threading.Semaphore(0)

def waiter():
    sem.acquire()
    print("B")

t = threading.Thread(target=waiter)
t.start()
print("A")
sem.release()
t.join()
```

**Answer: (d)** The waiter blocks on `acquire()` until the main thread calls `release()`, and the main thread does that only after `print("A")`, so `A` always precedes `B`.

- (a) It does not hang: `release()` is called, and `join()` waits for a finished thread.
- (b) `B` cannot print before the permit exists.
- (c) The order is forced by the semaphore, not left to the scheduler.

```text
A

```

**Deeper:** The thread may start and block before or after `print("A")`; either way the permit is only created later. Counting semaphores remember a `release()` that happens before the `acquire()`, which is the difference from `Condition.notify`, where a notification sent before anyone waits is lost.

B then A, always
Random — could be A then B, or B then A
A then B, always

questions.questionText:
This is meant to make "second" print only after "first," using semaphores, but it has a bug:

```python
import threading

class Foo:
    def __init__(self):
        self.sem = threading.Semaphore(1)  # BUG is here

    def first(self):
        print("first")
        self.sem.release()

    def second(self):
        self.sem.acquire()
        print("second")
```

What is wrong and what's the fix?
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (c)** With `Semaphore(1)` the first `acquire()` succeeds immediately, so `second()` can print before `first()` has run. It must start at 0 so it blocks until `first()` releases.

- (a) A `Lock` guards a critical section; it does not make `second()` wait for `first()`, and the real defect is the initial permit count.
- (b) Swapping the method names changes nothing about the synchronisation.
- (d) If `second()` released instead of acquiring, nothing would ever wait.

**Deeper:** The bug is invisible in testing if `first()` usually runs first by luck, and appears as a rare ordering failure in production. Always test ordering code by starting threads in the worst order, for example third, second, first.

questions.questionText: For the "ZeroEvenOdd" problem (three threads: one prints only 0s, one prints only evens, one prints only odds, in strict interleaved order), which setup is closest to correct?
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (d)** Three semaphores form a baton pass: `zero_sem` starts at 1, and each thread releases exactly the semaphore of the thread that must run next.

- (a) Semaphores solve it fine; the standard reference solution does exactly this.
- (b) Tuned `sleep` delays are timing luck, not synchronisation, and fail under load.
- (c) A single shared lock gives mutual exclusion but no ordering between three roles.

The `zero` thread chooses to release the `even` or `odd` semaphore depending on the parity of the next number, and `even`/`odd` release `zero_sem` again.

**Deeper:** Explicit hand-off is easy to reason about because each wait has exactly one releaser. A `Condition` with a shared "turn" variable also works, but needs `notify_all` and a predicate loop.

options.optionText: It cannot be done with semaphores; only Condition will work
Use time.sleep() with carefully tuned delays to control the order
Use one single Lock shared by all three threads with no other coordination
Use three separate semaphores — e.g., a zero_sem starting at 1, and even_sem/odd_sem starting at 0 — so each thread's release() signals exactly which thread should run next

questions.questionText: What is a "critical section" in the context of threading.Lock?
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (b)** The critical section is the code between acquire and release, which at most one thread executes at a time.

- (a) Holding a lock says nothing about whether code is bug-free.
- (c) Using threads does not make a function a critical section.
- (d) Speed is irrelevant; critical sections are usually the slow, serialised part.

**Deeper:** Design critical sections to include the whole invariant (check and update together) and nothing more. Time spent inside a lock is time every other thread waits, so never include network or disk I/O. This is the sentence that interviewers want to hear before they ask about contention.

options.optionText: A section of code that never has bugs
The block of code that only one thread can execute at a time while holding the lock
Any function that uses threads
The part of code that runs fastest

questions.questionText: Why does a plain threading.Lock cause a deadlock if the same thread tries to acquire it twice (e.g., a locked function calling another locked function)?
questions.explanation:
**Answer: (c)** A plain `Lock` does not record its holder, so a second `acquire()` from the same thread waits for a release that only that same blocked thread could perform.

- (a) It blocks rather than raising an exception.
- (b) Nested calls are perfectly legal.
- (d) A lock can be acquired and released many times.

**Deeper:** `RLock` records the owner and a recursion count, so re-entry is allowed. The deeper fix is design: avoid public locked methods calling each other, and put the invariant in one place with unlocked private helpers. A self-deadlock shows up in a thread dump as a single thread waiting in `acquire` on a lock that it already holds.

Python doesn't allow nested function calls
A Lock has no memory of who is holding it, so it just waits forever for a release that never comes from itself
Locks can only be used once per program
